title: Multispecies Stock Assessment: Mathematical Methods, Data, and Software
section: Chapter Structure
text:
Chapter Structure
This monograph provides a six-chapter mathematical and statistical review of multispecies stock assessment models, length-structured integrated assessments, stomach content observation models, and dynamic statistical calibration methods for size-spectrum models, accompanied by a comprehensive References section.



Chapter
Title & Core Scope
Key Models & Methodologies Covered




Chapter 1
Taxonomy and Theoretical Foundations of Multispecies Stock Assessment Models
Strategic vs. Tactical MICE “sweet spot”; State-space coordinate systems (Age, Age-Length, Length, Continuous Mass, Biomass Pools); One-Way (\(M2\)-only) vs. Two-Way (Bioenergetic) trophic feedback; Andersen & Ursin (1977) differential equations and Livingston (1983) nonlinear sensitivity analysis, and how SMS vs. mizer diverged; Jacobian community matrices (\(\mathbf{J}\)) and quadratic multispecies yield approximations.


Chapter 2
Age-Structured Multispecies Stock Assessment Models
MSVPA/MSFOR iterative cohort equations; SMS / smsR seasonal survival, separable \(F\), Andersen–Ursin size preference, evacuation rations, exact \(M2\), and Lognormal + Dirichlet likelihoods; MSASA / MSCAA / Hydra and 7 predator functional responses including Pre-emption and Ecosim Foraging Arena; CEATTLE / Rceattle temperature-dependent generalized VBGF, Wisconsin bioenergetics, 12 MBRP harvest control rules, and hybrid predator scaling.


Chapter 3
Age-Length and Length-Structured Assessment Models
Gadget2 & gadget3 5D state tensor \(N_{s,a,l,r,t}, W_{s,a,l,r,t}\), MULTSPEC/Jones consumption-coupled growth, Beta-Binomial discrete bin transitions (g3a_grow_impl_bbinom), Type II/III predation with dif_pmin overconsumption cap, Stefánsson’s two-stage iterative reweighting, and Baltic cod–herring–sprat–Saduria case study; MULTIFAN-CL robustified normal length likelihood; Stock Synthesis (SS3) growth morphs/platoons & Rosa Lee’s phenomenon; Size-Transition Matrices \(\mathbf{X}_{l,l'}\); LIME length-based mixed effects; LeMans / LeMaRns and CSMS / CSM.


Chapter 4
Continuous Size-Spectrum (mizer) and State-Space Food-Web Models
mizer complete PDEs, bioenergetics, reproduction, starvation, and semi-implicit upwind discretization; Jump-Growth Fokker–Planck PDE and second-order growth diffusion \(d_i(w,t)\); Regulation without SRR; Ecopath, Ecosim, Ecospace, Rpath, Walters’ Foraging Arena Theory (\(v_{ij}\) exchange), and EcoState TMB state-space ODE model.


Chapter 5
Stomach Content Data, Gastric Evacuation Physics, and Diet Likelihood Formulations
Biophysical cylinder model of gastric evacuation (\(\frac{dS}{dt} = -\rho L^\lambda e^{\delta T} E^{-\mu} S^{0.5}\)); Jensen’s inequality pooling bias and Taylor correction; Prey condition & %F vs. %W; ICES & DAPSTOM databases, FishStomachs CPUE raising, and sdmTMB Tweedie spatiotemporal diet standardization; Multinomial, Dirichlet, Dirichlet-Multinomial, Logistic-Normal, and Exponential Family / Gamma log-PPMR likelihoods.


Chapter 6
Statistical Estimation, Data Weighting, Uncertainty Quantification, and mizer Roadmap
Master comparative table across 8 model families; Francis TA1.8 vs. McAllister–Ianelli vs. Dirichlet-Multinomial data weighting; TMB Laplace approximation; GA + Parallel Tempering MCMC and History Matching + SMC + Multi-Model Ensembles; Five-Pillar Architectural Blueprint for Dynamic Statistical Stock Assessment in mizer.

title: 1  Taxonomy and Theoretical Foundations of Multispecies Stock Assessment Models
text:
1.1 Introduction: From Single-Species to Multispecies Tactical Assessment
Traditional fisheries stock assessment relies on the single-species paradigm (Beverton and Holt 1957; Cadima 2003; Lart 2022), in which each exploited population is modeled in isolation from its biological community. In single-species Virtual Population Analysis (VPA), Statistical Catch-at-Age (SCAA), or integrated assessment models such as Stock Synthesis (Methot and Wetzel 2013) and SAM (Nielsen and Berg 2014), all non-fishing mortality is aggregated into a single natural mortality rate \(M_{s,a,t}\) that is frequently assumed constant across time and often across ages (or scaled empirically with body size and life-history parameters; Gislason et al. (2010)). Somatic growth (weight-at-age \(w_{s,a,t}\)) and maturity ogives (\(\text{Mat}_{s,a,t}\)) are typically entered as empirical covariates rather than state variables coupled to prey availability.
Decades of empirical and modeling work in the North Sea, Baltic Sea, Barents Sea, Iceland, Bering Sea, and Georges Bank have demonstrated that this single-species simplification breaks down in strongly interacting fish communities:
crumbs: 1  Taxonomy and Theoretical Foundations of Multispecies Stock Assessment Models

title: 1  Taxonomy and Theoretical Foundations of Multispecies Stock Assessment Models
text:
Non-Stationary Predation Mortality (\(M2\)): Predation mortality inflicted by piscivorous fish, marine mammals, and seabirds typically exceeds fishing mortality \(F\) on juvenile age classes and forage fish, and varies by orders of magnitude as predator biomasses fluctuate (Lewy and Vinther 2004; Trijoulet et al. 2019). Ignoring time-varying \(M2\) biases historical stock-recruitment relationships, reference points (\(F_{\text{MSY}}\), \(B_{\text{lim}}\)), and short-term catch forecasts (ICES 2023).
Prey-Driven Somatic Growth and Starvation: Predators are food-limited across parts of their ontogeny. Depletion of forage fish (e.g., capelin Mallotus villosus in the Barents Sea and Icelandic waters, or sprat Sprattus sprattus in the Baltic Sea) directly reduces cod (Gadus morhua) feeding levels, somatic growth rates, condition factors, and reproductive output (Stefánsson and Pálsson 1998; Taylor and Stefánsson 2004; Hartvig et al. 2011).
Ontogenetic Size-Structured Omnivory and Cannibalism: In marine ecosystems, “who eats whom” is governed primarily by body size rather than taxonomic identity alone (Ursin 1973; Andersen 2020). Large piscivores grow through five to six orders of magnitude in body weight from egg to adult, transitioning from planktivory to benthivory/piscivory and cannibalism, which creates strong internal regulatory feedback loops (Canales et al. 2020).
Incompatibility of Single-Species \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) Targets: Attempting to simultaneously harvest all predator and prey stocks at their single-species \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) targets is frequently biologically impossible because rebuilding predator stocks erodes prey yields and vice versa (Pope et al. 2006, 2019; Andersen 2020).

title: 1  Taxonomy and Theoretical Foundations of Multispecies Stock Assessment Models
section: 1.2 The Complexity Spectrum: Strategic Models, Tactical Assessments, and MICE
text:
1.2 The Complexity Spectrum: Strategic Models, Tactical Assessments, and MICE
Fisheries ecosystem models span a wide continuum of structural complexity, taxonomic resolution, and statistical rigor (Plagányi et al. 2014; Collie et al. 2016; Karp et al. 2023):





flowchart LR
    A["<b>Single-Species Assessments</b><br/>(SAM, SS3, MULTIFAN-CL)<br/>High statistical rigor<br/>Zero trophic coupling"] --> B["<b>Extended Single-Species (ESAM)</b><br/>Predator index covariates<br/>on M or Q"]
    B --> C["<b>Tactical Multispecies / MICE</b><br/>(SMS, CEATTLE, Gadget, Hydra,<br/>EcoState, Dynamic mizer)<br/>Formal likelihood fitting<br/>Focused food web (3–15 spp.)"]
    C --> D["<b>Whole-Ecosystem / End-to-End</b><br/>(EwE, Atlantis, OSMOSE)<br/>30–100+ functional groups<br/>Strategic / MSE focus<br/>Limited formal parameter estimation"]






1.2.1 Models of Intermediate Complexity for Ecosystem Assessments (MICE)
Plagányi et al. (2014) and Collie et al. (2016) formalized the concept of MICE (Models of Intermediate Complexity for Ecosystem assessments) as the “sweet spot” for tactical fisheries management. As model complexity increases, structural bias (from omitting trophic interactions) decreases, whereas parameter estimation uncertainty (from fitting hundreds of poorly identified interaction rates to noisy data) increases rapidly (Collie et al. 2016, fig. 1).
A model qualifies as a tactical multispecies assessment or MICE when it satisfies four operational criteria (Plagányi et al. 2014; Karp et al. 2023):

Context-Driven Taxonomic Scope: It models only the core interacting species (typically \(3\text{--}12\) commercial predator and prey stocks plus \(1\text{--}3\) aggregated “other food” or resource pools) responsible for the majority of predation mortality and fishery yield.
Formal Statistical Estimation: Parameters are estimated by maximizing a formal likelihood (or posterior density) against empirical time series of commercial catches, scientific survey indices, age/size compositions, and stomach contents, rather than relying purely on literature plug-in values or manual tuning.
Diagnostic and Uncertainty Quantification: It provides standard stock assessment diagnostics (residual patterns, retrospective Mohn’s \(\rho\), profile likelihoods, Hessian/Laplace standard errors, or MCMC/SMC credible intervals).
Operational Cadence: It can be updated on the 1–5 year assessment cycle used by management bodies (e.g., ICES Working Group on Multispecies Assessment Methods [WGSAM] key runs supplying time-varying \(M = M1 + M2\) matrices to single-species SAM assessments, or NOAA NPFMC Bering Sea CEATTLE runs).

title: 1  Taxonomy and Theoretical Foundations of Multispecies Stock Assessment Models
section: 1.3 Fundamental Axes of Structural Classification
text:
1.3 Fundamental Axes of Structural Classification
Every multispecies stock assessment model can be positioned along three fundamental mathematical axes (Stefánsson and Pálsson 1998; Andersen et al. 2016; Pennino et al. 2025):

1.3.1 Axis 1: Individual State Space (Age vs. Length vs. Continuous Body Mass)










State Space
State Variable
Governing Dynamical Equation
Representative Models
Primary Strengths & Limitations




1. Biomass Pool / Multi-Stanza
\(B_{i}(t)\)
Coupled system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs): \(\frac{dB_i}{dt} = g_i \sum_j Q_{ij} - \sum_k Q_{ki} - (M0_i + F_i) B_i\)
Ecopath with Ecosim (Walters et al. 1997), Rpath (Lucey et al. 2020), EcoState (Thorson et al. 2024)
Fast; low state dimension; captures whole-food-web energy flow; cannot directly fit length/age compositions without multi-stanza delay-difference approximations.


2. Discrete Age-Structured
\(N_{i,a,t}\)
Difference equation along cohort diagonals: \(N_{i,a+1,t+1} = N_{i,a,t} \exp(-Z_{i,a,t})\) with empirical weight-at-age \(w_{i,a,t}\)
MSVPA/MSFOR, SMS (Lewy and Vinther 2004), MSCAA/Hydra, CEATTLE
Directly compatible with single-species age-based assessments; simple cohort tracking; requires aging data (otoliths); size-based predation must be mapped through fixed \(w_{i,a,t}\) or age-length keys.


3. Joint Age-Length Structured
\(N_{i,a,l,t}\) and \(W_{i,a,l,t}\)
Advection-dispersion across length bins within each discrete age class: \(\mathbf{N}_{i,a,t+\Delta t} = \mathbf{G}_{i,a,t} \mathbf{S}_{i,a,t} \mathbf{N}_{i,a,t}\)
MULTSPEC, BORMICON, Gadget2, gadget3 (Stefánsson and Pálsson 1998; Begley and Howell 2004)
Separates chronological age from physical size; resolves size-selective mortality effects on mean length-at-age; computationally intensive due to \((s \times a \times l \times r)\) state tensor.


4. Discrete Length-Structured (Age-Free)
\(N_{i,l,t}\)
Matrix projection across length bins: \(\mathbf{N}_{i,t+1} = \mathbf{X}_i \mathbf{S}_{i,t} \mathbf{N}_{i,t} + \mathbf{R}_{i,t}\)
LeMans (Hall et al. 2006), LeMaRns (Spence et al. 2020), CSMS (Pope et al. 2006)
Requires no otolith aging; matches survey length-frequency data directly; deterministic fractional bin transition (\(\phi_{i,l}\)) introduces numerical cohort diffusion unless stochastic transition matrix \(\mathbf{X}_{l,l'}\) is used.


5. Continuous Body-Mass Spectrum
\(N_i(w,t)\) (\(\text{numbers}\cdot\text{g}^{-1}\))
McKendrick–von Foerster PDE (or Fokker-Planck Jump-Growth PDE): \(\frac{\partial N_i}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (g_i N_i)}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2 (d_i N_i)}{\partial w^2} - \mu_i N_i\)
mizer (Hartvig et al. 2011; Scott et al. 2014; Datta et al. 2010)
Mechanistic mass and energy conservation from plankton to top predators; emergent growth, maturity, and mortality; requires PDE discretization and diffusion treatment to track cohorts dynamically.






1.3.2 Axis 2: Direction of Trophic Feedback (One-Way vs. Two-Way Coupling)
A critical distinction in multispecies stock assessment—emphasized by Stefánsson and Pálsson (1998) and Andersen et al. (2016)—is whether trophic interactions operate one-way (top-down only) or two-way (top-down predation mortality + bottom-up bioenergetic growth/reproduction):

One-Way Trophic Feedback (“Predation-Only” / Fixed-Ration Models):

Used in MSVPA, SMS, LeMans/LeMaRns, and standard modes of MSCAA/Hydra.
Predator abundance determines the predation mortality rate \(M2\) experienced by prey: \[\text{Predator Abundance } N_{\text{pred}} \implies \text{Prey Mortality } M2_{\text{prey}}\]
However, predator somatic growth rate, weight-at-age \(w_{a,t}\), and per-capita total food consumption rate \(R_{a,t}\) are independent of prey abundance. Even if all modeled fish prey collapse, predators maintain their prescribed ration \(R_{a,t}\) (implicitly compensating by consuming an inexhaustible “other food” pool \(B_{\text{other}}\)) and follow fixed growth curves.
Consequence: In forward projections under high forage-fish fishing mortality, one-way models predict that piscivores suffer zero loss of growth or reproductive output when their prey are fished down (Jacobsen et al. 2016; Pope et al. 2019).

Two-Way Trophic Feedback (“Bioenergetic / Size-Spectrum” Models):

Used in mizer, MULTSPEC/Gadget (when configured with g3a_grow_length_multspec or g3a_grow_weight_weightjones), bioenergetic CEATTLE, and Ecosim/EcoState.
Every predation event simultaneously removes biomass from the prey cohort (\(M2_{\text{prey}}\)) and supplies assimilable energy to the predator cohort, driving somatic growth \(g_{\text{pred}}\), energy reserves/condition \(W_{\text{pred}}\), egg production \(R_{p,\text{pred}}\), and (when energy intake falls below metabolic maintenance) starvation mortality \(\mu_{s,\text{pred}}\): \[\text{Prey Abundance } N_{\text{prey}} \Longleftrightarrow \begin{cases} \text{Top-Down: Predation Mortality } M2_{\text{prey}} \\ \text{Bottom-Up: Predator Growth } g_{\text{pred}}, \text{ Reproduction } R_{p,\text{pred}}, \text{ Starvation } \mu_{s,\text{pred}} \end{cases}\]





1.3.3 Axis 3: Calibration Paradigm (Deterministic VPA vs. Pattern-Oriented/History Matching vs. Integrated Statistical Likelihood)

Deterministic / Iterative Backward VPA (MSVPA): Assumes catch-at-age and stomach contents are known without error; solves for historical \(N_{a,t}\), \(F_{a,t}\), and \(M2_{a,t}\) via fixed-point iteration.
Equilibrium / Pattern-Oriented / History Matching (mizer steady-state, LeMaRns SMC, EwE): Calibrates time-averaged catch or biomass against a steady-state reference period, or uses rejection/Sequential Monte Carlo sampling with implausibility metrics (Spence, Thorpe, et al. 2021) to identify ensembles of plausible parameter vectors.
Integrated Maximum Likelihood / State-Space Assessment (SMS, Gadget/gadget3, CEATTLE, MSCAA/Hydra, EcoState): Formulates a differentiable forward process model coupled to explicit statistical observation models for each raw data stream (commercial catch-at-age/length, survey CPUE indices, stomach content proportions), optimizing the joint log-likelihood (or marginal Laplace likelihood in TMB) via automatic differentiation.

title: 1  Taxonomy and Theoretical Foundations of Multispecies Stock Assessment Models
section: 1.4 The Andersen & Ursin (1977) Theoretical Foundation and Livingston’s (1983) Evaluation
text:
1.4 The Andersen & Ursin (1977) Theoretical Foundation and Livingston’s (1983) Evaluation
Virtually all modern size- and age-structured multispecies models—including MSVPA, SMS, Gadget, LeMans/LeMaRns, CSMS, and mizer—trace their mathematical lineage to the landmark monograph by K. P. Andersen and Erik Ursin (1977), “A Multispecies Extension to the Beverton and Holt Theory of Fishing, with Accounts of Phosphorus Circulation and Primary Production”, Ursin’s (1973) empirical analysis of prey size preferences in cod and dab, and Patricia Livingston’s (1983) mathematical evaluation and sensitivity analysis of the Andersen–Ursin equations for North Pacific fisheries.
Because Andersen and Ursin (1977) is the shared ancestor of both statistical multispecies assessments (SMS, MSCAA, CEATTLE) and continuous size-spectrum models (mizer), examining its exact differential equations and parameter sensitivities—as documented by Livingston (1983, 2–11, Table 1)—clarifies how these two branches diverged.

1.4.1 Core Coupled Differential Equations of Andersen & Ursin (1977)
Andersen and Ursin (1977) extended the three basic Beverton and Holt (1957) differential equations for individual body weight \(w_i(t)\), cohort abundance \(N_i(t)\), and fishery yield \(Y_i(t)\) of computational entity \(i\) (a species-age group) (Livingston 1983, Eqs. 1–8):

Bioenergetic Pütter / Generalized von Bertalanffy Somatic Growth: The rate of food consumption \(\frac{dR_i}{dt}\) by an individual of entity \(i\) with body mass \(w_i\) is proportional to its allometric absorbing surface \(w_i^m\) and its dimensionless feeding level \(f_i \in [0, 1]\) (capped in the full model at a critical feeding level \(f_c = 0.44\)): \[\frac{dR_i}{dt} = f_i \, h_i \, w_i^m \qquad (0 \le f_i \le f_c \le 1)\] Only a fraction \(v_i = (1 - \alpha)\beta\) of consumed food is net-assimilated into tissue, where \(\beta = 0.80\) is the digested fraction of food and \(\alpha = 0.40\) is the fraction of digested energy lost in specific dynamic action / energy transfer costs (so \(v_i = 0.48\) universally; Livingston (1983, Table 1, p. 11)). Subtracting fasting metabolic catabolism \(k_i w_i^n\) gives the individual weight ODE: \[\frac{dw_i}{dt} = v_i \frac{dR_i}{dt} - k_i w_i^n = (1 - \alpha)\beta \, f_i \, h_i \, w_i^m - k_i w_i^n\] where Andersen and Ursin (1977) estimated universal exponents \(m = 0.56\) (or \(m = 2/3\) in the simplified skeleton model) and \(n = 0.83\) (or \(n = 1\) in the skeleton model) across 81 fish species (Ursin 1967).
Ursin’s (1973) Lognormal Size-Preference Kernel and Suitability (\(G_{ij}\)): Analyzing thousands of stomach records of cod (Gadus morhua) and dab (Limanda limanda), Ursin (1973, Eq. 2) demonstrated that predator \(i\) of weight \(w_i\) evaluates a potential prey item \(j\) of weight \(w_j\) according to a symmetric Gaussian distribution on the logarithmic predator-prey mass ratio \(\ln(w_i / w_j)\): \[g_{ij}(w_i, w_j) = \exp\!\left( -\frac{\left(\ln\frac{w_i}{w_j} - \eta_i\right)^2}{2\sigma_i^2} \right)\] where \(\eta_i\) is the preferred log predator-prey weight ratio (“a prey twice the preferred size is as acceptable as a prey half the preferred size”; Livingston (1983, 3, Fig. 1)) and \(\sigma_i\) is the standard deviation of diet breadth. Multiplying by species-specific behavioral/habitat vulnerability \(\rho_{ij} \in (0, 1]\) gives total suitability: \[G_{ij} = \rho_{ij} \, g_{ij}(w_i, w_j)\]
Available Food (\(\Psi_i\)), Search Volume (\(q_i w_i^r\)), and Feeding Level (\(f_i\)): Total suitable food biomass encountered by predator \(i\) is \(\Psi_i = \sum_j \Psi_{ij} = \sum_j G_{ij} w_j N_j\). The feeding level \(f_i\) follows a Holling Type II saturation curve (Livingston 1983, Eqs. 5–6): \[f_i = \frac{\Psi_i}{\Psi_i + Q_i}, \qquad Q_i = \frac{V \text{ (or } A\text{)}}{q_i \, w_i^r}\] where \(V\) (pelagic water volume) or \(A\) (demersal seabed area) scales the half-saturation food biomass \(Q_i\), \(r = 0.15\) is the universal search rate exponent, and \(q_i\) is the search rate coefficient (\(23\text{ m}^3\text{ g}^{-(1+r)}\) for pelagic habitat or \(0.53\text{ m}^2\text{ g}^{-(1+r)}\) for demersal habitat; Livingston (1983, Table 1, p. 10)).
Cohort Mortality Partitioning (\(F_i\), \(\hat{M}_i\), \(M2_i\)) and Discrete Spawning: Cohort numbers \(N_i(t)\) decay according to (Livingston 1983, Eqs. 2A, 8): \[\frac{dN_i}{dt} = -\left(F_i + \hat{M}_i + M2_i\right) N_i, \qquad \frac{dY_i}{dt} = F_i \, N_i \, w_i\] where predation mortality \(M2_i\) inflicted on prey \(i\) by all predator groups \(j\) is the ratio of total biomass of \(i\) consumed per unit time to the standing biomass \(N_i w_i\) of \(i\): \[M2_i = \frac{1}{N_i w_i} \sum_{j} \frac{dR_j}{dt} \, N_j \, \frac{\Psi_{ji}}{\Psi_j}\] Residual natural mortality \(\hat{M}_i = M1_i + M4_i + M5_i + M6_i\) comprises density-dependent larval mortality \(M1_i\) plus background disease (\(M4_i \approx 0.03\text{ yr}^{-1}\)), senescence (\(M5_i\)), and spawning stress (\(M6_i\)). At discrete spawning dates, mature age groups lose a weight fraction \(\pi_i\) to release \(E = \sum \pi_i(1-\pi_{\text{male}}) N_i w_i / \omega_i\) eggs of weight \(\omega_i\), which hatch into age-0 recruits via a Beverton–Holt density-dependent survival function (Livingston 1983, Eq. 9, p. 13): \[E1 = E \left(\frac{C}{C + E}\right)\]



1.4.2 Nonlinear Parameter Sensitivity of the Andersen–Ursin System (Livingston 1983)
By perturbing each parameter of the 14-entity Andersen–Ursin skeleton model (phytoplankton, 3 zooplankton age classes, 4 herring age classes, 6 cod age classes) by \(\pm 10\%\) and \(\pm 20\%\) and fitting the nonlinear power-law response \(y = \alpha x^\beta\) (Livingston 1983, 13–27, Tables 4–6), Livingston discovered a striking hierarchy of parameter sensitivities:

Low Sensitivity (\(|\beta| \le 0.5\), Table 4): Spawning fraction \(\pi\), residual natural mortality \(M1\), fish egg weights \(\omega_2, \omega_3\), and herring fishing mortalities \(F_6\text{--}F_8\) had weak, nearly linear effects on equilibrium numbers and body weights.
Moderate Sensitivity (\(0.5 < |\beta| \le 1.5\), Table 5): Predator search rate scalar \(Q\), density-dependent larval recruitment caps \(C_2, C_3\), and adult cod fishing mortality \(F_{14}\) had moderate effects; increasing \(Q\) (i.e., reducing search efficiency \(q_i\)) lowered individual body weights \(W_i\) (\(\beta = -0.34\) to \(-0.66\)) while increasing prey numbers \(N_i\) (\(\beta = +0.12\) to \(+0.53\)) via reduced predation.
High, Strongly Nonlinear Sensitivity (\(|\beta| > 1.5\), Table 6): The anabolic growth and assimilation parameters (\(v, H_1, H_2, H_3, m\)), catabolic exponent (\(n\)), and mean prey size preference (\(\eta\)) produced massive, strongly nonlinear responses across the food web (e.g., \(\beta = +7.17\) for total weight with respect to anabolic exponent \(m\), and \(\beta = +2.39\text{ to }+3.37\) for cod weight with respect to assimilation efficiency \(v\)).
Mathematical Rationale: In a two-way size-structured model, increasing anabolic growth (\(H_i, m, v\)) simultaneously (1) increases predator body mass \(w_j\), (2) increases per-capita predator ration \(h_j w_j^m\), and (3) shifts the predator’s preferred prey size window \(w_j e^{-\eta_j}\) across the prey size spectrum, creating a multiplicative trophic cascade across cohorts (Livingston 1983, 26–27).



1.4.3 The Fundamental Divergence: How SMS/MSVPA vs. mizer Simplified Andersen & Ursin (1977)





flowchart TD
    AU["<b>Andersen & Ursin (1977)</b><br/>Full Bioenergetic Multispecies Model (83 coupled ODEs)<br/>Feeding level: f<sub>j</sub> = Ψ<sub>j</sub> / (Ψ<sub>j</sub> + Q<sub>j</sub>)<br/>Growth: dw/dt = (1 − α)β f<sub>j</sub> h w<sup>m</sup> − k w<sup>n</sup>"]
    AU -->|"<b>Simplification 1: Helgason & Gislason (1979) / Pope (1979)</b><br/>Assume f<sub>j</sub> = const (fixed ration R<sub>j</sub> = f<sub>j</sub> h<sub>j</sub> w<sub>j</sub><sup>m</sup>)<br/>Fix empirical weight-at-age w<sub>a,t</sub>"| MSVPA["<b>MSVPA & SMS (Lewy & Vinther 2004)</b><br/>M2<sub>i,a</sub> = ∑<sub>j</sub> (N<sub>j</sub> R<sub>j</sub> G<sub>ij</sub>) / Φ<sub>j</sub><br/>Exact match to stomach proportions<br/>One-way trophic feedback"]
    AU -->|"<b>Simplification 2: Hartvig, Andersen & Beyer (2011)</b><br/>Continuous size-spectrum PDE<br/>Volumetric search rate γ<sub>j</sub> w<sub>j</sub><sup>q</sup><br/>Dynamic growth g<sub>j</sub>(w) & reproduction R<sub>p,j</sub>"| MIZER["<b>mizer (Scott et al. 2014)</b><br/>Full two-way bioenergetic feedback<br/>Emergent growth, maturity & M2<br/>Historically lacked time-series likelihoods"]






The MSVPA / SMS Simplification (Helgason and Gislason 1979; Pope 1979; Lewy and Vinther 2004):

In the late 1970s, the ICES Multispecies Working Group realized that Andersen & Ursin’s full 83-ODE system had too many unknown bioenergetic parameters to estimate directly from fisheries data, unless one assumed that feeding level \(f_j\) (and thus total consumption rate \(R_j(w_j) = f_j h_j w_j^n\) and somatic growth \(w_{a,t}\)) was known externally from gastric evacuation studies and commercial weight-at-age sampling.
Under this assumption, the fraction of predator \(j\)’s diet consisting of prey \((i, w_i)\) is simply the ratio of suitable prey biomass to total suitable food: \[\text{Diet Proportion } D_{ij} = \frac{G_{ij} B_i}{\Phi_j}\]
Consequently, the instantaneous predation mortality rate \(M2_i\) on prey \(i\) simplifies to: \[M2_i = \sum_{j} \frac{\bar{N}_j \, R_j \, G_{ij}}{\Phi_j}\]
This brilliant simplification made \(G_{ij}/\Phi_j\) directly observable in stomach content data (since stomach content weight proportions after evacuation correction estimate \(D_{ij}\)), launching the entire MSVPA and SMS assessment tradition. However, the price paid was the loss of dynamic growth feedback (\(dw/dt\)).

The mizer Reformulation (Hartvig et al. 2011; Scott et al. 2014):

Thirty-four years after Andersen and Ursin (1977), Hartvig et al. (2011) restored the full bioenergetic growth and reproduction equations of Andersen & Ursin within a continuous McKendrick–von Foerster PDE framework, replacing the arbitrary species-specific half-saturation constants \(Q_j(w_j)\) with a mechanistic volumetric search rate \(\gamma_j(w_j) = \gamma_j w_j^q\).
In mizer, the encounter rate of food is \(E_j(w_j) = \gamma_j(w_j) \Phi_j(w_j)\), which implies an emergent half-saturation food density \(Q_j(w_j) = \frac{h_j w_j^n}{\gamma_j w_j^q}\). All life-history parameters scale allometrically with individual weight \(w\) and asymptotic species size \(W_{\infty, j}\), reducing the parameter space from hundreds of cohort-specific constants to a compact set of scaling exponents and species traits.

section: 1.5 Community-Level Dynamics and the Multispecies Jacobian Matrix

1.5 Community-Level Dynamics and the Multispecies Jacobian Matrix
When comparing multispecies stock assessment models across these structural paradigms (Tsou and Collie 2001; Aydin et al. 2005; Jacobsen et al. 2016; Spence et al. 2018; Pope et al. 2019), Pope et al. (2006), Pope et al. (2019), and Jacobsen et al. (2016) introduced two unifying analytical diagnostics:

1.5.1 The Yield Vector and Jacobian Interaction Matrix (\(\mathbf{J}\))
Let \(\mathbf{F} = (F_1, F_2, \dots, F_S)^\top\) be the vector of long-term fishing mortality rates across \(S\) species, and let \(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{F}) = (Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_S)^\top\) and \(\mathbf{SSB}(\mathbf{F}) = (\text{SSB}_1, \dots, \text{SSB}_S)^\top\) be the resulting equilibrium yield and spawning stock biomass vectors. Near a reference fishing vector \(\mathbf{F}_0\), the response of the multispecies community is characterized by the Jacobian matrix (Pope et al. 2019, 5):
\[J_{ik} = \left.\frac{\partial \ln \text{SSB}_i}{\partial F_k}\right|_{\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}_0} \quad \text{or} \quad J^{(Y)}_{ik} = \left.\frac{\partial Y_i}{\partial F_k}\right|_{\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}_0}\]

Diagonal elements (\(J_{ii} < 0\)): Measure the direct single-species depletion + intraspecific cannibalism recovery response of species \(i\) to its own fishing mortality \(F_i\). Strong cannibalism (e.g., cod, whiting, hake) dampens \(|J_{ii}|\) because fishing down large adults releases juveniles from cannibalistic \(M2\).
Off-diagonal elements (\(J_{ik}\) for \(i \neq k\)):

In one-way models (SMS, LeMans), \(J_{\text{prey}, \text{pred}} > 0\) (fishing down a predator increases prey SSB by reducing \(M2\)), while \(J_{\text{pred}, \text{prey}} \approx 0\) (fishing down a prey has zero direct effect on predator SSB, or only an indirect “prey-switching/shielding” effect if total suitable food \(\Phi_{\text{pred}}\) changes cannibalism rates).
In two-way bioenergetic models (mizer, Gadget, Ecosim), \(J_{\text{pred}, \text{prey}} < 0\) because fishing down forage fish reduces predator feeding level \(f_{\text{pred}}\), slowing predator somatic growth \(g_{\text{pred}}\) and lowering reproductive output \(R_{p,\text{pred}}\).




1.5.2 Quadratic Approximation of Total Multispecies Yield
Pope et al. (2006) and Pope et al. (2019) showed that across widely different multispecies models of the North Sea (SMS, Gadget, EwE, LeMans, mizer, CSMS, CSM), the equilibrium yield of species \(i\) as a function of the fishing mortality vector \(\mathbf{F}\) is well approximated by a coupled quadratic form (a multispecies generalization of the Schaefer surplus production parabola):
\[Y_i(\mathbf{F}) \approx a_i F_i + \sum_{k=1}^{S} b_{ik} F_i F_k\]
In matrix notation, total community yield \(Y_{\text{tot}}(\mathbf{F}) = \sum_{i=1}^S Y_i(\mathbf{F}) = \mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{F} + \mathbf{F}^\top \mathbf{B} \mathbf{F}\). An unconstrained community-wide MSY exists at \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{MSY}} = -\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{B}^\top)^{-1}\mathbf{a}\) only if the symmetric part of the interaction matrix \(\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{B}^\top)\) is negative definite; in practice, strong predation terms \(b_{ik} > 0\) often make the unconstrained optimum corner-valued (“fish out the predators to maximize forage fish yield”), necessitating conservation constraints (\(B_i \ge B_{\text{lim}, i}\)) or value-weighted objective functions (Pope et al. 2019).

2.1 Overview of the Age-Structured Multispecies Family
Age-structured multispecies models are direct extensions of single-species Virtual Population Analysis (VPA) and Statistical Catch-at-Age (SCAA) models. They partition total instantaneous mortality \(Z_{s,a,y,q}\) of species \(s\), age class \(a\), year \(y\), and season/quarter \(q\) into three additive components (first formalized by Helgason and Gislason (1979) and Pope (1979)):
\[Z_{s,a,y,q} = F_{s,a,y,q} + M1_{s,a,q} + M2_{s,a,y,q}\]
where:
Because these models track discrete age cohorts \((s, a)\) rather than continuous body size, individual body weight \(w_{s,a,y,q}\) and length \(l_{s,a,y,q}\) are typically treated as known empirical inputs (measured from port and survey sampling), or mapped via pre-computed age-length keys (\(\text{ALK}_{s,a,l,y,q}\)).
Four major model lineages define this family:

text:
\(F_{s,a,y,q}\) is the instantaneous fishing mortality rate,
\(M1_{s,a,q}\) is the residual (background) natural mortality rate due to disease, senescence, abiotic stress, and predation by unmodeled predators,
\(M2_{s,a,y,q}\) is the endogenous predation mortality rate inflicted by the modeled predators in the ecosystem.




Foundations and MSVPA: Ursin (1967), Ursin (1973), and Andersen and Ursin (1977) established the size-based bioenergetic and prey-suitability equations, evaluated for North Pacific stocks by Livingston (1983) and simplified into operational MSVPA by Helgason and Gislason (1979), Pope (1979), and Sparre (1980).
Stochastic Multispecies Model (SMS / smsR): Lewy and Vinther (2004) formulated the seasonal age-length statistical multispecies model and Dirichlet stomach-content likelihood used in ICES key runs (ICES 2021, 2023).
North American Statistical Catch-at-Age (MSASA / MSCAA / Hydra): Jurado-Molina et al. (2005), Kinzey and Punt (2009), Van Kirk et al. (2010), Curti et al. (2013), and Trijoulet et al. (2019) developed and tested forward-projecting multispecies catch-at-age models across alternative predator functional responses and diet observation error regimes.
Climate-Enhanced Multispecies Assessment (CEATTLE / Rceattle): Holsman and Aydin (2015), Holsman et al. (2016), and Adams et al. (2022) coupled temperature-dependent von Bertalanffy growth (Essington et al. 2001) and Wisconsin bioenergetics (Kitchell et al. 1977; Thornton and Lessem 1978) with age-structured stock assessment and multispecies biological reference points.

section: 2.2 Multispecies Virtual Population Analysis (MSVPA) and MSFOR
text:
2.2 Multispecies Virtual Population Analysis (MSVPA) and MSFOR

2.2.1 Historical Development
Developed simultaneously by Helgason and Gislason (1979) and Pope (1979) following the Andersen and Ursin (1977) monograph, MSVPA was the standard operational multispecies model of the ICES Multispecies Working Group (MSWG) throughout the 1980s and 1990s, motivating the massive 1981 and 1991 ICES “Years of the Stomach” sampling programs in the North Sea (Stefánsson and Pálsson 1998; Lewy and Vinther 2004). MSFOR is its forward-projection counterpart used to evaluate management scenarios given recruitment assumptions.


2.2.2 Mathematical Formulation of MSVPA
Within each quarter \(q \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) of year \(y\), cohort abundance \(N_{i,a,y,q}\) of prey species \(i\), age \(a\) decays exponentially:
\[N_{i,a,y,q+1} = N_{i,a,y,q} \exp\!\left(-Z_{i,a,y,q}\right), \qquad \bar{N}_{i,a,y,q} = N_{i,a,y,q} \frac{1 - \exp(-Z_{i,a,y,q})}{Z_{i,a,y,q}}\]
Observed catch-at-age in numbers \(C_{i,a,y,q}\) is assumed exact (zero observation error), obeying the Baranov catch equation:
\[C_{i,a,y,q} = \frac{F_{i,a,y,q}}{Z_{i,a,y,q}} N_{i,a,y,q} \left(1 - \exp(-Z_{i,a,y,q})\right) = F_{i,a,y,q} \bar{N}_{i,a,y,q}\]
The predation mortality \(M2_{i,a,y,q}\) on prey \((i, a)\) by all predator species \(j\) and predator ages \(b\) is:
\[M2_{i,a,y,q} = \sum_{j} \sum_{b} \frac{\bar{N}_{j,b,y,q} \, R_{j,b,q} \, S_{i,a,j,b,q}}{\Phi_{j,b,y,q}}\]
where:

\(R_{j,b,q}\) is the prescribed per-capita quarterly food ration (in mass) consumed by predator \((j, b)\) in quarter \(q\),
\(S_{i,a,j,b,q} \in [0, 1]\) is the suitability coefficient of prey \((i, a)\) for predator \((j, b)\) in quarter \(q\),
\(\Phi_{j,b,y,q}\) is the total available (suitable) food biomass for predator \((j, b)\):

\[\Phi_{j,b,y,q} = \sum_{k} \sum_{c} S_{k,c,j,b,q} \, \bar{N}_{k,c,y,q} \, w_{k,c,y,q} + S_{\text{other}, j, b, q} \, B_{\text{other}, q}\]


2.2.3 Iterative Fixed-Point Solution Algorithm
In classic MSVPA, suitability \(S_{i,a,j,b,q}\) is not parameterized as a smooth function of predator-prey size ratio; instead, it is estimated directly from observed average stomach content weight proportions \(\bar{W}_{i,a,j,b,y,q}\) via fixed-point iteration:

Initialize: Set \(M2^{(0)}_{i,a,y,q} = 0\) (or a prior guess) and run standard backward VPA on each species to obtain initial cohort abundances \(\bar{N}^{(0)}_{i,a,y,q}\) and fishing mortalities \(F^{(0)}_{i,a,y,q}\).
Update Suitabilities: For years \(y \in \mathcal{Y}_{\text{stom}}\) with stomach content observations \(\bar{W}_{i,a,j,b,y,q}\), compute empirical suitabilities: \[\tilde{S}_{i,a,j,b,y,q} = \frac{\bar{W}_{i,a,j,b,y,q}}{\bar{N}_{i,a,y,q} \, w_{i,a,y,q}}\] Normalize so \(\sum_{i,a} \tilde{S}_{i,a,j,b,y,q} = 1\), and average across stomach-sampling years \(y \in \mathcal{Y}_{\text{stom}}\) (weighted by predator stomach sample size) to obtain time-invariant quarter-specific suitabilities \(S^{(m)}_{i,a,j,b,q}\).
Update \(M2\): Substitute \(S^{(m)}_{i,a,j,b,q}\) and \(\bar{N}^{(m-1)}\) into the \(M2\) equation to compute \(M2^{(m)}_{i,a,y,q}\).
Update VPA: Re-run backward VPA for all species using \(Z^{(m)}_{i,a,y,q} = F^{(m)}_{i,a,y,q} + M1_{i,a,q} + M2^{(m)}_{i,a,y,q}\) to obtain \(\bar{N}^{(m)}_{i,a,y,q}\).
Iterate: Repeat Steps 2–4 until \(\max |M2^{(m)} - M2^{(m-1)}| < \epsilon\).



2.2.4 Limitations of MSVPA
As analyzed by Stefánsson and Pálsson (1998) and Lewy and Vinther (2004):

No Observation Error: MSVPA treats commercial catch-at-age and stomach content proportions as exact deterministic quantities. Sampling noise in rare stomach items propagates directly into suitability \(S_{i,a,j,b,q}\).
Over-Parameterization of Suitability: Estimating a free suitability parameter for every \((i, a, j, b, q)\) combination requires thousands of parameters and leaves zero degrees of freedom for prey age classes not observed in a particular predator age’s stomachs.
No Uncertainty Estimates: Because there is no statistical likelihood function, MSVPA cannot produce confidence intervals on \(M2\), SSB, or recruitment, nor can it perform formal hypothesis testing (e.g., AIC/LRT between functional responses).

section: 2.3 The Stochastic Multispecies Model (SMS and smsR)
text:
2.3 The Stochastic Multispecies Model (SMS and smsR)
To overcome the deterministic limitations of MSVPA, Peter Lewy and Morten Vinther at DTU Aqua developed SMS (Stochastic Multispecies Model; Lewy and Vinther (2004)), implemented in ADMB (Auto Differentiation Model Builder) and recently ported to TMB/R as smsR (Nis Sand Jacobsen et al.; ICES (2021); ICES (2023)).
SMS is the flagship operational multispecies stock assessment model in ICES, providing the official time-varying natural mortality matrices (\(M = M1 + M2\)) used in single-species stock assessments (e.g., SAM and SS3) for the North Sea and Baltic Sea (ICES 2023).

2.3.1 State-Space Indexing and Population Dynamics
SMS is a forward-projecting, seasonal (typically quarterly, \(q \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\)), age-structured statistical catch-at-age model. In addition to tracked dynamic VPA species (which can act as both predators and prey), SMS includes “other predators” (e.g., seabirds, grey seals, harbour porpoises, horse mackerel, hake) whose abundance time series \(N_{A,a,y,q}\) are entered as known external covariates, and an “other food” biomass pool \(B_{\text{OF}}\) (Lewy and Vinther 2004, 7).
Following the notation of Lewy and Vinther (2004):

Let \((A, a)\) denote a predator species \(A\) of age (or size class) \(a\), with mean weight \(w_{A,a,y,q}\).
Let \((B, b)\) denote a prey species \(B\) of age (or size class) \(b\), with mean weight \(w_{B,b,y,q}\).

Stock survival across seasons \(q\) within year \(y\) follows: \[N_{s,a,y,q+1} = N_{s,a,y,q} \exp\!\left(-Z_{s,a,y,q}\right), \qquad q = 1, 2, 3\] At the transition from the final quarter \(q=4\) of year \(y\) to \(q=1\) of year \(y+1\): \[N_{s,a+1,y+1,1} = N_{s,a,y,4} \exp\!\left(-Z_{s,a,y,4}\right), \qquad a < a_{\max}-1\] and for the plus-group \(a_{\max}\): \[N_{s,a_{\max},y+1,1} = N_{s,a_{\max}-1,y,4} \exp\!\left(-Z_{s,a_{\max}-1,y,4}\right) + N_{s,a_{\max},y,4} \exp\!\left(-Z_{s,a_{\max},y,4}\right)\]
Recruitment \(N_{s,a_{\text{rec}},y,q_{\text{rec}}}\) is parameterized either as free log-parameters \(\ln R_{s,y}\) or via a stochastic stock-recruitment relationship (Ricker, Beverton-Holt, or hockey-stick) with lognormal process error: \[N_{s,a_{\text{rec}},y,q_{\text{rec}}} = f_{\text{SRR}}\!\left(\text{SSB}_{s,y-a_{\text{rec}}}\right) \exp\!\left(\epsilon_{R,s,y}\right), \qquad \epsilon_{R,s,y} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{R,s}\right)\]


2.3.2 Separable Fishing Mortality Model
To prevent overfitting catch-at-age noise, SMS models instantaneous fishing mortality \(F_{s,a,y,q}\) using a partially separable structure across age \(a\), year \(y\), and season \(q\) within multi-year regime blocks \(Y_j\) (Lewy and Vinther 2004, Eq. 2):
\[F_{s,a,y,q} = v_{s,a,Y_j} \, F^{(y)}_{s,y} \, F^{(q)}_{s,a,Y_j,q}\]
where:

\(v_{s,a,Y_j}\) is the age effect (fishery selectivity at age \(a\) in year-block \(Y_j\)),
\(F^{(y)}_{s,y}\) is the annual fishing effort/mortality multiplier in year \(y\),
\(F^{(q)}_{s,a,Y_j,q}\) is the seasonal allocation fraction of fishing mortality in quarter \(q\) (constrained so the mean across seasons equals \(0.25\)).

Expected commercial catch-at-age \(\hat{C}_{s,a,y,q}\) is given by the Baranov equation: \[\hat{C}_{s,a,y,q} = \frac{F_{s,a,y,q}}{Z_{s,a,y,q}} N_{s,a,y,q} \left(1 - \exp(-Z_{s,a,y,q})\right) = F_{s,a,y,q} \bar{N}_{s,a,y,q}\]


2.3.3 Parametric Suitability and the Andersen–Ursin Size-Selection Submodel
Instead of MSVPA’s non-parametric empirical suitabilities, SMS parameterizes the suitability \(S(B, b, A, a, q)\) of prey \((B, b)\) for predator \((A, a)\) in season \(q\) as a multiplicative product of three biological components (Lewy and Vinther 2004, Eq. 5):
\[S(B, b, A, a, y, q) = \text{vul}(B, A) \times \text{size}(B, b, A, a, y, q) \times \text{overlap}(B, A, q)\]

Species Vulnerability (\(\text{vul}(B, A)\)): Time-invariant parameter measuring the behavioral/morphological vulnerability of prey species \(B\) to predator species \(A\) (with \(\text{vul}(\text{Other Food}, A) \equiv 1\) as the reference baseline).
Spatial/Seasonal Overlap (\(\text{overlap}(B, A, q)\)): Parameter representing the spatial co-occurrence of prey \(B\) and predator \(A\) in season \(q\) (fixed to \(1\) in seasons with full overlap, estimated in seasons with migratory separation).
Asymmetric Lognormal Size Preference (\(\text{size}(B, b, A, a, y, q)\)): Following Andersen and Ursin (1977), SMS models size preference as a Gaussian (or asymmetric split-Gaussian) function of the log predator-to-prey weight ratio \(\xi = \ln\!\left(\frac{w_{A,a,y,q}}{w_{B,b,y,q}}\right)\), restricted to the physiologically feasible range \([\xi_{\min, A}, \xi_{\max, A}]\) (Lewy and Vinther 2004, Eq. 6):

\[\text{size}(B, b, A, a, y, q) = \begin{cases} \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\left(\ln\frac{w_{A,a}}{w_{B,b}} - \eta_A\right)^2}{2\sigma_{1,A}^2}\right) & \text{if } \xi_{\min,A} \le \ln\frac{w_{A,a}}{w_{B,b}} \le \eta_A \\[12pt] \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\left(\ln\frac{w_{A,a}}{w_{B,b}} - \eta_A\right)^2}{2\sigma_{2,A}^2}\right) & \text{if } \eta_A < \ln\frac{w_{A,a}}{w_{B,b}} \le \xi_{\max,A} \\[10pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
When SMS is run in length-class stomach mode (because ICES stomach databases record predator and prey lengths \(l\), not ages \(a\)), SMS converts age abundances \(N_{s,a,y,q}\) into length classes \(l\) using seasonal empirical Age-Length Keys (\(\text{ALK}_{s,a,l,y,q}\)) before evaluating \(\text{size}(B, l_B, A, l_A)\) using constant length-weight relationships \(w_s(l) = \alpha_s l^{\beta_s}\), and then maps \(M2\) back from length classes to age classes (Lewy and Vinther 2004, 8–9).


2.3.4 Gastric-Evacuation-Based Consumption Rate (\(R_{A,a,y,q}\))
Total quarterly food intake (ration) \(R_{A,a,y,q}\) of predator \((A,a)\) is input as an empirical covariate derived from average observed stomach fullness \(\bar{S}_{A,a,q}\) and temperature-dependent gastric evacuation models (Andersen and Beyer 2005; Lewy and Vinther 2004, Eqs. 7–8):
\[R_{A,a,y,q} = \alpha_{R,A} \, w_{A,a,y,q}^{\beta_{R,A}} \quad \text{or} \quad R_{A,a,y,q} = \rho_A \, \bar{S}_{A,a,q}^{\gamma_A} \, \exp(\delta_A T_{y,q}) \, L_{A,a}^{\lambda_A} \, D_q\]
where \(T_{y,q}\) is ambient water temperature and \(D_q\) is the number of hours in quarter \(q\).


2.3.5 Predation Mortality (\(M2\)) and Exact Integration Over the Quarter
Let \(\bar{B}_{B,b,y,q} = \bar{N}_{B,b,y,q} w_{B,b,y,q}\) be the mean quarterly biomass of prey \((B, b)\), and let total available food for predator \((A, a)\) be:
\[\Phi(A, a, y, q) = \sum_{B} \sum_{b} \bar{B}_{B,b,y,q} \, S(B, b, A, a, y, q) + B_{\text{OF}, A} \, S(\text{OF}, A, a, y, q)\]
In differential form at instant \(t \in [q, q+1]\), the instantaneous predation rate is \(M2_{B,b}(t) = \sum_{A,a} \frac{N_{A,a}(t) r_{A,a} S(B,b,A,a)}{\Phi(A,a,t)}\). Assuming \(\Phi(A,a,t)\) is approximately constant within a single quarter (since \(B_{\text{OF}}\) is large and individual prey decline is offset across cohorts), integrating over the quarter yields the exact discrete-time SMS \(M2\) equation (Lewy and Vinther 2004, Eq. 11):
\[M2_{B,b,y,q} = \sum_{A} \sum_{a} \frac{\bar{N}_{A,a,y,q} \, R_{A,a,y,q} \, S(B, b, A, a, y, q)}{\Phi(A, a, y, q)}\]
Since \(\bar{N}_{B,b,y,q} = N_{B,b,y,q}\frac{1 - e^{-Z_{B,b,y,q}}}{Z_{B,b,y,q}}\) depends on \(M2_{B,b,y,q}\) (and predator survival also depends on \(M2\) for intermediate predators like whiting or young cod), SMS performs \(2\text{--}4\) internal Newton/fixed-point iterations per quarter evaluation within the ADMB/TMB objective function, or uses the explicit beginning-of-quarter biomass approximation when quarterly time steps are short.


2.3.6 Expected Stomach Content Proportions
Under the SMS equations, the expected proportion by weight \(\hat{W}(B, b, A, a, y, q)\) of prey \((B, b)\) in the stomach of predator \((A, a)\) in year \(y\), quarter \(q\) is (Lewy and Vinther 2004, Eq. 12):
\[\hat{W}(B, b, A, a, y, q) = \frac{\bar{B}_{B,b,y,q} \, S(B, b, A, a, y, q)}{\Phi(A, a, y, q)}\]
Note that \(\sum_{B,b} \hat{W}(B, b, A, a, y, q) + \hat{W}(\text{OF}, A, a, y, q) = 1\).


2.3.7 Statistical Likelihood Function of SMS
SMS estimates all parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\ln N_{\text{init}}, \ln R_{s,y}, v_{s,a}, F^{(y)}_{s,y}, F^{(q)}_{s,q}, q_{\text{survey}}, \text{vul}(B,A), \eta_A, \sigma_A, \text{overlap}, \dots)\) by minimizing the negative joint log-likelihood across four data types (Lewy and Vinther 2004, 10–16):
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{catch}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{CPUE}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{stomach}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{SRR}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\]

1. Commercial Catch-at-Age Likelihood (Lognormal)
Observed catch-at-age \(C_{s,a,y,q}\) is assumed lognormally distributed around expected catch \(\hat{C}_{s,a,y,q}\): \[\ln C_{s,a,y,q} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\ln \hat{C}_{s,a,y,q},\; \sigma^2_{\text{catch}, s, a, q}\right)\] contributing to the negative log-likelihood: \[-\ln L_{\text{catch}} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{s,a,y,q} \left[ \ln\!\left(2\pi \sigma^2_{\text{catch},s,a,q}\right) + \frac{\left(\ln C_{s,a,y,q} - \ln \hat{C}_{s,a,y,q}\right)^2}{\sigma^2_{\text{catch},s,a,q}} \right]\]


2. Survey Abundance Index (CPUE) Likelihood (Lognormal)
For survey fleet \(f\) operating from season fraction \(\alpha_{f}\) to \(\beta_{f}\) in quarter \(q\), the expected survey index \(\hat{I}_{f,s,a,y}\) is: \[\hat{I}_{f,s,a,y} = Q_{f,s,a} \, N_{s,a,y,q} \frac{\exp(-\alpha_f Z_{s,a,y,q}) - \exp(-\beta_f Z_{s,a,y,q})}{(\beta_f - \alpha_f) Z_{s,a,y,q}}\] with lognormal negative log-likelihood: \[-\ln L_{\text{CPUE}} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{f,s,a,y} \left[ \ln\!\left(2\pi \sigma^2_{\text{CPUE},f,s,a}\right) + \frac{\left(\ln I_{f,s,a,y} - \ln \hat{I}_{f,s,a,y}\right)^2}{\sigma^2_{\text{CPUE},f,s,a}} \right]\]


3. Stomach Content Composition Likelihood (Dirichlet vs. Multinomial)
Let \(U = (A, a, y, q)\) index a specific predator-age-year-quarter sampling stratum, and let \(k \in \{1, \dots, K_U\}\) index the \(K_U\) prey entities \((B, b)\) (plus “other food”) observed in that predator’s diet, with observed weight proportions \(\mathbf{W}_U = (W_{1,U}, \dots, W_{K_U,U})\) satisfying \(\sum_{k=1}^{K_U} W_{k,U} = 1\), and model expectations \(\hat{p}_{k,U} = \hat{W}(k, U)\).
Lewy and Vinther (2004, 11–14) derived two alternative likelihood formulations for continuous stomach weight proportions:

Option A: Multinomial Approximation on Effective Prey Counts Defining an effective number of independent prey observations \(N_{\text{stom}, U}\) (e.g., number of stomachs or hauls sampled), \(N_{\text{stom}, U} \mathbf{W}_U\) is treated as a multinomial vector with log-likelihood kernel: \[\ln L_{\text{stom, Mult}} = \sum_{U} N_{\text{stom}, U} \sum_{k=1}^{K_U} W_{k,U} \ln \hat{p}_{k,U}\]
Option B: Exact Dirichlet Distribution (Default in SMS) Because \(W_{k,U} \in (0, 1)\) is a continuous biomass proportion rather than a discrete integer count, Lewy and Vinther (2004, Eqs. 19–24) modeled \(\mathbf{W}_U\) using a Dirichlet distribution with concentration parameters \(\alpha_{k,U} = v_U \hat{p}_{k,U}\) and total precision sum \(v_U = \sum_{k=1}^{K_U} \alpha_{k,U}\):
\[f_{\text{Dir}}(\mathbf{W}_U \mid v_U \hat{\mathbf{p}}_U) = \frac{\Gamma(v_U)}{\prod_{k=1}^{K_U} \Gamma(v_U \hat{p}_{k,U})} \prod_{k=1}^{K_U} W_{k,U}^{v_U \hat{p}_{k,U} - 1}\]
Under the Dirichlet distribution, the expectation and variance of each prey share \(W_{k,U}\) are: \[\mathbb{E}[W_{k,U}] = \hat{p}_{k,U}, \qquad \text{Var}(W_{k,U}) = \frac{\hat{p}_{k,U}(1 - \hat{p}_{k,U})}{v_U + 1}\] Defining the variance-scaling factor \(V_U = \frac{1}{v_U + 1} \iff v_U = \frac{1}{V_U} - 1\), SMS relates \(V_U\) to the predator species’ overall diet dispersion parameter \(\theta_{\text{stom}, A}\) and the number of stomachs/hauls sampled \(N_{\text{haul}, U}\) via: \[V_U = \frac{\theta_{\text{stom}, A}}{N_{\text{haul}, U}} \implies v_U = \frac{N_{\text{haul}, U}}{\theta_{\text{stom}, A}} - 1\] This allows \(\theta_{\text{stom}, A}\) to be estimated directly inside the maximum likelihood optimization via the exact Gamma-function log-likelihood! (Wait: to handle observed zeros \(W_{k,U} = 0\), SMS pools unobserved interior age classes with adjacent age classes or applies a small threshold; see Chapter 5 for full details).

section: 2.4 Statistical Multispecies Catch-at-Age (MSASA, MSCAA, and Hydra)
text:
2.4 Statistical Multispecies Catch-at-Age (MSASA, MSCAA, and Hydra)
In North America (particularly NOAA AFSC for the Aleutian Islands, Gulf of Alaska, and Bering Sea, and NOAA NEFSC for Georges Bank and the Gulf of Maine), a family of Multispecies Statistical Catch-at-Age (MSASA / MSCAA) models was developed in ADMB and TMB by Kinzey and Punt (2009), Van Kirk et al. (2010), Curti et al. (2013), Gaichas et al. (Hydra MSE operating model), and evaluated in simulation studies by Trijoulet et al. (2019).

2.4.1 Kinzey & Punt (2009): Aleutian Islands Age–Length Hybrid MSCAA and the Seven Predator Functional Responses
Kinzey and Punt (2009) developed a foundational integrated multispecies statistical catch-at-age framework in ADMB and applied it to the Aleutian Islands (1960–2003) for walleye pollock (Theragra chalcogramma, ages 0–15+, \(1\text{--}80\text{ cm}\) in \(5\text{ cm}\) bins), Atka mackerel (Pleurogrammus monopterygius, ages 0–15+, \(1\text{--}65\text{ cm}\)), and Pacific cod (Gadus macrocephalus, ages 0–12+, \(1\text{--}120\text{ cm}\), harvested by 3 fleets: trawl, pot, and longline).

Predation Mortality (\(P_{k,a,y}\)), Gamma Length-Ratio Selectivity (\(\gamma^{r,u}_{k,a}\)), and Age–Length Transition Mapping (\(\chi^{r,u,l}\)): Total mortality on prey species \(k\), age \(a\) in year \(y\) is \(Z_{k,a,y} = \sum_f F^f_{k,a,y} + P_{k,a,y} + M_k\), where predation mortality \(P_{k,a,y}\) inflicted by all predator species \(r\) and predator ages \(u\) is (Kinzey and Punt 2009, Eqs. 6–7, p. 77): \[P_{k,a,y} = \sum_{r,u} V^{r,u}_{k,a,y}, \qquad V^{r,u}_{k,a,y} = N_{r,u,y} \, \phi^{r,u}_{k,a,y} \, \gamma^{r,u}_{k,a}\] Instead of a symmetric lognormal weight-ratio kernel, Kinzey and Punt (2009, Eq. 18, p. 80) parameterize predator \((r, u)\) size selectivity \(\gamma^{r,u}_{k,a} \in (0, 1]\) for prey \((k, a)\) as a skewed Gamma function of the log predator-to-prey expected length ratio \(G^{r,u}_{k,a} = \ln(\bar{L}_{r,u} / \bar{L}_{k,a})\), normalized to equal \(1\) at its mode \(\tilde{G}^r = (\alpha^r - 1)\beta^r\): \[\gamma^{r,u}_{k,a} = \left(\frac{G^{r,u}_{k,a}}{\tilde{G}^r}\right)^{\alpha^r - 1} \exp\!\left[-\frac{G^{r,u}_{k,a} - \tilde{G}^r}{\beta^r}\right], \qquad \tilde{G}^r = (\alpha^r - 1)\beta^r\] The total number of prey \((k, a)\) eaten by predator \((r, u)\) in year \(y\) follows the Baranov predation equation: \[E^{r,u}_{k,a,y} = \frac{V^{r,u}_{k,a,y}}{Z_{k,a,y}} N_{k,a,y} \left(1 - e^{-Z_{k,a,y}}\right)\] Because stomach samples (\(1,987\) pollock, \(1,033\) mackerel, and \(3,278\) cod stomachs) are recorded by \(5\text{ cm}\) predator length bin \(l\) and \(5\text{ cm}\) prey length bin \(m\), Kinzey & Punt map age-specific predation into length space using prespecified empirical age-to-length transition matrices \(\chi^{r,u,l}\) (Kinzey and Punt 2009, Eqs. 9–14 & Table 3, pp. 77–84):

Prey numbers eaten by predator length class \((r, l)\): \(E^{r,l}_{k,a,y} = \sum_u E^{r,u}_{k,a,y} \chi^{r,u,l}\).
Predicted prey length composition \(\tilde{T}^{r,l}_{k,m}\) inside predator \((r, l)\) stomachs (fitted in multinomial likelihood \(L_6\)): \[\tilde{T}^{r,l}_{k,m} = \frac{\sum_y n^{r,l}_y \sum_a \chi^{k,a,m} E^{r,l}_{k,a,y}}{\sum_y n^{r,l}_y \sum_{a'} E^{r,l}_{k,a',y}}\]
Predicted prey species mass \(Q^{r,u}_{k,y}\) and diet weight proportions \(\tilde{Q}^{r,l}_{k,y}\) (fitted in multinomial likelihood \(L_7\)): \[Q^{r,u}_{k,y} = \begin{cases} \sum_{a=0}^{A_{L,k}} E^{r,u}_{k,a,y} w_{k,a} & \text{modeled prey } k \\[6pt] Q^r_0 \left(1 - e^{-\phi^{r,u}_o N_{r,u,y}}\right) & \text{"other" prey} \end{cases}, \qquad Q^{r,l}_{k,y} = \sum_u Q^{r,u}_{k,y} \chi^{r,u,l}, \qquad \tilde{Q}^{r,l}_{k,y} = \frac{Q^{r,l}_{k,y}}{\sum_{k'} Q^{r,l}_{k',y}}\]
Predicted vs. Bioenergetic Daily Ration (\(\hat{\Omega}^{r,u}_y\), fitted in likelihood \(L_5\)): \[\hat{\Omega}^{r,u}_y = \frac{\sum_k Q^{r,u}_{k,y}}{365 \, N_{r,u,y} e^{-Z_{r,u,y}/2}}, \qquad L_5 = \sum_{r,u} \frac{\left(\Omega^{r,u} - \bar{\hat{\Omega}}^{r,u}\right)^2}{2\sigma_d^2}\] where \(\Omega^{r,u} = \frac{1}{365}\frac{K^r}{A^r}(w^{r,u})^{d^r}(w^{r,\infty})^{d^r - 1}\) is the Essington et al. (2001) bioenergetic daily ration!

Unified Equilibrium-Normalized Parameterization of Seven Functional Responses (Table 1, p. 79): To compare prey-dependent and predator-dependent functional responses on an equal footing, Kinzey and Punt (2009, Eqs. 15–17 & Table 1) define the predator age-effect \(\theta^{r,u} = 1 + \frac{\omega^r \tilde{\omega}^r}{u + \tilde{\omega}^r}\) and normalize available prey abundance \(\Phi^{r,u}_y\) and competing predator abundance \(\Psi^{k,a}_y\) relative to their unfished equilibrium values in year \(y_P = 1960\): \[\Phi^{r,u}_y = \frac{\sum_{k,a} N_{k,a,y} \gamma^{r,u}_{k,a}}{\sum_{k,a} N_{k,a,y_P} \gamma^{r,u}_{k,a}}, \qquad \Psi^{k,a}_y = \frac{\sum_{r,u} N_{r,u,y} \gamma^{r,u}_{k,a}}{\sum_{r,u} N_{r,u,y_P} \gamma^{r,u}_{k,a}}\] Because \(\Phi^{r,u}_{y_P} = \Psi^{k,a}_{y_P} = 1\) at unfished equilibrium, all seven functional responses for \(\phi^{r,u}_{k,a,y}\) share the exact same unfished baseline \(\phi^{r,u}_{k,a,y_P} = v^r_k \theta^{r,u}\):

Key Empirical Findings (Kinzey and Punt 2009, 89–101):

Dominance of Predator-Dependent Functional Responses (Types V & VII): The two best-fitting functional responses by AIC were Type V (Predator Pre-emption, \(\Delta\text{AIC} = 0\)) and Type VII (Ecosim Foraging Arena, \(\Delta\text{AIC} = 351\)), both of which outperformed standard prey-only Holling Type II (\(\Delta\text{AIC} = 384\)) and Type III (\(\Delta\text{AIC} = 611\)). In Type V, predator interference \(\Psi^{k,a}_y\) multiplicatively dampens per-capita attack rates at low and intermediate prey densities, preventing unrealistic over-depletion when predator stocks are large.
Divergence Between Single-Species and Multispecies Trajectories: The multispecies model estimated that Aleutian pollock spawning biomass declined over \(3\times\) more steeply from 1964 to 2003 than estimated by the single-species model (with non-overlapping 95% confidence bands in the 1960s–1980s, Fig. 9), and estimated age-0 pollock predation mortality \(P_{1,0,y} \approx 5.0\text{ yr}^{-1}\) (only \(\sim 0.5\%\) survival from age 0 to age 1).





2.4.2 Van Kirk et al. (2010): Gulf of Alaska MSASA and Simultaneity vs. Identifiability
Van Kirk et al. (2010) constructed an ADMB-based Multispecies Age-Structured Assessment (MSASA) model for three strongly interacting species in the Gulf of Alaska (1981–2001): walleye pollock (Theragra chalcogramma, ages 1–10+), Pacific cod (Gadus macrocephalus, ages 1–12+), and arrowtooth flounder (Atheresthes stomias, ages 1–15+), fitted to commercial catch, NMFS triennial bottom-trawl survey data, and \(2,704\) predator stomachs from the AFSC REEM database.

Predation Mortality (\(P_{i,a,t}\)) and Beginning-of-Year Approximation: Total mortality is \(Z_{i,a,t} = M^r_{i,a,t} + F_{i,a,t} + P_{i,a,t}\). Because true instantaneous predation mortality \(P^{\text{inst}}_{i,a,t} = \frac{1}{\bar{B}_{i,a,t}}\sum_j \sum_b I_{j,b} \bar{N}_{j,b,t} \frac{\varphi_{i,a,j,b,t}}{\varphi_{j,b,t}}\) is implicitly recursive in \(\bar{N}_{i,a,t}\) and \(\bar{B}_{i,a,t}\), MSASA uses the explicit beginning-of-year abundance approximation (Van Kirk et al. 2010, Eqs. 1–6): \[P_{i,a,t} = \frac{1}{B_{i,a,t}} \sum_{j} \sum_{b} I_{j,b} \, N_{j,b,t} \, \frac{\varphi_{i,a,j,b,t}}{\varphi_{j,b,t}}\] where \(I_{j,b}\) (\(\text{kg} \cdot \text{yr}^{-1}\)) is the annual predator ration derived from Essington et al. (2001) / Aydin et al. (2005) von Bertalanffy bioenergetics, and available prey biomass is: \[\varphi_{i,a,j,b,t} = \nu_{i,a,j,b} \, B_{i,a,t}, \qquad \varphi_{j,b,t} = B_{\text{oth}} + \sum_{i} \sum_{a} \nu_{i,a,j,b,t} \, B_{i,a,t}\] with constant non-modeled prey biomass \(B_{\text{oth}} = e^{15}\) (\(\nu_{\text{oth}} \equiv 1\)) and Andersen–Ursin suitability: \[\nu_{i,a,j,b} = \rho_{i,j} \, g_{i,a,j,b}, \qquad g_{i,a,j,b} = \exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2\sigma_j^2}\left(\ln\frac{w_{j,b}}{w_{i,a}} - \eta_j\right)^2\right]\]
Joint Objective Function and \(\sqrt{n}\)-Weighted Stomach Least Squares: Unlike SMS (which uses a Dirichlet stomach likelihood), MSASA combines lognormal total catch and survey biomass, multinomial catch-at-age and survey-at-age/length (with fixed effective sample size \(w = 100\)), and a weighted least-squares (normal) objective function on stomach content weight proportions (Van Kirk et al. 2010, Table 4, p. 1139): \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{stom}} = \sum_{p=1}^{3} w_{\text{stom}, p} \sum_{i,a,j,b,t \in p} \left[ \left(\frac{\varphi_{i,a,j,b,t}}{\varphi_{j,b,t}} + 0.0001\right) - \left(\frac{\hat{\varphi}_{i,a,j,b,t}}{\hat{\varphi}_{j,b,t}} + 0.0001\right) \right]^2\] where stomach proportions are pooled into three 7-year blocks (\(p \in \{1981\text{--}1987,\, 1988\text{--}1994,\, 1995\text{--}2001\}\)) with weights set to the square root of predator stomach sample sizes (\(w_{\text{stom}} = \{11, 26, 44\}\)).
Key Lessons on Parameter Estimability (Van Kirk et al. 2010, 1140–45):

Temporal Pooling of Stomach Data is Essential for Convergence: Attempting to fit unpooled annual stomach proportions failed to converge in ADMB, and pooling all 21 years into a single time-invariant average (M1) produced a singular Hessian unless stomach weights were inflated so high that catch and survey fits degraded. Dividing diets into 7-year regime blocks (M2–M4) with time-varying species preference \(\rho_{i,j}\) (M3, \(\text{AIC} = 2121.68\)) and size preference \(\eta_j, \sigma_j\) (M4, \(\text{AIC} = 2050.65\)) achieved positive-definite Hessians and captured the tripling of arrowtooth flounder predation on age-1 pollock.
Confounding of Survey Catchability (\(Q_i\)) and Residual Mortality (\(M^r_i\)) with \(P_{i,a,t}\): When Van Kirk et al. attempted to estimate survey catchability \(Q_i\) or residual natural mortality \(M^r_i\) freely alongside predation mortality \(P_{i,a,t}\), ADMB pushed prey abundance upward, drove \(Q_i \to 0\), or counter-intuitively increased \(M^r_i\) to absorb the extra older cohorts generated by high juvenile recruitment. Thus, \(Q_i\) and \(M^r_i\) had to be fixed externally.





2.4.3 Curti et al. (2013): Georges Bank MSCAA, Ecosystem Biomass Closure, and Monte Carlo Error Propagation
Curti et al. (2013) developed an ADMB MSCAA model for Georges Bank (1978–2007) covering Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua), silver hake (Merluccius bilinearis), and Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus), introducing three important methodological refinements:

Sparre (1980) Stationary Total Ecosystem Biomass Closure: Instead of assuming a constant biomass of “other food” \(B_{\text{other}}\), Curti et al. (2013, Eqs. 6–10) followed Sparre (1980) and Tsou and Collie (2001) in assuming a stationary total ecosystem biomass \(\text{EB} = 15 \times 10^6\text{ metric tons}\) (and tested \(\text{EB} = 7.34 \times 10^6\text{ t}\) from Rochet et al. (2011) in a sensitivity analysis), so that non-modeled “other food” varies dynamically each year as the complement of modeled fish biomass: \[B_{\text{other}, t} = \text{EB} - \sum_{i} \sum_{a} B_{i,a,t}\] Suitabilities \(v_{i,a,j,b,t} = \rho_{i,j} g_{i,a,j,b,t}\) (with \(v_{\text{other}} = \rho_{\text{other}} g_{\text{other}} = 1\)) are normalized across all prey categories for each predator \((j, b)\): \[\tilde{v}_{i,a,j,b,t} = \frac{v_{i,a,j,b,t}}{\sum_{k}\sum_{c} v_{k,c,j,b,t} + v_{\text{other}}}, \qquad \phi_{i,a,j,b,t} = \tilde{v}_{i,a,j,b,t} B_{i,a,t}, \qquad \phi_{j,b,t} = \tilde{v}_{\text{other}} B_{\text{other}, t} + \sum_{k,c} \phi_{k,c,j,b,t}\] and predation mortality is driven by age-specific consumption-to-biomass ratios \((CB)_{j,b}\): \[M2_{i,a,t} \approx \frac{1}{N_{i,a,t} W_{i,a,t}} \sum_{j} \sum_{b} (CB)_{j,b} \, B_{j,b,t} \, \frac{\phi_{i,a,j,b,t}}{\phi_{j,b,t}}\] Crucial Scaling Invariance Result (Curti et al. 2013, 478): Halving assumed total ecosystem biomass \(\text{EB}\) from \(15\text{ Mt}\) to \(7.34\text{ Mt}\) changed estimated recruitment, abundance, and \(M2_{i,a,t}\) by less than \(3.5\%\) (\(0.53\%\), \(0.59\%\), and \(3.49\%\) maximum differences, respectively!), because the estimated vulnerability parameters \(\rho_{i,j}\) (defined relative to \(\rho_{\text{other}} = 1\)) automatically scaled down by \(51\text{--}53\%\) to preserve the observed diet proportions \(\phi_{i,a,j,b,t}/\phi_{j,b,t}\)!
Empirical Pre-Estimation of Size Preference \((\eta_{i,j}, \sigma_{i,j})\) vs. Internal Estimation of \(\ln(\rho_{i,j})\): Because NEFSC Food Web Dynamics stomach records routinely measure predator length and prey species mass, but only a subset (\(1,900\) records) measured individual prey lengths, Curti et al. found that attempting to estimate \((\eta_{i,j}, \sigma_{i,j})\) inside the integrated model caused severe parameter confounding. They therefore computed \(\eta_{i,j}\) and \(\sigma_{i,j}\) externally from the \(1,900\) paired predator-prey weight records (Table 5, p. 477) and estimated only the log species-preference coefficients \(\ln(\rho_{i,j})\) inside ADMB against 5-year-binned multinomial food-habits proportions weighted by McAllister–Ianelli effective sample sizes (McAllister and Ianelli 1997).
Regularizing Penalty Functions (Curti et al. 2013, Table 3, p. 474): To prevent biologically unrealistic boundary solutions during optimization and Monte Carlo runs, Curti et al. added three smooth quadratic penalties to the negative log-likelihood:

Initial Cohort Decay Penalty (\(Yp_i\)): Penalizes deviations of first-year abundances \(N_{i,a,1}\) from exponential decay \(\text{Yr1}_{i,a,1} = N_{i,a-1,1} e^{-\bar{Z}_{i,a-1}}\): \[Yp_i = \sum_{a > 1} \left(N_{i,a,1} - \text{Yr1}_{i,a,1}\right)^2\]
Log-Recruitment CV Threshold Penalty (\(Rp_i\)): Prevents the coefficient of variation of log-recruitment from exceeding species thresholds \(\text{Rth}_i \in \{1.0, 0.7, 0.4\}\): \[Rp_i = 0.01 \left[\text{CV}(\ln N_{i,1,t}) - \text{Rth}_i\right]^2 \cdot \mathbb{I}\!\left(\text{CV}(\ln N_{i,1,t}) > \text{Rth}_i\right)\]
Minimum Age-Specific Biomass Threshold Penalty (\(Bp_i\)): Prevents any cohort biomass \(B_{i,a,t}\) from collapsing below \(\text{Bth}_i = 10\text{ kg}\) during trial steps: \[Bp_i = 0.01 \sum_{a,t} \left(B_{i,a,t} - \text{Bth}_i\right)^2 \cdot \mathbb{I}\!\left(B_{i,a,t} < \text{Bth}_i\right)\]

Monte Carlo Error-Propagation Findings (Curti et al. 2013, 474–82, Figs. 4–7): Running \(400\text{--}500\) Monte Carlo replicates across progressively higher observation error levels in commercial catch (\(\sigma_{\text{TC}} \in \{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8\}\), \(N_{\text{eff,CP}} \in \{1000, 500, 75, 40, 20\}\)), survey indices (\(\sigma_{\text{TS}} \in \{0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8\}\), \(N_{\text{eff,SP}} \in \{1000, 200, 100, 60\}\)), and predator diets (\(N_{\text{eff,FH}} \in \{2500, 500, 100, 50, 10\}\)) revealed a clear separation of information sources:

Fishing mortality \(F_{i,t}\) is most sensitive to measurement error in commercial catches.
Recruitment \(N_{i,1,t}\) and predation mortality \(M2_{i,a,t}\) are most sensitive to measurement error in trawl survey indices (breaking down when survey lognormal \(\sigma_{\text{TS}} \ge 0.6\)).
Robustness to Noisy Diet Data: Across all parameters, increasing noise in predator stomach contents (even down to an effective sample size of \(N_{\text{eff,FH}} = 10\) per 5-year block) had the smallest impact on recruitment, \(F\), and \(M2\) precision, because the temporal trajectory of \(M2_{i,a,t}\) is primarily driven by predator and prey abundance trajectories anchored by the catch and survey datasets!





2.4.4 Alternative Functional Responses in MSCAA and Hydra
Whereas SMS uses the fixed-ration Andersen–Ursin equation (which corresponds to a Holling Type II functional response in the limit where total consumption rate \(R_{A,a}\) is held constant by adjusting “other food”), Kinzey and Punt (2009) and Gaichas et al. (Hydra) formulated MSCAA to allow explicit comparison of alternative functional response forms for the per-predator consumption rate \(I_{i,a,j,b,t}\) of prey \((i, a)\) by predator \((j, b)\):
Let \(\tilde{B}_{i,a,j,b,t} = S_{i,a,j,b} \, \bar{N}_{i,a,t} \, w_{i,a,t}\) be the suitable prey biomass of \((i, a)\) for predator \((j, b)\), and let \(\Phi_{j,b,t} = \sum_{k,c} \tilde{B}_{k,c,j,b,t} + S_{\text{OF},j,b} B_{\text{OF}}\) be total suitable food.

Holling Type I (Linear / Lotka-Volterra): \[M2_{i,a,t} = \sum_{j,b} \alpha_{j,b} \, S_{i,a,j,b} \, \bar{N}_{j,b,t}\]
Holling Type II (Hyperbolic Satiation / Standard Andersen-Ursin-SMS): \[M2_{i,a,t} = \sum_{j,b} \frac{R_{j,b,t} \, \bar{N}_{j,b,t} \, S_{i,a,j,b}}{\Phi_{j,b,t} + H_{j,b}}\] (Note: when \(H_{j,b} = 0\) and \(S_{\text{OF},j,b} B_{\text{OF}} > 0\), this reduces identically to the SMS equation).
Holling Type III (Sigmoid / Prey-Switching with Exponent \(\theta_{j} > 1\)): \[M2_{i,a,t} = \sum_{j,b} \frac{R_{j,b,t} \, \bar{N}_{j,b,t} \, S_{i,a,j,b} \, \left(\bar{N}_{i,a,t} w_{i,a,t}\right)^{\theta_j - 1}}{\sum_{k,c} S_{k,c,j,b} \left(\bar{N}_{k,c,t} w_{k,c,t}\right)^{\theta_j} + \left(S_{\text{OF},j,b} B_{\text{OF}}\right)^{\theta_j}}\] When \(\theta_j = 2\), rare prey experience disproportionately low predation mortality (\(M2_{i,a,t} \to 0\) as \(B_{i,a,t} \to 0\)), providing an automatic stabilizing refuge at low stock size.
Predator Interference & Pre-emption (Beddington–DeAngelis / Crowley–Martin): Adds a predator-abundance interference term \(\gamma_{j} \bar{N}_{j,b,t}\) (additively as in Type IV or multiplicatively as in Type V of Kinzey and Punt (2009)) to the denominator of the functional response: \[M2_{i,a,t} = \sum_{j,b} \frac{R_{j,b,t} \, \bar{N}_{j,b,t} \, S_{i,a,j,b}}{\Phi_{j,b,t} + H_{j,b}\left(1 + \gamma_j \bar{N}_{j,b,t}\right)}\] This dampens top-down control when predator abundance spikes, mimicking the behavioral foraging-arena limitation of Ecosim (Walters et al. 1997).



2.4.5 Simulation-Estimation Findings (Trijoulet et al. 2019)
Using a self-test and cross-test simulation framework in the TMB-based multispecies model ms-keyrun / MSCAA, Trijoulet et al. (2019) demonstrated that:

Ignoring trophic interactions (fitting single-species SCAA with constant \(M\) to data generated from a multispecies food web) produces severe, systematic biases in SSB (\(>30\%\)), recruitment (\(>50\%\)), and \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) reference points for both forage fish and cannibalistic predators.
Even when diet composition data are noisy (effective sample size \(N_{\text{stom}} = 20\text{--}50\)), MSCAA models accurately recover the temporal trajectory of \(M2_{i,a,t}\) and eliminate the retrospective bias seen in constant-\(M\) single-species assessments.
