text:
2.5 Climate-Enhanced Multispecies Stock Assessment (CEATTLE / Rceattle)
Developed by Kirstin Holsman, Jim Ianelli, Kerim Aydin, André Punt, Grant Adams, and colleagues at NOAA AFSC and the University of Washington (Holsman et al. 2016; Adams et al. 2022; ICES 2021, 2023), CEATTLE (Climate-Enhanced, Age-based model with Temperature-specific Trophic Linkages and Energetics) and its open-source TMB/R package Rceattle represent the state-of-the-art in integrating temperature-dependent growth, Wisconsin bioenergetics, and multispecies harvest control rules into an age-structured statistical stock assessment.
Originally built in ADMB for the Eastern Bering Sea complex—walleye pollock (Gadus chalcogrammus, ages 1–12), Pacific cod (Gadus macrocephalus, ages 1–12), and arrowtooth flounder (Atheresthes stomias, ages 1–21, sex-structured)—and subsequently ported to TMB (Rceattle) and expanded to the Gulf of Alaska (adding Pacific halibut Hippoglossus stenolepis; Adams et al. (2022)), California Current, and Baltic Sea, CEATTLE is used operationally by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council (NPFMC).

2.5.1 Temperature-Dependent Generalized von Bertalanffy Growth (Holsman et al. 2016)
Unlike standard age-structured models that treat weight-at-age \(W_{ij,y}\) solely as an empirical look-up table, Holsman et al. (2016, Eqs. 1–2 & Table 1 Eqs. T1.10a–c, pp. 12–14, 50) derived a temperature-dependent generalized von Bertalanffy growth function (VBGF) based on Essington et al. (2001) and Holsman and Aydin (2015), fitted to \(21,388\) pollock, \(14,362\) Pacific cod, and \(772\) arrowtooth flounder otolith weight-at-age records:
\[W_{ij,y} = W_{\infty, iy} \left(1 - \exp\!\left(-K_i \left(1 - d_{i,y}\right)\left(j - t_{0,i}\right)\right)\right)^{\frac{1}{1 - d_{i,y}}} e^{\varepsilon}, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \sigma_{d,i}^2\right)\]
where:

\(W_{\infty, iy} = \left(\frac{H_i}{K_i}\right)^{\frac{1}{1 - d_{i,y}}}\) is the time-varying asymptotic body mass of species \(i\) in year \(y\), determined by the bioenergetic assimilation constant \(H_i\) (\(\text{kg}\cdot\text{kg}^{-d}\cdot\text{yr}^{-1}\); e.g., \(16.34\) for pollock, \(9.30\) for cod) and catabolic energy loss constant \(K_i\) (\(\text{kg}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}\cdot\text{yr}^{-1}\); \(0.22\) for pollock, \(0.45\) for cod; Table 3, p. 54),
\(d_{i,y}\) is the realized allometric slope of consumption, which varies annually as an exponential-linear function of bottom temperature \(T_y\) (\(^\circ\text{C}\)): \[d_{i,y} = \exp\!\left(\alpha_{d,i,y} + \alpha 0_{d,i} + \beta_{d,i} T_y\right)\] allowing both the growth rate and asymptotic weight \(W_{\infty, iy}\) to respond dynamically to historical and IPCC-projected bottom temperatures!
For sexually dimorphic species (arrowtooth flounder, where males have higher natural mortality \(M_{\text{male}} = 0.35\) vs. \(M_{\text{fem}} = 0.20\) and smaller asymptotic size), sex-specific weights \(W^{\text{fem}}_{ij,y}, W^{\text{male}}_{ij,y}\) and residual mortalities are combined using the surviving female cohort proportion (Holsman et al. 2016, Eqs. T1.18–T1.21, p. 51): \[\omega_{ij} = \frac{e^{-j M_{\text{fem}}}}{e^{-j M_{\text{fem}}} + e^{-j M_{\text{male}}}}, \qquad W_{ij,y} = \omega_{ij} W^{\text{fem}}_{ij,y} + (1 - \omega_{ij}) W^{\text{male}}_{ij,y}\]



2.5.2 Wisconsin Bioenergetics Consumption and Thermal Scaling (\(f(T_y)_p\))
In CEATTLE, the individual specific annual ration \(\delta_{pa,y}\) (\(\text{kg prey} \cdot \text{kg predator}^{-1} \cdot \text{yr}^{-1}\)) of predator species \(p\), age \(a\) in year \(y\) is modeled via the Wisconsin Bioenergetics allometric equation (Holsman et al. 2016, Table 2, Eqs. T2.4–T2.5, p. 52; Adams et al. 2022, Eqs. 10–11):
\[\delta_{pa,y} = \hat{\varphi}_p \, \alpha_\delta \, W_{pa,y}^{(1 + \beta_\delta)} \, f(T_y)_p\]
where:

\(\hat{\varphi}_p\) is the annual relative foraging rate (\(\text{d}\cdot\text{yr}^{-1}\) scalar),
\(\alpha_\delta\) and \(\beta_\delta < 0\) are the intercept and allometric slope of maximum specific consumption (\(\beta_\delta = -0.460\) for pollock, \(-0.122\) for cod, \(-0.245\) for arrowtooth flounder; Table 3, p. 53),
\(f(T_y)_p\) is the Kitchell et al. (1977) dome-shaped temperature scaling algorithm: \[f(T_y)_p = V^X \exp\!\left(X (1 - V)\right)\] with: \[V = \frac{T^{\text{cm}}_p - T_y}{T^{\text{cm}}_p - T^{\text{co}}_p}, \qquad X = \frac{Z^2 \left(1 + \left(1 + 40/Y\right)^{0.5}\right)^2}{400}\] \[Z = \ln(Q^c_p)\left(T^{\text{cm}}_p - T^{\text{co}}_p\right), \qquad Y = \ln(Q^c_p)\left(T^{\text{cm}}_p - T^{\text{co}}_p + 2\right)\] where \(T^{\text{co}}_p\) is the physiological optimum consumption temperature (\(10.0^\circ\text{C}\) for pollock, \(13.7^\circ\text{C}\) for cod, \(19.6^\circ\text{C}\) for arrowtooth), \(T^{\text{cm}}_p\) is the maximum lethal physiological temperature (\(15.0^\circ\text{C}\), \(21.0^\circ\text{C}\), \(34.13^\circ\text{C}\)), and \(Q^c_p\) is the \(Q_{10}\) thermal slope (\(2.60, 2.41, 2.18\)). (Rceattle also supports the Thornton and Lessem (1978) two-logistic thermal curve and energy-density caloric scaling \(\mathcal{E}_{\text{pred}} / \sum \hat{W} \mathcal{E}_{\text{prey}}\)).



2.5.3 Predation Mortality (\(M2_{ij,y}\)) and Analytical/Iterative Suitability (\(\bar{S}_{paij}\))
Following Jurado-Molina et al. (2005), CEATTLE expresses predation mortality \(M2_{ij,y}\) on prey species \(i\), age \(j\) in year \(y\) as a Holling Type II functional response where suitability \(\bar{S}_{paij} \in [0, 1]\) of modeled prey \((i, j)\) and suitability \(1 - \sum_{ij} \bar{S}_{paij}\) of “other prey” \(B^{\text{other}}_p\) sum to unity (Holsman et al. 2016, Table 2, Eqs. T2.1–T2.3, p. 52):
\[M2_{ij,y} = \sum_{p} \sum_{a} \left( \frac{N_{pa,y} \, \delta_{pa,y} \, \bar{S}_{paij}}{\sum_{i,j} \left(\bar{S}_{paij} B_{ij,y}\right) + B^{\text{other}}_p \left(1 - \sum_{i,j} \bar{S}_{paij}\right)} \right)\]
Instead of adding thousands of noisy diet cells to the likelihood, Holsman et al. (2016) and Adams et al. (2022) calculate \(\bar{S}_{paij}\) analytically from observed gravimetric stomach proportions \(U_{paij,y}\) (converted from length-based stomach samples to age-based proportions using annual empirical age-length transition matrices \(\text{ALK}_y\)) and model-estimated biomasses \(B_{ij,y}\):
\[\bar{S}_{paij} = \frac{1}{n_y} \sum_{y} \left( \frac{\dfrac{\bar{U}_{paij}}{B_{ij,y}}}{\sum_{i,j} \left(\dfrac{\bar{U}_{paij}}{B_{ij,y}}\right) + \dfrac{1 - \sum_{i,j} \bar{U}_{paij}}{B^{\text{other}}_p}} \right)\]
In Rceattle (Adams et al. 2022, sec. 2.4, p. 4), the single-species assessment models are first optimized (tuning McAllister–Ianelli effective sample sizes for age/length compositions; McAllister and Ianelli (1997)), and then the multispecies model is iteratively re-optimized, updating \(\bar{S}_{paij}\) at each outer step until convergence (which occurs in 3 iterations).


2.5.4 Multispecies Biological Reference Points (MBRPs) and Harvest Control Rules (Holsman et al. 2016)
A major contribution of Holsman et al. (2016, sec. 2.3 & Table 5, pp. 15–20, 57) is the rigorous mathematical formalization of 12 Multispecies Biological Reference Point (MBRP) harvest scenarios under NPFMC Tier 3 control rules (where target Acceptable Biological Catch proxy biomass is \(\overline{\text{SSB}}_{F,i} = 0.40 \, \overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,i}\) and the minimum MSY biomass limit is \(B_{\text{MSY}, i} = 0.35 \, \overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,i}\)):

Non-Uniqueness of “Unfished Biomass” (\(\overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,i}\)) and Fishing-Order Dependence (Scenarios 1.1–1.4):

Under Scenario 1.1, \(\overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,i}\) is defined by setting \(F_i = 0\) for all species simultaneously: \[\overline{\text{SSB}}_{F,i} = 0.40 \, \overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,i} \Big|_{F_1 = F_2 = F_3 = 0}\]
Under Scenarios 1.3 & 1.4, \(\overline{\text{SSB}}'_{0,1}\) for prey (pollock) is defined conditionally on predators (cod and arrowtooth) being fished at their target \(F^*_{\text{ABC}, 2}, F^*_{\text{ABC}, 3}\): \[\overline{\text{SSB}}'_{0,1} = \left(\overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,1} \;\middle|\; F_1 = 0,\, \overline{\text{SSB}}_{F,2},\, \overline{\text{SSB}}_{F,3}\right)\]
Mathematical Insight: When predators are unfished (\(F_2 = F_3 = 0\)), predator biomass expands and inflicts massive \(M2_{1,a}\) on juvenile pollock (plus intense pollock cannibalism, which triggers over-compensatory damped oscillations in projected SSB; Fig. 10, p. 60). Consequently, simultaneous unfished pollock biomass \(\overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,1}\) can actually be lower than harvested pollock biomass when predators are fished!

Spawning Biomass-Per-Recruit Approach (Scenario 2.1, Eqs. T5.2.1a–b): Solves for \(F_{x,i}\) such that \(\text{SPR}_{F,i} = 0.40 \left(\text{SPR}_{F,i} \mid F_{x,i} = 0\right)\), where: \[\text{SPR}_{F,i} = \frac{1}{R_{i,1}} \sum_{j=1}^{A_i} \rho_{ij} \, \bar{W}_{ij} \, N_{ij} \exp\!\left(-\left(F_{x,i} s^f_{ij} + M1_{ij} + \overline{M2}_{ij}\right)\right)\]
System-Wide Aggregate Biomass Proxies (Scenarios 3.1–3.4, Eqs. T5.3.1–T5.3.4): Finds a system-wide multiplier \(F_{\text{ALL}}\) such that total community female spawning biomass satisfies \(\sum_i \overline{\text{SSB}}_{F,i} = 0.40 \sum_i \overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,i}\), scaling species-specific fishing mortality either by total natural mortality \(F_{x,i} = F_{\text{ALL}} (\bar{M}_i / \sum_k \bar{M}_k)\) or by unfished biomass \(F_{x,i} = F_{\text{ALL}} (\overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,i} / \sum_k \overline{\text{SSB}}_{0,k})\), with (Scenarios 3.2, 3.4) or without (Scenarios 3.1, 3.3) the conservation constraint \(\text{SSB}_{F,i,y} \ge 0.35 \, \text{SSB}_{0,i}\).
Simplex Optimization of Individual vs. Aggregate MSY (Scenarios 4.1–4.3, Eqs. T5.4.1–T5.4.3): Uses 8 iterations of Nelder–Mead simplex optimization to find \(\mathbf{F}_x = (F_{x,1}, F_{x,2}, F_{x,3})\) maximizing either individual species yield \(\max(\overline{\text{ABC}}_{x,i} \mid F_{x,i})\) (Scenario 4.1) or total combined community yield \(\max\left(\sum_i \overline{\text{ABC}}_{x,i} \mid \mathbf{F}_x\right)\) without (Scenario 4.2) or with (Scenario 4.3) the minimum biomass threshold \(\text{SSB}_{F,i,y} \ge 0.35 \, \text{SSB}_{0,i}\):

Predator Eradication Paradox: Unconstrained maximization of aggregate yield (Scenario 4.2) achieved \(3.2\text{ million t}\) by fishing Pacific cod and arrowtooth flounder to extinction in order to eliminate predation on pollock (since annual predation on juvenile pollock is \(2\text{--}5\times\) the annual fishery harvest!). Imposing the biodiversity constraint \(\text{SSB}_{F,i} \ge 0.35 \, \text{SSB}_{0,i}\) (Scenario 4.3) prevented predator collapse and demonstrated that MBRPs are not inherently more or less conservative than single-species BRPs; rather, their conservatism depends on whether single-species or aggregate targets are used and whether minimum biomass thresholds are enforced.





2.5.5 Gulf of Alaska Rceattle Ensemble and Hybrid “Predators-as-Fleets” Scaling (Adams et al. 2022)
In adapting Rceattle (implemented in TMB with recruitment and initial cohort deviations treated as Laplace-integrated random effects) to the Gulf of Alaska for pollock, Pacific cod, arrowtooth flounder, and Pacific halibut (Hippoglossus stenolepis), Adams et al. (2022) addressed a universal practical problem in multispecies assessment: how to include an important apex predator (Pacific halibut) whose stock assessment is conducted externally on a coastwide spatial scale (by the International Pacific Halibut Commission, IPHC, using a 4-model Stock Synthesis ensemble).
Adams et al. (2022) evaluated 16 model configurations across 3 time-series durations (\(1977\text{--}2018\), \(1993\text{--}2018\), \(1996\text{--}2018\)) grouped into 4 ensemble averages:

Ensemble Avg 1 (Single-Species) vs. Ensemble Avg 2 (3-Species MS without Halibut): Including predation by arrowtooth flounder (the dominant predator in the GOA), cod, and pollock increased average estimated pollock total biomass by \(2.03\text{--}2.21\times\) and pollock SSB by \(1.70\text{--}1.84\times\) relative to single-species models.
Ensemble Avg 3 (Fixed External Predator Abundance): Inputs sex-specific mid-year halibut numbers-at-age directly from each of the 4 IPHC Stock Synthesis ensemble models (scaled by the proportion of age-5+ halibut survey biomass in IPHC Regulatory Areas 3A & 3B) without fitting halibut data in the Rceattle likelihood.
Ensemble Avg 4 (Relative Predator Survey Index with Estimated Scaling \(\tilde{q}_i\)): Inputs relative halibut abundance-at-age from the IPHC setline survey multiplied by a freely estimated scaling parameter \(\tilde{q}_{\text{halibut}}\).

Critical Identifiability Warning (Adams et al. 2022, sec. 3.1 & 4.2, pp. 6, 11): When \(\tilde{q}_{\text{halibut}}\) was freely estimated inside the multispecies likelihood (Models 11 & 16), the optimizer drove \(\tilde{q}_{\text{halibut}} \to 0\) (\(0.0021\text{--}0.0025\) with large standard errors), shrinking halibut predation mortality to zero and reproducing the 3-species no-halibut model! Even though Models 11 & 16 achieved a slightly lower AIC on the pollock/cod/arrowtooth survey and catch data by removing the external constraint of halibut predation, doing so was biologically spurious—a textbook demonstration of why predator abundance indices in “predators-as-fleets” extensions cannot have unanchored scaling parameters \(\tilde{q}_i\) without informative priors on predator scale.

title: 3  Age-Length and Length-Structured Assessment Models (Gadget/gadget3, SS3, MULTIFAN-CL, LeMans/LeMaRns, CSMS/CSM)
text:
3.1 Why Track Length in Addition to (or Instead of) Age?
In marine ecosystems, nearly every ecological and fishery interaction—gape-limited predation, trawl mesh selection, gillnet dome-shaped selectivity, metabolic rate, and fecundity—is a direct physical function of body size (length \(L\) or weight \(W\)) rather than chronological age \(a\) (Stefánsson and Pálsson 1998; Punt et al. 2016). Purely age-structured models (MSVPA, SMS, CEATTLE) suffer from three structural limitations when size-dependent processes are strong:
crumbs: 3  Age-Length and Length-Structured Assessment Models (`Gadget`/`gadget3`, `SS3`, `MULTIFAN-CL`, `LeMans`/`LeMaRns`, `CSMS`/`CSM`)

title: 3  Age-Length and Length-Structured Assessment Models (Gadget/gadget3, SS3, MULTIFAN-CL, LeMans/LeMaRns, CSMS/CSM)
text:
Rosa Lee’s Phenomenon (Size-Selective Mortality Within an Age Class): When fishing or predation selectively removes the fastest-growing (or slowest-growing) individuals within an age cohort, the surviving individuals of age \(a\) have a distorted length and weight distribution that cannot be represented by a fixed empirical weight-at-age \(w_{s,a,t}\) (Methot and Wetzel 2013; Begley and Howell 2004).
Consumption-Driven Growth Plasticity: When forage fish collapse, predators grow more slowly in length and lose body condition (weight-at-length). A joint age-length-weight model can track both stunted length growth and starvation-induced weight loss dynamically (Stefánsson and Pálsson 1998).
Direct Observation of Length Frequencies: Measuring fish lengths at sea or port is fast and cheap, whereas reading otolith ages is expensive, prone to reader bias, and unavailable for crustaceans (shrimp, Nephrops, crabs), cephalopods, and many tropical or data-limited stocks (Fournier et al. 1998; Punt et al. 2016).

section: 3.2 Gadget (Gadget2 and gadget3): Statistical Age-Length-Structured Multispecies Framework
text:
3.2 Gadget (Gadget2 and gadget3): Statistical Age-Length-Structured Multispecies Framework

3.2.1 Lineage and Architecture
Gadget (Globally Applicable Area Disaggregated General Ecosystem Toolbox) evolved from two Nordic multispecies research models of the late 1980s and 1990s (Stefánsson and Pálsson 1998; Begley and Howell 2004), synthesized under the EU dst2 project (Stefánsson 2003, 2004; Begley 2004; Begley and Howell 2004):

MULTSPEC (Bogstad et al. 1997, IMR Norway): An area-, age-, and length-structured model of Barents Sea cod, capelin, herring, harp seals, and minke whales.
BORMICON (Boreal Migration and Consumption model; Stefánsson and Pálsson (1997), MRI Iceland): A statistical multi-area age-length assessment model of Icelandic cod, capelin, and northern shrimp (Pandalus borealis) (Taylor and Stefánsson 2004; Taylor et al. 2004, 2007).

Originally written in C++ (Gadget2, Begley (2004)) and optimized via Hooke & Jeeves pattern search, Simulated Annealing, and BFGS, with applications ranging from Icelandic cod–capelin–shrimp interactions (Taylor and Stefánsson 2004; Taylor et al. 2004, 2007) and Mediterranean hake (Bartolino et al. 2011) to Eastern Baltic cod ontogenetic diet shifts (Kulatska et al. 2019), the framework has recently been re-engineered as gadget3 (g3) (Lentz and Elvarsson 2024; ICES 2021), which compiles modular R model definitions (g3a_grow_*, g3a_predate_*, g3l_distribution_*) directly into TMB C++ templates with exact automatic differentiation.


3.2.2 State-Space Tensor (\(N_{s,a,l,r,t}\) and \(W_{s,a,l,r,t}\))
Gadget tracks sub-stocks \(s\) (which may represent species, sex, or immature vs. mature life stages, e.g., immature hake vs. mature hake in Bartolino et al. (2011)) across discrete time steps \(t\) (typically monthly or quarterly, \(\Delta t = 1/12\) or \(1/4\text{ yr}\)), spatial areas \(r\), discrete ages \(a \in \{a_{\min}, \dots, a_{\max}\}\), and discrete length bins \(l \in \{1, \dots, n_L\}\) with bin boundaries \([L_{\min, l}, L_{\max, l})\) and midpoint \(L_l\).
Crucially, in every \((s, a, l, r, t)\) cell, Gadget tracks two coupled state variables (Begley and Howell 2004, 4; Lentz and Elvarsson 2024):

\(N_{s,a,l,r,t}\): The number of individuals in cell \((s, a, l, r)\) at time \(t\).
\(W_{s,a,l,r,t}\): The mean body weight of individuals in cell \((s, a, l, r)\) at time \(t\) (which can either follow a fixed length-weight curve \(W_l = \alpha_s L_l^{\beta_s}\) or vary dynamically in response to food intake and growth).

Within each time step \(t\), biological and fishery processes are executed sequentially in a strict order: \[\text{1. Migration } (\mathbf{M}) \longrightarrow \text{2. Predation \& Fishing } (\mathbf{P}) \longrightarrow \text{3. Somatic Growth \& Maturation } (\mathbf{G}) \longrightarrow \text{4. Ageing } (\mathbf{A}) \longrightarrow \text{5. Spawning \& Recruitment } (\mathbf{R})\]



3.2.3 Somatic Growth and the Beta-Binomial Length-Transition Distribution
In a discrete length-bin model, somatic growth during time step \(\Delta t\) must specify:

The mean length increment \(\Delta L_l\) and mean weight increment \(\Delta W_l\) of fish currently in length bin \(l\), and
The probability distribution \(p(\Delta j \mid l)\) that a fish in length bin \(l\) jumps up by \(\Delta j \in \{0, 1, \dots, \Delta j_{\max}\}\) length bins during \(\Delta t\).


A. Mean Length & Weight Increments (g3a_grow_*)
Gadget provides two classes of growth equations (Begley and Howell 2004, 8–10; Lentz and Elvarsson 2024):

Consumption-Independent von Bertalanffy Growth (g3a_grow_lengthvbsimple / g3a_grow_weightsimple): \[\Delta L_l = \left(L_{\infty, s} - L_l\right)\left(1 - \exp(-\kappa_s \Delta t)\right)\] \[\Delta W_l = \alpha_s \left(L_l + \Delta L_l\right)^{\beta_s} - \alpha_s L_l^{\beta_s}\]
Consumption-Dependent (Two-Way Bioenergetic) Growth (g3a_grow_length_multspec and g3a_grow_weight_weightjones): Let \(\psi_{s,l,r,t} \in [0, 1]\) be the predator’s realized feeding level in length bin \(l\) during time step \(t\) (ratio of actual biomass consumed to maximum possible consumption \(M_{s,l,t}\); see Section 3.2.4), and let \(T_{r,t}\) be ambient temperature.

MULTSPEC Length & Weight Increment (g3a_grow_length_multspec / g3a_grow_weight_multspec): \[\Delta L_l = \Delta t \cdot p_{0,s} \, L_l^{p_{1,s}} \, \psi_{s,l,r,t} \left(p_{2,s} T_{r,t} + p_{3,s}\right)\] \[\Delta W_l = \Delta t \cdot q_{0,s} \, W_{s,a,l}^{q_{1,s}} \left(\psi_{s,l,r,t} - q_{2,s}\right)\left(q_{3,s} T_{r,t} + q_{4,s}\right)\] where \(q_{2,s}\) is the maintenance feeding level below which fish lose weight (\(\Delta W_l < 0\), while \(\Delta L_l \ge 0\) since fish skeletons do not shrink!).
Jones (1976) Bioenergetic Weight Increment (g3a_grow_weight_weightjones, Jones (1976)): \[\Delta W_l = \frac{\Delta t \left( \frac{C_{s,l,t}}{\Delta t} - r_{0,s} W_{s,a,l}^{r_{1,s}} \exp(r_{2,s} T_{r,t}) \right)}{r_{3,s}}\] coupled to length growth via a condition-factor feedback function \(f(\delta W_l)\) that suppresses length growth \(\Delta L_l\) whenever actual body weight \(W_{s,a,l}\) falls below reference weight \(W_{\text{ref}, l} = \alpha_s L_l^{\beta_s}\) (Begley and Howell 2004, 9; Lentz and Elvarsson 2024).




B. The Beta-Binomial Length-Bin Jump Distribution (g3a_grow_impl_bbinom)
Once the mean length increment \(\Delta L_l\) is computed (and normalized by the bin width \(\delta L\) to give mean bin growth \(\mu_l = \Delta L_l / \delta L\)), Gadget distributes growing individuals across integer bin jumps \(\Delta j \in \{0, 1, \dots, n_{\max}\}\) using a Beta-Binomial distribution (Stefánsson and Pálsson 1998; Taylor et al. 2004, Eq. 5; Lentz and Elvarsson 2024):
Given:

\(n_{\max}\): Maximum allowed number of length-bin jumps in a single time step \(\Delta t\),
\(\mu_l = \frac{\Delta L_l}{\delta L} \in [0, n_{\max}]\): Expected number of bin jumps,
\(\beta_s > 0\): Single free dispersion parameter controlling variance in individual growth rates,

define \(\alpha_l\) via the mean constraint \(\mu_l = \frac{n_{\max} \alpha_l}{\alpha_l + \beta_s}\): \[\alpha_l = \frac{\beta_s \, \mu_l}{n_{\max} - \mu_l}\] Then the probability \(G_{l, l + \Delta j} = \Pr(\text{Jump} = \Delta j \mid l)\) of growing by \(\Delta j \in \{0, 1, \dots, n_{\max}\}\) bins in \(\Delta t\) is:
\[G_{l, l + \Delta j} = \binom{n_{\max}}{\Delta j} \frac{\text{B}(\Delta j + \alpha_l,\; n_{\max} - \Delta j + \beta_s)}{\text{B}(\alpha_l, \beta_s)} = \frac{\Gamma(n_{\max} + 1)}{\Gamma(\Delta j + 1)\Gamma(n_{\max} - \Delta j + 1)} \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_l + \beta_s)}{\Gamma(n_{\max} + \alpha_l + \beta_s)} \frac{\Gamma(\Delta j + \alpha_l)\Gamma(n_{\max} - \Delta j + \beta_s)}{\Gamma(\alpha_l)\Gamma(\beta_s)}\]
In gadget3 (Lentz and Elvarsson 2024), this is evaluated efficiently via an exact forward recurrence relation in \(\Delta j\) so that no lgamma calls are needed inside the inner loop, and both cohort numbers \(N_{s,a,l'}\) and cell mean weights \(W_{s,a,l'}\) are updated cleanly via matrix multiplication: \[N_{s,a,l',t+\Delta t} = \sum_{\Delta j = 0}^{n_{\max}} G_{l' - \Delta j, l'} \, N_{s,a,l'-\Delta j, t}, \qquad (NW)_{s,a,l',t+\Delta t} = \sum_{\Delta j = 0}^{n_{\max}} G_{l' - \Delta j, l'} \, N_{s,a,l'-\Delta j, t} \left(W_{s,a,l'-\Delta j, t} + \Delta W_{l'-\Delta j, \Delta j}\right)\]

[!TIP] Why the Beta-Binomial Growth Implementation is a Major Lesson for mizer: With only one extra parameter (\(\beta_s\)) beyond the deterministic growth rate \(\Delta L_l\), g3a_grow_impl_bbinom generates realistic, strictly non-negative, bounded discrete-bin dispersion around the mean growth trajectory, completely eliminating the numerical vs. biological diffusion problem of deterministic first-order PDE schemes while remaining \(C^\infty\)-differentiable in TMB!





3.2.4 Predation, Functional Response, and Overconsumption Protection (g3a_predate)
In Gadget, both commercial/survey fishing fleets and biological predators are unified under a single mathematical abstraction (g3a_predate in Lentz and Elvarsson (2024)).
For a biological predator \(p\) in length group \(L\) preying on prey stock \(i\) in length group \(l\) (Begley and Howell 2004, 13–15; Taylor and Stefánsson 2004, Eqs. 7–11; Lentz and Elvarsson 2024):

Predator-Prey Length Suitability (\(S_{p,i}(L, l)\)): Gadget offers several parametric suitability functions of predator length \(L\) and prey length \(l\), most commonly:

Andersen & Ursin Log-Ratio Suitability (g3_suitability_andersen): \[S_{p,i}(L, l) = p_0 + p_2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{\left(\ln\frac{L}{l} - p_1\right)^2}{p_3 \text{ (or } p_4\text{)}}\right)\]
Richards / Asymmetric Logistic Suitability (g3_suitability_richards): \[S_{p,i}(L, l) = \left(\frac{p_3}{1 + \exp(-p_0 - p_1 l - p_2 L)}\right)^{1/p_4}\]

Maximum Possible Consumption (\(M_{p,L,t}\), g3a_predate_maxconsumption): The maximum biomass a single predator of length \(L\) can consume in time step \(\Delta t\) at temperature \(T_t\) is: \[M_{p,L,t} = \Delta t \cdot m_{0,p} \, L^{m_{1,p}} \exp\!\left(m_{2,p} T_t - m_{3,p} T_t^3\right)\]
Desired Consumption and Holling Type II/III Functional Response (g3a_predate_catchability_predator): Let \(B_{i,l,t} = N_{i,l,t} W_{i,l,t}\) be the available prey biomass of \((i, l)\), and let the suitability-weighted prey energy/biomass be: \[E_{p,L,i,l,t} = \left(S_{p,i}(L, l) \, \mathcal{E}_i \, N_{i,l,t} \, W_{i,l,t}\right)^{d_{i}}\] where \(d_i = 1\) yields a Holling Type II functional response and \(d_i > 1\) yields a Holling Type III (prey-switching) functional response. The predator’s feeding level \(\psi_{p,L,t} \in [0, 1]\) is given by the half-saturation parameter \(H_p\): \[\psi_{p,L,t} = \frac{\sum_{i,l} E_{p,L,i,l,t}}{\sum_{i,l} E_{p,L,i,l,t} + H_p \, \Delta t + E_{\text{other}, p}}\] and the total desired consumption \(C^{\text{des}}_{p,L,i,l,t}\) of prey \((i, l)\) by all \(N_{p,L,t}\) predators in length group \(L\) is: \[C^{\text{des}}_{p,L,i,l,t} = N_{p,L,t} \, M_{p,L,t} \, \psi_{p,L,t} \, \frac{E_{p,L,i,l,t}}{\sum_{k,m} E_{p,L,k,m,t} + E_{\text{other}, p}}\]
Differentiable Overconsumption Cap and Understocking Penalty: During optimization, parameter trial values may cause total desired consumption across all predators and fleets \(D_{i,l,t} = \sum_{p,L} C^{\text{des}}_{p,L,i,l,t} + \sum_{f} C^{\text{des}}_{f,i,l,t}\) to exceed the available prey biomass \(B_{i,l,t} = N_{i,l,t} W_{i,l,t}\). In gadget3 (Lentz and Elvarsson 2024), total consumption is smoothly capped at \(95\%\) of available biomass (\(0.95 B_{i,l,t}\)) using a differentiable logistic minimum function (dif_pmin), scaling each predator’s actual consumption down proportionally: \[C^{\text{act}}_{p,L,i,l,t} = C^{\text{des}}_{p,L,i,l,t} \cdot \text{dif\_pmin}\!\left(1,\; \frac{0.95 \, B_{i,l,t}}{D_{i,l,t}}\right)\] Simultaneously, any “unmet demand” (understocking \(U_{i,l,t} = \max(0, D_{i,l,t} - 0.95 B_{i,l,t})\)) adds a smooth quadratic penalty \(\ell_{\text{understock}} = w_U \sum_{i,l,t} U_{i,l,t}^p\) to the objective function, guiding the gradient optimizer away from biologically infeasible regions where prey stocks are driven negative.




3.2.5 Composite Likelihoods and Two-Stage Iterative Reweighting in Gadget
Gadget fits simultaneously to arbitrary combinations of raw, unaggregated observations (Begley and Howell 2004, 18–23; Lentz and Elvarsson 2024):

Survey Abundance Indices (g3l_distribution_surveyindices_log / linear): \[\ell_{\text{index}} = \sum_{t} \left(\ln I_{t} - \left(\alpha + \beta \ln \hat{I}_{t}\right)\right)^2\] where \(\alpha = \ln q\) is log catchability and \(\beta\) is either fixed at \(1\) (linear proportionality) or estimated (hyperstability/hyperdepletion).
Length-Frequency & Age-Length Compositions (g3l_distribution_sumofsquares, multinomial, mvlogistic):

Sum of Squares of Proportions: \(\ell_{\text{SS}} = \sum_{t,a,l} \left(\pi_{t,a,l} - \hat{\pi}_{t,a,l}\right)^2\), where \(\pi_{t,a,l} = N^{\text{obs}}_{t,a,l} / \sum_{a',l'} N^{\text{obs}}_{t,a',l'}\).
Multinomial: \(\ell_{\text{mult}} = 2 \sum_{t} \left[\ln\Gamma(N_t + 1) - \sum_{a,l} \ln\Gamma(N^{\text{obs}}_{t,a,l} + 1) + \sum_{a,l} N^{\text{obs}}_{t,a,l} \ln \hat{\pi}_{t,a,l}\right]\).

Stomach Content Proportions (StomachContent / g3l_distribution_sumofsquares): Compares observed prey species/length weight ratios \(W^{\text{obs}}_{p,L,i,l,t}\) in predator \((p, L)\) stomachs against model-predicted consumption fractions: \[\hat{W}_{p,L,i,l,t} = \frac{C^{\text{act}}_{p,L,i,l,t}}{\sum_{k,m} C^{\text{act}}_{p,L,k,m,t}}\]


Stefánsson’s (1998) Two-Stage Iterative Likelihood Reweighting
Because a typical Gadget model combines \(10\text{--}30\) disparate likelihood components \(\ell_c\) (\(c = 1, \dots, C\)) with different units and sample sizes, Stefánsson and Pálsson (1998), Stefánsson (2003), and Taylor et al. (2004) developed an objective two-stage reweighting procedure (gadget.iterative):

Stage 1 (Independent Component Minima): For each likelihood group \(g\), run an optimization assigning a very high weight to group \(g\) to determine the minimum achievable residual sum of squares \(\ell_g^*\) (representing the intrinsic observation variance \(\hat{\sigma}_g^2 = \ell_g^* / \text{df}_g\) of dataset \(g\) without model-conflict bias).
Stage 2 (Inverse-Variance Weighting): Set the weight \(w_g\) of each likelihood component equal to its inverse estimated variance: \[w_g = \frac{\text{df}_g}{\ell_g^*}\] so that in the final joint optimization \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{tot}} = \sum_{g} w_g \ell_g(\boldsymbol{\theta})\), every well-specified likelihood component has an expected weighted score of \(\approx \text{df}_g\) (chi-square degrees of freedom).





3.2.6 Case Study: Baltic Sea Multispecies Gadget Model and Ontogenetic Diet Shifts (Kulatska et al. 2019)
Kulatska et al. (2019) constructed a quarterly (1974–2013) age-length multispecies Gadget model (using Rgadget and the Marine Fisheries Database MFDB) for the Baltic Sea (ICES Subdivisions 25–32), providing a template for how benthic and pelagic prey functional groups are parameterized in a length-structured assessment:

Dynamic Fish Stocks vs. Constant-Biomass Invertebrate Pools: Eastern Baltic cod (Gadus morhua, split into juvenile substock ages 0–1, \(4\text{--}35\text{ cm}\) and adult substock ages 2–12+, \(10\text{--}120\text{ cm}\) at \(1\text{ cm}\) resolution) is modeled as the active predator on two dynamic pelagic clupeid stocks—Central Baltic herring (Clupea harengus, ages 0–10+, \(3.5\text{--}32\text{ cm}\)) and Baltic sprat (Sprattus sprattus, ages 0–8+, \(3\text{--}17\text{ cm}\))—plus three constant-biomass benthic/invertebrate prey pools: the benthic isopod Saduria entomon (\(0.5\text{--}9\text{ cm}\)), pelagic/hyperbenthic mysids (Mysis mixta, \(0.5\text{--}3\text{ cm}\)), and “other food”.
Empirical Identification of Ontogenetic Predator Size Classes via Bray–Curtis Clustering: Rather than choosing arbitrary predator length bins for the stomach likelihood (StomachContent), Kulatska et al. (2019, sec. 2.3.1, p. 341) applied hierarchical cluster analysis with Bray–Curtis dissimilarity (\(\text{BC} \ge 0.2\) threshold) to \(1974\text{--}2013\) EU/ICES Baltic cod stomach records (Quarters 1 and 4, using only digestion stages 1–2 and excluding stage 0 intact prey to eliminate trawl-net feeding!), identifying five ontogenetic cod diet regimes: \[L_{\text{cod}} \in \big\{[16, 25),\; [25, 35),\; [35, 60),\; [60, 80),\; [80, 112]\text{ cm}\big\}\] reflecting the ontogenetic transition from mysids and Saduria (\(<25\text{ cm}\)) to sprat (\(25\text{--}60\text{ cm}\)) and large herring (\(>60\text{ cm}\)).
Prey-Specific Suitability Functions (\(S(L, l)\)) and Evacuation Ration (\(M_L\)):

Size-Structured Prey (Herring, Sprat, and Saduria entomon): Modeled via the symmetric Andersen–Ursin logarithmic length-ratio suitability curve (Kulatska et al. 2019, Eq. 4, p. 340): \[S_{\text{prey}}(L, l) = p_0 + p_2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{\left(\ln\frac{L}{l} - p_1\right)^2}{p_3}\right)\] yielding optimal prey lengths \(l^* = L e^{-p_1}\) equal to \(19\%\) of cod length for sprat and \(28\%\) of cod length for herring.
Mysids (Mysis mixta): Because mysids span a narrow size range (\(0.5\text{--}3\text{ cm}\)) eaten primarily by juvenile cod, suitability is parameterized as a decreasing exponential function of predator length \(L\) alone: \[S_{\text{mysid}}(L) = \frac{\gamma}{1 + \exp(-\alpha - \beta L)}\]
Maximum Consumption Rate (\(M_L\)): Estimated externally from observed stomach content weights \(S_k\) (including empty stomachs) via the Jones (1978) evacuation rate model, yielding the quarterly allometric ration: \[M_L = \Delta t_{\text{days}} \cdot m_0 \, L^{m_1}, \qquad m_0 = 3.167 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{d}^{-1}\cdot\text{cm}^{-m_1},\quad m_1 = 2.66\]

Diagnosing Regime Shifts and Spatial Mismatch (Kulatska et al. 2019, 343–47): Optimized across 21 likelihood components using Simulated Annealing \(\to\) Hooke & Jeeves \(\to\) BFGS with Stefánsson (2003) / Taylor et al. (2007) iterative inverse-variance reweighting, the model accurately captured both ontogenetic diet shifts and interdecadal clupeid switches during \(1974\text{--}1988\) (Bray–Curtis dissimilarity \(0.08\text{--}0.28\)), but exhibited higher diet residuals in \(2007\text{--}2013\) (\(\text{BC} = 0.24\text{--}0.52\)). Kulatska et al. showed that this residual pattern was diagnostic of two unmodeled physical processes in the recent Baltic regime: (a) expanding bottom hypoxia decimating benthic Saduria entomon biomass, and (b) spatial predator–prey mismatch (Eastern Baltic cod contracting southwestward into ICES SD 25 while sprat and herring shifted northeastward into SD 28–32).

section: 3.3 Single-Species Length-Based & Integrated Assessments as a Methodological Bridge
text:
3.3 Single-Species Length-Based & Integrated Assessments as a Methodological Bridge
Building on classical cohort and yield theory (Beverton and Holt 1956, 1957; Cadima 2003; Lart 2022), single-species integrated assessment models (MULTIFAN-CL (Fournier et al. 1998), Stock Synthesis SS3 (Methot and Wetzel 2013), Reviewed by Maunder and Punt (2013)), size-transition matrix assessments (Punt et al. 2016), and non-equilibrium length-based mixed-effects models (LIME (Rudd and Thorson 2018)) solved several fundamental statistical problems in fitting length-composition data that are directly applicable to size-spectrum models like mizer.

3.3.1 MULTIFAN-CL and Fournier’s Robustified Length-Frequency Likelihood
Developed by David Fournier, John Hampton, and John Sibert (Fournier et al. 1998) for Western and Central Pacific tuna assessments, MULTIFAN-CL was the first large-scale ADMB integrated model to estimate age-structured dynamics directly from length-frequency data.

Length-at-Age Mixture Model: At any time \(t\), the lengths of fish in age class \(a \in \{1, \dots, A\}\) are assumed normally distributed with mean \(\mu_{a,t}\) (following a von Bertalanffy curve with seasonal oscillations and cohort-specific growth deviations) and standard deviation \(\sigma_a\) (scaling linearly with mean length): \[\sigma_a = \sigma_1 \exp\!\left(\lambda_{\sigma} \left(\frac{\mu_a - \mu_1}{\mu_A - \mu_1}\right)\right)\] Crucially, fishery selectivity \(s_{f,a}\) is parameterized as a smooth cubic-spline function of mean length \(\mu_a\) rather than age (length-dependent selectivity), reducing the number of selectivity parameters and linking cohorts across growth variations.
Fournier’s Robustified Normal Likelihood for Length Compositions: Standard multinomial likelihoods \(\sum_l \tilde{P}_l \ln P_l\) are notoriously sensitive to outliers in the tails (a single large fish caught in a bin where \(\hat{P}_l = 10^{-6}\) creates a massive log-likelihood penalty) and overdispersion from schooling (fish of similar sizes school together, so haul length samples have much smaller effective sample size \(\tau_t\) than the number of fish measured). Fournier et al. (1998, Eq. 3.6) derived the robustified normal likelihood for observed length proportions \(\tilde{p}_{f,t,l}\) vs. predicted proportions \(\hat{p}_{f,t,l}\) across \(L\) length bins:
\[\ln L_{\text{MFCL}} = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{f,t} \sum_{l=1}^{L} \ln\!\left(2\pi \left(\xi_{f,t,l} + \frac{0.1}{L}\right)\right) + \sum_{f,t} \sum_{l=1}^{L} \ln\!\left[ \exp\!\left(-\frac{\left(\tilde{p}_{f,t,l} - \hat{p}_{f,t,l}\right)^2}{2\left(\xi_{f,t,l} + \frac{0.1}{L}\right) / \tau_{f,t}}\right) + 0.01 \right]\]
where \(\xi_{f,t,l} = (1 - \tilde{p}_{f,t,l})\tilde{p}_{f,t,l}\), \(\tau_{f,t} = \min(N_{\text{fish}, f, t}, 1000)\) is the effective sample size, \(+ \frac{0.1}{L}\) prevents the variance from vanishing in bins where \(\tilde{p}_{f,t,l} \approx 0\) so empty tail bins do not dominate the variance weight, and \(+ 0.01\) inside the logarithm caps the maximum penalty of any single outlier bin at \(\ln(0.01) \approx -4.605\) (equivalent to a \(3\sigma\) normal residual!).



3.3.2 Stock Synthesis (SS3): Age-Length Kernels and Growth Morphs/Platoons
In Stock Synthesis (Methot and Wetzel 2013, 86–90), population numbers \(N_{t,g,a}\) are tracked by age \(a\) and growth morph/platoon \(g\), and mapped at every time step to discrete population length bins \(l \in \{1, \dots, n_L\}\) via an age-length transition matrix \(\varphi_{l, g, a}\):
\[\varphi_{l, g, a} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{L_{\max, l} - \tilde{L}_{g,a}}{\sigma_{g,a}}\right) - \Phi\!\left(\frac{L_{\min, l} - \tilde{L}_{g,a}}{\sigma_{g,a}}\right)\]
where \(\Phi(\cdot)\) is the standard normal CDF, \(\tilde{L}_{g,a}\) is the mean length at exact mid-season age for morph \(g\), and \(\sigma_{g,a}\) is its standard deviation.

Combined Age- and Length-Specific Selectivity: For fleet \(f\) with age selectivity \(S^{(A)}_{f,a}\) and length selectivity \(S^{(L)}_{f,l}\), the effective survival and catch-at-age are integrated over the length distribution within each age class (Methot and Wetzel 2013, Eq. A.1.24): \[F_{t,f,g,a} = E_{t,f} \, S^{(A)}_{f,a} \sum_{l=1}^{n_L} \varphi_{l,g,a} \, S^{(L)}_{f,l}\]
Capturing Rosa Lee’s Phenomenon via Platoons: To prevent the assumption that the normal length distribution \(\varphi_{l,g,a}\) resets every year regardless of size-selective fishing on the right tail of the cohort, SS3 splits each recruiting cohort into \(3\) or \(5\) growth platoons \(g\) (slow, medium-slow, average, medium-fast, fast growers with initial Gaussian weights). Because fast-growing platoons enter the length-selective fishery earlier, they are depleted faster (\(F_{t,f,\text{fast},a} > F_{t,f,\text{slow},a}\)), naturally shifting the surviving cohort’s mean length downward!



3.3.3 Pure Size-Structured Assessments and Size-Transition Matrices (\(\mathbf{X}_{l,l'}\))
In their comprehensive review of size-structured stock assessments (used worldwide for lobsters, crabs, abalone, scallops, prawns, and tropical finfish), Punt et al. (2016) formalized the general discrete-time, discrete-size population equation:
\[\mathbf{N}_{t+1} = \mathbf{X}_t \, \mathbf{S}_t \, \mathbf{N}_t + \mathbf{R}_{t+1}\]
where:

\(\mathbf{N}_t = (N_{1,t}, N_{2,t}, \dots, N_{n_L,t})^\top\) is the vector of numbers across \(n_L\) size bins,
\(\mathbf{S}_t = \text{diag}\!\left(\exp(-Z_{1,t}), \dots, \exp(-Z_{n_L,t})\right)\) is the diagonal survival matrix during time step \(t\),
\(\mathbf{X}_t\) is the lower-triangular (since animals do not shrink in length) \(n_L \times n_L\) Size-Transition Matrix, where \(X_{l', l}\) is the probability that an individual in size bin \(l\) grows into size bin \(l' \ge l\) at the end of the time step (\(\sum_{l' \ge l} X_{l', l} = 1\)).


Parameterizing the Size-Transition Matrix \(\mathbf{X}_{l', l}\) (Punt et al. 2016, Eqs. 2–5)
Instead of estimating \(n_L(n_L-1)/2\) free transition probabilities, size-structured assessments model the continuous growth increment \(\Delta L = L_{t+1} - L_l \ge 0\) of an individual at midpoint \(L_l\) using a Gamma distribution (or truncated Normal / Log-normal distribution) with mean increment \(\bar{\Delta}_l = (L_\infty - L_l)(1 - e^{-k \Delta t})\) and variance \(\sigma^2_{\Delta, l} = \beta_{\Delta} \bar{\Delta}_l\) (so shape \(\alpha_l = \bar{\Delta}_l / \beta_{\Delta}\) and scale \(\beta_{\Delta}\)):
\[X_{l', l} = \int_{L_{\min, l'} - L_l}^{L_{\max, l'} - L_l} \frac{\Delta^{\alpha_l - 1} \exp(-\Delta / \beta_{\Delta})}{\Gamma(\alpha_l) \, \beta_{\Delta}^{\alpha_l}} \, d\Delta, \qquad l' \ge l\]

[!IMPORTANT] Critical Insight from Punt et al. (2016) for Fitting mizer to Length Data: Punt et al. (2016, 50–53) prove via simulation that in any size-structured assessment model, asymptotic size \(L_\infty\) (or growth rate \(g(w)\)), natural mortality \(M(w)\), and dome-shaped vs. asymptotic gear selectivity \(S_f(w)\) are strongly confounded when fitted to commercial length compositions alone:

Absence of large fish in the catch can be explained equally well by: (a) slower growth / lower \(L_\infty\), (b) higher predation/natural mortality \(M\), (c) higher fishing mortality \(F\), or (d) dome-shaped selectivity \(S_f(w)\).
How to break the confounding: (1) Use scientific trawl survey length distributions with known asymptotic selectivity, (2) include mean weight-at-age / conditional age-at-length data where available, or (3) include stomach content / predator-prey size data which independently anchors \(M2(w)\) and growth!






3.3.4 LIME: Length-Based Integrated Mixed Effects for Non-Equilibrium Length Data (Rudd & Thorson 2018)
Traditional length-only assessment methods for data-limited stocks—such as Length-Based Spawning Potential Ratio (LB-SPR, Hordyk et al. (2015)) and mean-length mortality estimators (Beverton and Holt 1956; Gedamke and Hoenig 2006)—assume strict steady-state equilibrium (constant recruitment \(R_t = R_0\) and constant fishing mortality \(F_t = F\)). In reality, recruitment pulses and time-varying \(F_t\) distort single-year length compositions, causing severe bias in equilibrium length estimators.
To relax these equilibrium assumptions while requiring as little as 1 year of length-composition data plus known basic life-history parameters (\(L_\infty, k, t_0, M, L_{m}^{50}, \alpha, \beta, \text{CV}_L\)), Merrill Rudd and James Thorson (Rudd and Thorson 2018) developed LIME (Length-based Integrated Mixed Effects), implemented in R and TMB:

Age-Length Transition Matrix (\(\varphi_{a,l}\)) and Length-Based Selectivity (\(S_l\)): Given von Bertalanffy mean length-at-age \(L_a = L_\infty\left(1 - e^{-k(a - t_0)}\right)\) and length standard deviation \(\sigma_{L,a} = L_a \cdot \text{CV}_L\) (typically \(\text{CV}_L = 0.10\)), the probability \(\varphi_{a,l}\) of an individual of age \(a\) falling into length bin \(l\) with bounds \([l_{\text{low}}, l_{\text{high}})\) is (Rudd and Thorson 2018, Table 1, Eq. 5, p. 29): \[\varphi_{a,l} = \begin{cases} \Phi\!\left(\dfrac{l_{\text{high}} - L_a}{\sigma_{L,a}}\right) & l = 1 \\[10pt] \Phi\!\left(\dfrac{l_{\text{high}} - L_a}{\sigma_{L,a}}\right) - \Phi\!\left(\dfrac{l_{\text{low}} - L_a}{\sigma_{L,a}}\right) & 1 < l < n_l \\[10pt] 1 - \Phi\!\left(\dfrac{l_{\text{low}} - L_a}{\sigma_{L,a}}\right) & l = n_l \end{cases}\] Gear selectivity is parameterized as a two-parameter logistic function of length \(x_l\) (with parameters \(L_s^{50}\) and \(L_s^{95}\)) and mapped to age \(a\) by integrating across the age-length matrix: \[S_l = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\ln(19)\left(x_l - L_s^{50}\right)}{L_s^{95} - L_s^{50}}\right)}, \qquad S_a = \sum_{l=1}^{n_l} \varphi_{a,l} \, S_l\]
Mixed-Effects State-Space Dynamics (Random-Walk \(F_t\) and Laplace-Integrated Recruitment \(R_t\)):

Autocorrelated Recruitment Random Effects: Annual recruitment \(R_t\) is modeled as a lognormal random effect (with optional \(\text{AR}(1)\) autocorrelation \(\rho_R\) and TMB epsilon bias-correction; Rudd and Thorson (2018, Table 2, Eqs. 7, 17–19, p. 30)): \[R_t \sim \text{Lognormal}\!\left(\ln R_0 - \frac{\sigma_R^2}{2},\; \sigma_R^2\right)\] where recruitment standard deviation \(\sigma_R\) is estimated with a hierarchical lognormal prior centered on the meta-analytic fish average (\(\sigma_R \sim \text{Lognormal}(\ln(0.737),\, 0.353^2)\); Thorson et al. (2014)).
Random-Walk Penalty on Fishing Mortality \(F_t\): Annual fishing mortality \(F_t\) is estimated as a fixed effect constrained by a first-difference random-walk penalty in log-space (\(\sigma_F = 0.20\)): \[\ln F_t \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\ln F_{t-1},\; \sigma_F^2\right)\]
Predicted Catch Length Proportions (\(\hat{p}_{t,l}\)): Predicted catch-at-age \(\hat{C}_{t,a} = \frac{F_t S_a}{M + F_t S_a} N_{t,a}\left(1 - e^{-M - F_t S_a}\right)\) is projected into length bins via \(\hat{C}_{t,l} = \sum_{a} \hat{C}_{t,a} \varphi_{a,l}\), giving predicted length proportions \(\hat{p}_{t,l} = \hat{C}_{t,l} / \sum_{l'} \hat{C}_{t,l'}\).

Self-Weighting Dirichlet-Multinomial Length Likelihood and Derived Reference Points: LIME fits observed catch length counts \(\tilde{\pi}_{t,l}\) using the Dirichlet-Multinomial (DM) likelihood of Thorson et al. (2017) (see Section 5.6.2), estimating the DM linear overdispersion parameter \(\theta\) (log_theta) simultaneously with \(F_t, L_s^{50}, L_s^{95}, \sigma_R\), and integrating over the latent recruitment vector \(\mathbf{r} = \{R_t\}\) via TMB’s Laplace approximation (Rudd and Thorson 2018, Table 2, Eqs. 16, 22). From the estimated parameters, LIME computes annual Spawning Potential Ratio: \[\text{SPR}_t = \frac{\text{SBPR}_t}{\text{SBPR}_0} = \frac{\sum_{a} \text{Mat}_a \, W_a \, N_{F_t, a}}{\sum_{a} \text{Mat}_a \, W_a \, N_{F=0, a}}\] Notice that because \(\varphi_{a,l}\) allows cohorts of different ages to overlap in length, LIME can separate a recruitment pulse \(\epsilon_{R,t}\) (which creates a mode in juvenile length bins that propagates across years at rate \(g(L)\)) from an increase in fishing mortality \(F_t\) (which truncates the right tail of the length distribution across all adult cohorts simultaneously)—a key mechanism for dynamic length-based calibration in mizer!

section: 3.4 Discrete Length-Structured Multispecies Models (LeMans, LeMaRns, CSMS, CSM)
text:
3.4 Discrete Length-Structured Multispecies Models (LeMans, LeMaRns, CSMS, CSM)

3.4.1 LeMans and LeMaRns (Hall et al. 2006; Rochet et al. 2011; Thorpe et al. 2015; Spence et al. 2020, 2021)
Originally created by Stephen Hall, Collie, Jennings, Bravington, and Pope (Hall et al. 2006) for Georges Bank, extended to evaluate selective fishing across size-based models (Rochet et al. 2011), and adapted to the North Sea by Thorpe et al. (2015) and Michael Spence et al. as the R/C++ package LeMaRns (Spence et al. 2020; Spence, Dolder, et al. 2021; Spence, Thorpe, et al. 2021), LeMans (Length-based Multispecies analysis by numerical simulation) is a discrete-time, discrete-length-bin multispecies model with fixed von Bertalanffy growth and one-way predation mortality feedback.

Mathematical Equations of LeMaRns (Spence et al. 2020, 3–7)
Let \(N_{i,j,t}\) be the number of individuals of species \(i \in \{1, \dots, n_s\}\) in length class \(j \in \{1, \dots, n_l\}\) with bounds \([L_j, L_{j+1})\) and midpoint \(\bar{L}_j = (L_j + L_{j+1})/2\), body mass \(W_{i,j} = \alpha_i \bar{L}_j^{\beta_i}\), and maturity ogive \(m_{i,j} = \left(1 + \exp(-\kappa_{m,i}(\bar{L}_j - L_{\text{mat},i}))\right)^{-1}\).

Reproduction & Recruitment (Step 1): Spawning stock biomass is \(\text{SSB}_{i,t} = \sum_{j=1}^{n_l} m_{i,j} N_{i,j,t} W_{i,j}\). At the first time step of each year, recruits \(R_{i,t}\) enter the smallest length bin \(j = 1\) via a Hockey-Stick, Ricker, Beverton-Holt, or linear stock-recruitment relationship (with optional lognormal process error in Spence, Dolder, et al. (2021)): \[N^{(1)}_{i,1,t} = N_{i,1,t} + R_{i,t}, \qquad N^{(1)}_{i,j,t} = N_{i,j,t} \quad (j > 1)\]
Mortality: \(M1\), Fishing \(F\), and Predation \(M2\) (Step 2): Total mortality in time step \(\Delta t\) is \(Z_{i,j,t} = \Delta t \left(M1_{i,j} + F_{i,j,t} + M2_{i,j,t}\right)\), so surviving numbers are: \[N^{(2)}_{i,j,t} = N^{(1)}_{i,j,t} \exp(-Z_{i,j,t})\] where predation mortality \(M2_{i,j,t}\) on prey \((i, j)\) by all predators \((m, k)\) is governed by a Holling Type II (or Type III) functional response: \[M2_{i,j,t} = \sum_{m=1}^{n_s} \sum_{k=1}^{n_l} I_{m,k} \, N^{(1)}_{m,k,t} \, \frac{\theta_{m,k,i,j}}{\sum_{a=1}^{n_s} \sum_{b=1}^{n_l} \theta_{m,k,a,b} \, N^{(1)}_{a,b,t} W_{a,b} + W_{\text{other}}}\] Here:

\(I_{m,k} = W_{m,k} \left(L_{\infty, m} / \bar{L}_k\right)^{0.4} \cdot \text{ration\_scalar}_m\) is the maximum per-capita consumption rate of predator \((m, k)\),
\(\theta_{m,k,i,j} = \tau_{m,i} \cdot \psi_{m,k,i,j} \cdot o_{m,i}\) is the suitability product of taxonomic preference \(\tau_{m,i} \in \{0, 1\}\), spatial overlap \(o_{m,i}\), and Ursin lognormal weight-ratio preference: \[\psi_{m,k,i,j} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\left(\log_{10}\!\frac{W_{m,k}}{W_{i,j}} - \eta_m\right)^2}{2\sigma_m^2}\right)\]

Deterministic Fractional Somatic Growth (Step 3): Under deterministic von Bertalanffy growth, the time required for an individual of species \(i\) to grow from the lower boundary \(L_j\) to the upper boundary \(L_{j+1}\) of length bin \(j\) is: \[\delta t_{i,j} = \frac{1}{k_i} \ln\!\left(\frac{L_{\infty, i} - L_j}{L_{\infty, i} - L_{j+1}}\right)\] Therefore, in a discrete time step \(\Delta t\) (chosen small enough that \(\Delta t \le \min_{i,j} \delta t_{i,j}\), e.g., \(\Delta t = 0.1\text{ yr}\)), a fixed fraction \(\phi_{i,j}\) of individuals in length bin \(j\) advance to length bin \(j+1\): \[\phi_{i,j} = \frac{\Delta t}{\delta t_{i,j}} = \frac{\Delta t \cdot k_i}{\ln\!\left(\frac{L_{\infty, i} - L_j}{L_{\infty, i} - L_{j+1}}\right)}\] giving the state update: \[N_{i,j,t+1} = (1 - \phi_{i,j}) N^{(2)}_{i,j,t} + \phi_{i,j-1} N^{(2)}_{i,j-1,t}\] (Note: Mathematically, this update equation is identical to the explicit first-order upwind finite-difference scheme of the McKendrick–von Foerster PDE in mizer! Consequently, it exhibits the exact same numerical Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy [CFL] artificial cohort diffusion \(\approx \frac{1}{2} g \delta L (1 - \phi)\) analyzed by Datta et al. (2010)).





3.4.2 CSMS and CSM (Pope et al. 2006, 2019): Moment-Based Reduction of Length Spectra
John Pope and colleagues (Pope et al. 2006, 2019; Gislason et al. 2010) developed two remarkably parsimonious length-based multispecies models to explore multispecies MSY and community structure:

CSMS (Charmingly Simple Multispecies Size-based model; Pope et al. (2006)): Parameterizes an entire 13-species North Sea fish community using only 15 life-history scaling parameters (linking von Bertalanffy \(k_i = c_k L_{\infty,i}^{-0.31}\), maturity \(L_{\text{mat},i} = c_m L_{\infty,i}\), Ricker recruitment parameters, and Andersen-Ursin predation solely to each species’ asymptotic length \(L_{\infty,i}\)), reproducing the community size spectrum slope and steeper slopes under fishing.
CSM (Charmingly Simple Model; Pope et al. (2019)): Instead of tracking 50 discrete length bins per cohort, CSM notes that the log-length distribution of a cohort is approximately Gaussian and therefore tracks only the 0th through 4th moments \(\left(M_0 = N_{s,a},\; M_1 = \mathbb{E}[\ln L],\; M_2 = \text{Var}(\ln L),\; \dots\right)\) of each cohort’s size distribution! Because the product of a Gaussian cohort log-length density and a Gaussian Ursin log-size preference kernel has an exact closed-form Gaussian integral, CSM computes size-based predation mortality \(M2_{s,a}\) analytically without any discrete length bins, achieving a \(50\times\) speedup over bin-based models.

title: 4  Continuous Size-Spectrum (mizer) and State-Space Food-Web Models (EwE, Rpath, EcoState)
text:
4.1.1 Theoretical Lineage and Core Philosophy
Size-spectrum theory originated from the empirical discovery by Sheldon et al. (1972) and Sheldon et al. (1977) that pelagic marine biomass is approximately constant across logarithmic body-mass bins (\(B(w) dw \propto w^0 d(\ln w) \implies N(w) \propto w^{-2}\)), and from the continuous mass-balance and pelagic ecosystem derivations of Platt and Denman (1977), Silvert and Platt (1978), Benoît and Rochet (2004), Andersen and Beyer (2006), and Cuesta et al. (2018).
In a landmark synthesis, Hartvig et al. (2011) and Scott et al. (2014) resolved species identity within the continuous size spectrum to create the mizer framework (Multi-species size-spectrum ecological modelling in R; applied to North Sea reference points by Blanchard et al. (2014) and reviewed comprehensively by Andersen et al. (2016), Andersen (2019), Andersen (2020), and Pennino et al. (2025)).
Unlike age-structured models where somatic growth and natural mortality are external inputs, in mizer both individual somatic growth \(g_i(w,t)\) and predation mortality \(\mu_{p,i}(w,t)\) emerge dynamically from individual-level foraging and strict conservation of mass/energy.



4.1.2 Complete Mathematical Formulation of Standard mizer
Let \(N_i(w, t)\) (\(\text{numbers} \cdot \text{g}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}^{-3}\) or total numbers per weight interval) denote the number density of species \(i \in \{1, \dots, S\}\) at body mass \(w \in [w_0, w_{\max, i}]\) and time \(t\), and let \(N_R(w, t)\) denote the background plankton/benthic resource spectrum for \(w \in [w_{\text{cut}}, w_{\text{max}, R}]\).

1. Governing McKendrick–von Foerster Conservation PDE
The time evolution of \(N_i(w, t)\) is governed by the first-order hyperbolic continuity (advection-reaction) equation (Hartvig et al. 2011, Eq. 1; Scott et al. 2014, Eq. 3.1):
\[\frac{\partial N_i(w, t)}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial \left(g_i(w, t) N_i(w, t)\right)}{\partial w} = -\mu_i(w, t) N_i(w, t)\]
coupled to the boundary condition (recruitment flux) at egg weight \(w_0\):
\[g_i(w_0, t) N_i(w_0, t) = R_{\text{dd}, i}(t)\]


2. Volumetric Search Rate, Predation Kernel, and Encounter Rate (\(E_i(w,t)\))
A predator of species \(i\) and mass \(w\) searches a water volume at allometric rate \(\gamma_i(w) = \gamma_i w^q\) (\(q \approx 0.8\)). Its size preference for prey of mass \(w_p\) is described by a predation kernel \(\phi_i(w / w_p)\), most commonly the Andersen–Ursin lognormal kernel (Scott et al. 2014, Eq. 3.4):
\[\phi_i\!\left(\frac{w}{w_p}\right) = \exp\!\left( -\frac{\left(\ln\!\left(\frac{w}{\beta_i w_p}\right)\right)^2}{2\sigma_i^2} \right)\]
(or a power-law / box / double-logistic kernel). Given the species interaction (spatial overlap / vulnerability) matrix \(\theta_{ij} \in [0, 1]\), the total biomass of suitable prey encountered per unit time \(E_i(w, t)\) by predator \((i, w)\) is:
\[E_i(w, t) = \gamma_i(w) \int \phi_i\!\left(\frac{w}{w_p}\right) \left[ \theta_{iR} N_R(w_p, t) + \sum_{j=1}^{S} \theta_{ij} N_j(w_p, t) \right] w_p \, dw_p\]


3. Feeding Level (\(f_i(w,t)\)) and Holling Type II Satiation
Given physiological maximum intake rate \(I_{\max, i}(w) = h_i w^n\) (\(n \approx 0.67\text{--}0.75\)), the dimensionless feeding level \(f_i(w, t) \in [0, 1)\) follows a Holling Type II functional response:
\[f_i(w, t) = \frac{E_i(w, t)}{E_i(w, t) + h_i w^n}\]
Thus actual biomass consumption per predator per unit time is \(C_i(w, t) = f_i(w, t) h_i w^n\).


4. Bioenergetic Allocation, Somatic Growth (\(g_i(w,t)\)), and Reproduction (\(R_{p,i}(t)\))
Assimilated energy is a fraction \(\alpha_i \in (0, 1)\) of ingested food (\(\alpha_i \approx 0.6\)), from which standard metabolic maintenance \(k_{s,i} w^p\) (\(p \approx 0.7\text{--}1.0\)) is subtracted to give net available energy \(E_{\text{avail}, i}(w, t)\):
\[E_{\text{avail}, i}(w, t) = \alpha_i \, f_i(w, t) \, h_i w^n - k_{s,i} w^p\]
A size-dependent maturation ogive \(\psi_i(w)\) (transitioning from \(0\) to \(1\) around maturation weight \(w_{\text{mat}, i}\) and scaling with \(\left(w / w_{\max, i}\right)^{1-n}\) or \(1 - (w/w_{\max,i})^{p-n}\) so growth ceases at \(w_{\max, i}\)) partitions net positive energy between somatic growth \(g_i(w, t)\) and gonadal reproduction \(E_{r,i}(w, t)\):
\[g_i(w, t) = \max\!\Big(0,\; E_{\text{avail}, i}(w, t)\Big) \Big(1 - \psi_i(w)\Big)\]
\[\psi_i(w) = \left[1 + \left(\frac{w}{w_{\text{mat}, i}}\right)^{-U}\right]^{-1} \left(\frac{w}{w_{\max, i}}\right)^{1 - n}\]
The density-independent physiological egg production rate \(R_{\text{di}, i}(t)\) (\(\text{eggs} \cdot \text{yr}^{-1}\)) is obtained by integrating reproductive energy over all sizes, multiplying by reproductive efficiency \(\epsilon_{\text{rep}, i}\) and female fraction \(1/2\), and dividing by egg weight \(w_0\):
\[R_{\text{di}, i}(t) = \frac{\epsilon_{\text{rep}, i}}{2 w_0} \int_{w_0}^{w_{\max, i}} N_i(w, t) \max\!\Big(0,\; E_{\text{avail}, i}(w, t)\Big) \psi_i(w) \, dw\]
In standard mizer, external density dependence at the larval stage (e.g., limited larval habitat or unmodeled larval mortality) is represented by passing \(R_{\text{di}, i}(t)\) through a Beverton–Holt stock-recruitment function with maximum recruitment cap \(R_{\max, i}\):
\[R_{\text{dd}, i}(t) = \frac{R_{\max, i} \, R_{\text{di}, i}(t)}{R_{\text{di}, i}(t) + R_{\max, i}}\]


5. Total Mortality (\(\mu_i(w,t)\)): Background, Predation, Starvation, and Fishing
Total instantaneous mortality \(\mu_i(w, t)\) is the sum of four mechanistic components:
\[\mu_i(w, t) = \mu_{0, i}(w) + \mu_{p, i}(w, t) + \mu_{s, i}(w, t) + F_i(w, t)\]

Background / Senescence Mortality: \(\mu_{0, i}(w) = \mu_{0, i} w_{\max, i}^{n - 1}\) (allometrically scaled with \(w_{\max,i}\)).
Endogenous Predation Mortality (\(\mu_{p, i}(w_p, t) \equiv M2\)): By strict mass balance, every gram of prey \((j, w_p)\) eaten by predators \((i, w)\) must appear as mortality on \((j, w_p)\) (Scott et al. 2014, Eq. 3.11):
\[\mu_{p, j}(w_p, t) = \sum_{i=1}^{S} \theta_{ij} \int_{w_0}^{w_{\max, i}} \phi_i\!\left(\frac{w}{w_p}\right) \Big(1 - f_i(w, t)\Big) \gamma_i(w) \, N_i(w, t) \, dw\]
(Notice the identity \(\frac{f_i(w) h_i w^n}{E_i(w)} = 1 - f_i(w)\): when a predator is satiated [\(f_i(w) \to 1\)], its per-unit-prey clearance rate \((1 - f_i)\gamma_i(w)\) drops toward zero!)
Starvation Mortality (\(\mu_{s, i}(w, t)\)): Whenever available assimilated energy falls below metabolic maintenance (\(E_{\text{avail}, i}(w, t) < 0\)), individuals suffer starvation mortality proportional to the energy deficit divided by lipid energy stores \(\xi_{\text{store}} w\) (Scott et al. 2014, Eq. 3.12):
\[\mu_{s, i}(w, t) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{-E_{\text{avail}, i}(w, t)}{\xi_{\text{store}} w} & \text{if } E_{\text{avail}, i}(w, t) < 0 \\[8pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
Fishing Mortality (\(F_i(w, t)\)): Summed over fishing gears/fleets \(f\) with size selectivity \(S_{f,i}(w)\), catchability \(Q_{f,i}\), and fishing effort \(E_{f}(t)\):
\[F_i(w, t) = \sum_{f} S_{f, i}(w) \, Q_{f, i} \, E_{f}(t)\]
generating total fishery yield in weight \(Y_{f,i}(t) = \int_{w_0}^{w_{\max,i}} F_{f,i}(w, t) \, w \, N_i(w, t) \, dw\).



6. Resource Spectrum Dynamics (\(N_R(w,t)\))
The background plankton/benthos spectrum \(N_R(w, t)\) evolves via semi-chemostat (or logistic) renewal at rate \(r_R(w) = r_0 w^{n-1}\) toward carrying capacity \(\kappa_R(w) = \kappa w^{-\lambda}\) (\(\lambda \approx 2 + q - n \approx 2.05\)):
\[\frac{\partial N_R(w, t)}{\partial t} = r_R(w) \Big(\kappa_R(w) - N_R(w, t)\Big) - \mu_{p, R}(w, t) N_R(w, t)\]


7. Semi-Implicit Upwind Finite-Difference Discretization in mizer
On a logarithmically spaced weight grid \(w_j = w_0 \cdot 10^{(j-1)\Delta x}\) with bin widths \(\Delta w_j = w_{j+1} - w_j\), mizer solves the McKendrick–von Foerster PDE over time step \(\Delta t\) by evaluating encounter \(E_i\), feeding level \(f_i\), growth \(g_{i,j}^t\), and mortality \(\mu_{i,j}^t\) explicitly at time \(t\) (using Fast Fourier Transform [FFT] convolution on the log-weight grid for the integrals \(E_i\) and \(\mu_{p,i}\) when kernels are shift-invariant in \(\ln(w/w_p)\)), and then advancing \(N_{i,j}^{t+\Delta t}\) via a first-order upwind, backward-Euler (semi-implicit) scheme (Scott et al. 2014, Appendix A):
\[\frac{N_{i,j}^{t+\Delta t} - N_{i,j}^t}{\Delta t} + \frac{g_{i,j}^t N_{i,j}^{t+\Delta t} - g_{i,j-1}^t N_{i,j-1}^{t+\Delta t}}{\Delta w_j} = -\mu_{i,j}^t N_{i,j}^{t+\Delta t}\]
Solving for \(N_{i,j}^{t+\Delta t}\) gives a lower-bidiagonal linear system solved in \(O(n_w)\) forward substitution:
\[N_{i,j}^{t+\Delta t} = \frac{N_{i,j}^t + \frac{\Delta t}{\Delta w_j} g_{i,j-1}^t N_{i,j-1}^{t+\Delta t}}{1 + \Delta t \left(\frac{g_{i,j}^t}{\Delta w_j} + \mu_{i,j}^t\right)}\]

section: 4.2 The Jump-Growth Fokker–Planck PDE (Datta, Delius & Law 2010, 2011)
text:
4.2 The Jump-Growth Fokker–Planck PDE (Datta, Delius & Law 2010, 2011)

4.2.1 Why the First-Order McKendrick–von Foerster PDE Fails for Dynamic Cohort Fitting
In the standard McKendrick–von Foerster PDE \(\partial_t N + \partial_w (g N) = -\mu N\), somatic growth is treated as a purely deterministic continuous drift \(dw/dt = g(w, t)\). Consequently:

No Intrinsic Cohort Broadening: All individuals born at the same instant \(t_0\) at egg weight \(w_0\) travel along the exact same characteristic trajectory \(w(t)\) with zero variance in size-at-age! If recruitment is pulsed seasonally (or fluctuates interannually as in real stock assessments), a narrow delta-function pulse at \(w_0\) remains an unrealistically sharp spike (broadened only by numerical discretization error \(\propto \Delta w_j\) of the upwind scheme!).
Grid-Dependent Numerical Diffusion: In mizer’s first-order upwind scheme, changing the number of weight bins \(n_w\) or time step \(\Delta t\) alters the numerical diffusivity \(D_{\text{num}} \approx \frac{1}{2} g \Delta w\), which artificially changes how recruitment pulses smear across length compositions!
Deterministic Instability of the Community Size Spectrum: Without growth dispersion or an external stock-recruitment clamp, the continuous McKendrick–von Foerster PDE exhibits traveling-wave instabilities (cohort cycles) for realistic predator-prey mass ratios (\(\beta \sim 100\); Datta et al. (2011)).



4.2.2 Derivation of the Jump-Growth Equation (Datta, Delius & Law 2010)
Datta et al. (2010) resolved this fundamental limitation from first principles by observing that fish do not grow by absorbing a continuous fluid: they grow by discrete stochastic jumps \(\Delta w = \alpha w_p\) each time they capture and assimilate a discrete prey organism of body mass \(w_p\).
Starting from the exact Markov Master Equation for discrete prey-capture events in continuous time (Datta et al. 2010, Eq. 5): \[\frac{\partial N_i(w,t)}{\partial t} = \int dw_p \Big[ \text{Transition in from } (w - \alpha_i w_p) - \text{Transition out from } w \Big] - \mu_i(w,t) N_i(w,t)\] and performing a second-order Kramers–Moyal Taylor expansion in the prey mass increment \(\alpha_i w_p \ll w\), Datta et al. (2010) derived the Jump-Growth Fokker–Planck (Advection–Diffusion–Reaction) PDE:
\[\frac{\partial N_i(w, t)}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial \left(g_i(w, t) N_i(w, t)\right)}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^2 \left(d_i(w, t) N_i(w, t)\right)}{\partial w^2} - \mu_i(w, t) N_i(w, t)\]
where:

The first-order drift (mean somatic growth rate) \(g_i(w, t)\) is the first moment of assimilated prey mass: \[g_i(w, t) = \alpha_i \Big(1 - \psi_i(w)\Big) \Big(1 - f_i(w, t)\Big) \gamma_i(w) \int \phi_i\!\left(\frac{w}{w_p}\right) N_c(w_p, t) \, \mathbf{w_p} \, dw_p - k_{s,i} w^p \Big(1 - \psi_i(w)\Big)\]
The second-order macro-diffusion (growth variance) coefficient \(d_i(w, t)\) is the second moment of assimilated prey mass (Datta et al. 2010, Eq. 9): \[d_i(w, t) = \alpha_i^2 \Big(1 - \psi_i(w)\Big)^2 \Big(1 - f_i(w, t)\Big) \gamma_i(w) \int \phi_i\!\left(\frac{w}{w_p}\right) N_c(w_p, t) \, \mathbf{w_p^2} \, dw_p\]


[!IMPORTANT] Mathematical & Practical Significance of the Jump-Growth Diffusion Term \(d_i(w,t)\):

Zero Free Parameters: In the pure mechanistic derivation, \(d_i(w, t)\) requires no additional free parameters (or a single scaling multiplier if accounting for behavioral bout-feeding / schooling variation, analogous to Gadget’s Beta-Binomial \(\beta_s\)).
Physical Cohort Dispersion: A recruiting year-class pulse at \(w_0\) naturally broadens into a realistic bell-shaped size-at-age distribution as it advects to larger sizes, enabling direct likelihood fitting to time-series length-frequency distributions!
Grid-Independent Convergence: When solved on a sufficiently fine grid (or via Crank–Nicolson / implicit central differences for the \(\partial_w^2(d_i N_i)\) term), the physical diffusivity \(d_i(w, t)\) dominates numerical grid diffusivity, making model predictions invariant to grid resolution.

section: 4.3 Population Regulation Without Ad-Hoc Stock–Recruitment Relationships (Canales, Delius & Law 2020)
text:
4.3 Population Regulation Without Ad-Hoc Stock–Recruitment Relationships (Canales, Delius & Law 2020)
In standard fisheries models (including standard mizer, SMS, Gadget, and LeMaRns), population abundance is stabilized externally by imposing an ad-hoc Beverton–Holt or Ricker stock-recruitment relationship (SRR) at the boundary \(w_0\), with one or two free species-specific parameters (\(R_{\max, i}\) or steepness \(h_i\)) that have little direct physiological basis and strongly dictate MSY predictions.
Canales et al. (2020) demonstrated that in a size-spectrum model with linear density-independent reproduction (\(R_{\text{dd}, i} = R_{\text{di}, i}\), i.e., \(R_{\max, i} \to \infty\)), three endogenous biological mechanisms naturally regulate population abundance and coexistence without any ad-hoc SRR:

Density-Dependent Somatic Growth via Prey Competition: When a species’ abundance increases, it depletes its prey size range, lowering its feeding level \(f_i(w, t)\) and slowing juvenile growth \(g_i(w, t)\). Because juveniles spend longer in small vulnerable size classes (\(w < w_{\text{mat}, i}\)) while experiencing predation mortality \(\mu_{p,i}(w, t)\), cumulative survival to maturity \(\exp\!\left(-\int_{w_0}^{w_{\text{mat}}} \frac{\mu_i(w)}{g_i(w)} dw\right)\) drops sharply!
Early-Life Predation and Cannibalism: Extending the predation kernel to planktonic/larval stages and accounting for intra- and inter-specific predation on larvae creates a self-regulating mortality bottleneck.
Reproductive Allometry (\(m_i > n_i\)): When reproductive investment scales steeper with body mass than metabolic intake (matching empirical BOFFFF—Big Old Fat Fecund Female—observations), truncating the adult size structure via fishing directly reduces per-biomass egg output without needing an SRR curve.

text:
4.4 Mass-Balance, Foraging Arena, and State-Space Food-Web Models (Ecopath, Ecosim, Rpath, EcoState)
While size-spectrum models resolve continuous body mass, the most widely applied whole-ecosystem modeling framework in marine science is Ecopath with Ecosim (EwE)—originating with Polovina (1984) and Christensen and Pauly (1992), extended dynamically and spatially via Foraging Arena Theory in Ecosim and Ecospace by Walters et al. (1997), Walters et al. (1999), Christensen and Walters (2004), Christensen et al. (2005), and Christensen et al. (2024), critically evaluated by Plagányi and Butterworth (2004), and automated via stepwise fitting by Scott et al. (2016)—along with its reproducible R implementation Rpath (Lucey et al. 2020) and its recent TMB state-space stock assessment reformulation EcoState (Thorson et al. 2024).

4.4.1 Ecopath: Static Mass Balance at Reference Equilibrium
Ecopath partitions the ecosystem into \(i \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) functional groups (which may be single species, multi-species guilds, or juvenile/adult life stanzas). At a reference equilibrium period, production of group \(i\) equals the sum of all mortality and export fluxes (Christensen and Walters 2004, Eq. 1; Lucey et al. 2020, Eq. 1):
\[B_i \left(\frac{P}{B}\right)_i \cdot EE_i = Y_i + E_i + BA_i + \sum_{j=1}^{n} B_j \left(\frac{Q}{B}\right)_j DC_{ij}\]
where:

\(B_i\) is biomass, \((P/B)_i = Z_i\) is the production-to-biomass ratio (total mortality rate under equilibrium), and \((Q/B)_j\) is the consumption-to-biomass ratio of predator \(j\),
\(EE_i \in [0, 1]\) is Ecotrophic Efficiency (the fraction of production explained within the modeled system, so \(M0_i = (P/B)_i (1 - EE_i)\) is residual unexplained mortality),
\(Y_i\) is fishery catch, \(E_i\) is net migration, \(BA_i\) is biomass accumulation, and
\(DC_{ij}\) is the diet composition matrix (fraction by weight of predator \(j\)’s diet consisting of prey \(i\), with \(\sum_i DC_{ij} = 1\)). For each group \(i\), three of the four core parameters \(\{B_i, (P/B)_i, (Q/B)_i, EE_i\}\) are supplied along with \(DC_{ij}\) and \(Y_i\), and the linear system is solved for the missing parameter (typically \(EE_i\) or \(B_i\)).




4.4.2 Ecosim and Walters’ Foraging Arena Theory
When Ecopath is projected dynamically through time as a system of coupled ODEs (Ecosim; Walters et al. (1997)):
\[\frac{dB_i}{dt} = g_i \sum_{j} Q_{ji}(t) - \sum_{k} Q_{ik}(t) + I_i - \left(M0_i + F_i(t) + e_i\right) B_i(t)\]
where \(g_i = (P/Q)_i\) is net growth efficiency, a critical question arises: how should the consumption flux \(Q_{ij}(t)\) of prey \(i\) by predator \(j\) depend on \(B_i(t)\) and \(B_j(t)\)?
Walters et al. (1997) showed that if one uses standard mass-action Lotka–Volterra (\(Q_{ij} = a_{ij} B_i B_j\)) or standard Holling Type II in a complex 30-species food web, the ecosystem rapidly collapses via Gause competitive exclusion or violent predator-prey limit cycles.
To resolve this, Walters et al. (1997) formulated Foraging Arena Theory: at any given moment, total prey biomass \(B_i\) is partitioned with respect to predator \(j\) into an invulnerable (refuge/sheltered/un-overlapping) state \(B_i - V_{ij}\) and a small vulnerable foraging arena state \(V_{ij}\), with behavioural/spatial exchange rate \(v_{ij}\) between them:
\[\frac{dV_{ij}}{dt} = v_{ij}\left(B_i - V_{ij}\right) - v'_{ij} V_{ij} - a_{ij} V_{ij} B_j\]
Assuming the behavioral exchange \(V_{ij}\) equilibrates rapidly relative to annual population changes (\(dV_{ij}/dt \approx 0\), with \(v'_{ij} = v_{ij}\)), solving for \(V_{ij}\) yields the Foraging Arena Functional Response (Walters et al. 1997, Eq. 4; Christensen and Walters 2004, Eq. 5; Thorson et al. 2024, Eq. 4):
\[Q_{ij}(t) = a_{ij} V_{ij}(t) B_j(t) = \frac{a_{ij} \, v_{ij} \, B_i(t) \, B_j(t)}{2 v_{ij} + a_{ij} B_j(t)}\]
Calibrating to the Ecopath baseline \(Q_{ij,0} = B_{j,0} (Q/B)_{j,0} DC_{ij,0}\) at reference biomasses \((B_{i,0}, B_{j,0})\) eliminates \(a_{ij}\) in favor of a single dimensionless vulnerability multiplier \(X_{ij} = \frac{v_{ij} B_{i,0}}{Q_{ij,0}} \in (1, \infty)\) (default \(X_{ij} = 2\)):
\[Q_{ij}(t) = Q_{ij,0} \, \frac{X_{ij}}{X_{ij} - 1 + \frac{B_j(t)}{B_{j,0}}} \, \frac{B_i(t)}{B_{i,0}}\]

Low Vulnerability (\(X_{ij} \to 1\), “Bottom-Up / Donor Control”): As \(X_{ij} \to 1\), \(Q_{ij}(t) \to Q_{ij,0} \frac{B_i(t)}{B_{i,0}}\) is independent of predator biomass \(B_j(t)\)! Doubling predator abundance \(B_j\) simply means twice as many predators compete for the same trickle of prey entering the foraging arena, halving per-capita predator intake and preventing top-down prey extermination.
High Vulnerability (\(X_{ij} \to \infty\), “Top-Down / Lotka–Volterra Control”): As \(X_{ij} \to \infty\), \(Q_{ij}(t) \to Q_{ij,0} \frac{B_i(t)}{B_{i,0}} \frac{B_j(t)}{B_{j,0}}\) recovers mass-action top-down predation.

(For critique of EwE’s delay-difference multi-stanza assumptions and vulnerability overfitting when many \(X_{ij}\) are tuned to short time series, see Plagányi and Butterworth (2004) and the stepwise AIC fitting protocol of Scott et al. (2016)).



4.4.3 EcoState (Thorson et al. 2024): State-Space Mass-Balance Assessment in TMB
Historically, EwE was fitted by shooting (deterministic trajectory matching) without process errors or formal state-space marginal likelihoods. In 2024, James Thorson, Kirstin Holsman, Gaichas, Aydin, and Punt introduced EcoState (Thorson et al. 2024), which embeds the Ecopath + Ecosim ODEs directly inside a Template Model Builder (TMB) state-space stock assessment model:

Continuous-Time ODE with Annual Process Errors \(\epsilon_{i,t}\): Within each year \(t \in \{t_0, \dots, T\}\), biomass \(B_i(s)\) evolves over \(s \in [t, t+1]\) via the Ecosim Foraging Arena ODE augmented with an estimated annual unexplained process-error rate \(\epsilon_{i,t}\) (Thorson et al. 2024, Eq. 5): \[\frac{dB_i(s)}{ds} = g_i \sum_j Q_{ji}(s) - \sum_k Q_{ik}(s) - \Big(M0_i + F_{i,t} - \epsilon_{i,t}\Big) B_i(s)\] integrated numerically in TMB using a differentiable Runge–Kutta / Adams–Bashforth ODE solver (odeint), where \(\epsilon_{i,t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\text{proc}, i})\) are random effects marginalized via the Laplace approximation.
Simultaneous Joint Likelihood Across All Data Streams: EcoState estimates Ecopath baseline parameters (\(\ln B_{i,0}, EE_i, DC_{ij,0}\)), Ecosim vulnerabilities \(\ln(X_{ij}-1)\), fishing mortalities \(\ln F_{i,t}\), and process error variances \(\sigma_{\text{proc},i}\) simultaneously by fitting to:

Survey biomass indices: \(\ln I_{i,t} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\ln(q_i \hat{B}_{i,t}),\, \sigma^2_{I,i,t}\right)\),
Fishery catches: \(\ln C^{\text{obs}}_{i,t} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\ln \hat{C}_{i,t},\, \sigma^2_{C,i}\right)\),
Time-varying stomach diet proportions \(\mathbf{W}^{\text{obs}}_{j,t}\): modeled via a Dirichlet likelihood on predicted Ecosim consumption shares \(\hat{p}_{ij,t} = \frac{\hat{Q}_{ij,t}}{\sum_k \hat{Q}_{kj,t}}\)!

title: 5  Stomach Content Data, Gastric Evacuation Physics, and Diet Likelihood Formulations
text:
5.1 Why Stomach Content Data Cannot Be Treated as Direct Diet Proportions
A common pitfall when calibrating ecological models is to treat the wet weight \(S_{i,k}\) of prey \(i\) observed inside stomach \(k\) as a direct measure of the predator’s consumption rate \(C_i\). In reality, what is observed inside a sampled fish stomach is the standing stock of partially digested prey, which is related to the ingestion flux (consumption rate) only through the physics of gastric evacuation and spatial sampling design (Rindorf and Lewy 2004; Andersen and Beyer 2005; Buckland et al. 2017; Jacobsen et al. 2023):
\[\text{Ingestion Rate } C_i(t) \xrightarrow{\text{Digestion / Evacuation Rate } \frac{dS_i}{dt}} \text{True Stomach Content } S_i(t) \xrightarrow{\text{Trawl Survey \& Lab Protocol}} \text{Observed Stomach Data}\]

title: 5  Stomach Content Data, Gastric Evacuation Physics, and Diet Likelihood Formulations
section: 5.2 Biophysical Modelling of Gastric Evacuation (Andersen & Beyer 2005)
text:
5.2 Biophysical Modelling of Gastric Evacuation (Andersen & Beyer 2005)

5.2.1 The Square-Root Cylinder Evacuation Equation
Through extensive laboratory feeding experiments on gadoids and other predatory fishes, Andersen and Beyer (2005) established the mechanistic cylinder model of gastric evacuation.
Because digestive enzymes and hydrochloric acid are secreted by the stomach mucosa and act only on the outer surface area of the food bolus in the stomach (modeled as a cylinder of fixed length \(l_s \propto L_{\text{pred}}\) and radius \(r\), where volume/mass is \(S \propto l_s r^2\) and surface area is \(A_s \propto l_s r \propto S^{0.5}\)), the instantaneous gastric evacuation rate (GER) of total stomach mass \(S(t)\) (in \(\text{g} \cdot \text{h}^{-1}\)) follows a power law with exponent \(\alpha = 0.5\) (Andersen and Beyer 2005, Eqs. 1–3):
\[\frac{dS(t)}{dt} = -\rho \, S(t)^{\alpha}, \qquad \alpha \approx 0.5\]
where the rate parameter \(\rho\) scales with predator total length \(L\) (cm), ambient water temperature \(T\) (\(^\circ\text{C}\)), and meal energy density \(E\) (\(\text{kJ} \cdot \text{g}^{-1}\) wet weight):
\[\rho(L, T, E) = \rho_0 \, L^{\lambda} \, \exp(\delta T) \, E^{-\mu}\]
Typical empirical values for North Sea and Baltic piscivores (cod, whiting, saithe; Andersen and Beyer (2005, Table 1)) are:

Surface-to-volume exponent: \(\alpha = 0.50\),
Predator length scaling: \(\lambda \approx 1.30\text{--}1.44\) (since \(\lambda + 3\alpha \approx 2.8\text{--}2.95\), matching the allometric scaling of maximum consumption \(W^{0.75\text{--}0.8}\)),
Temperature coefficient: \(\delta \approx 0.08\text{--}0.10\text{ }^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\),
Prey energy-density resistance exponent: \(\mu \approx 0.85\text{--}0.90\) (lipid-rich, high-energy prey such as herring or sprat [\(E \approx 6\text{--}9\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{g}^{-1}\)] are evacuated significantly more slowly in wet weight per hour than lean fish or crustaceans [\(E \approx 3.5\text{--}4.5\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{g}^{-1}\)], so rate of energy delivery \(E \cdot |dS/dt| \propto E^{1-\mu} \approx E^{0.12}\) is nearly invariant across prey types!).



5.2.2 Evacuation of Individual Prey Items in Mixed Meals
When a predator stomach contains \(K\) distinct prey items/categories with individual wet masses \(S_1, S_2, \dots, S_K\) and total stomach mass \(S_{\text{tot}} = \sum_{k=1}^K S_k\), the evacuation rate of prey category \(i\) is proportional to its mass share \(S_i / S_{\text{tot}}\) in the cylinder multiplied by the total evacuation rate (Andersen and Beyer 2005, Eq. 6; Rindorf and Lewy 2004, Eq. 2):
\[\text{GER}_i = -\frac{dS_i}{dt} = \rho_i \left(\frac{S_i}{S_{\text{tot}}}\right) S_{\text{tot}}^{\alpha} = \rho_i \, S_i \, S_{\text{tot}}^{\alpha - 1}\]
where \(\rho_i = \rho_0 L^\lambda e^{\delta T} E_i^{-\mu}\) accounts for the specific energy density and cuticle/exoskeleton resistance of prey \(i\).
