title: 5  Stomach Content Data, Gastric Evacuation Physics, and Diet Likelihood Formulations
section: 5.3 The Nonlinear Stomach-Pooling Bias (Rindorf & Lewy 2004)
text:
5.3 The Nonlinear Stomach-Pooling Bias (Rindorf & Lewy 2004)
In over a century of stomach sampling (including the 1981 and 1991 ICES North Sea Stomach Sampling Projects), stomachs of predators of the same species and length class caught in the same trawl haul were physically pooled in a bucket aboard ship to save laboratory processing time, and only the mean stomach content weight \(\bar{S}_i = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n S_{i,k}\) across the \(n\) sampled predators (including empty stomachs) was recorded (Rindorf and Lewy 2004).

5.3.1 Proof of Jensen’s Inequality Bias
Over a stationary feeding period of duration \(D\), the true mean population consumption rate \(\bar{C}_i\) per predator is the expectation of the individual evacuation rate across all individual stomachs \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\):
\[\bar{C}_{\text{true}, i} = D \cdot \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \rho_i \, S_{i,k} \, S_{\text{tot}, k}^{\alpha - 1} \right] = \frac{D}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \rho_i \, S_{i,k} \, S_{\text{tot}, k}^{\alpha - 1}\]
However, when stomachs are pooled prior to calculation, only the sample means \(\bar{S}_i = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n S_{i,k}\) and \(\bar{S}_{\text{tot}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n S_{\text{tot},k}\) are known, and the naive pooled estimator is:
\[\hat{C}_{\text{pooled}, i} = D \, \rho_i \, \bar{S}_i \, \bar{S}_{\text{tot}}^{\alpha - 1}\]
For total consumption (\(S_i = S_{\text{tot}}\)), \(\bar{C}_{\text{true}} = D \rho \, \mathbb{E}[S_{\text{tot}}^\alpha]\) whereas \(\hat{C}_{\text{pooled}} = D \rho \, (\mathbb{E}[S_{\text{tot}}])^\alpha\). Because \(f(S) = S^\alpha\) is a strictly concave function for \(0 < \alpha < 1\) (\(\alpha \approx 0.5\)), Jensen’s Inequality guarantees that:
\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[S_{\text{tot}}^{\alpha}\right] < \Big(\mathbb{E}[S_{\text{tot}}]\Big)^{\alpha} \implies \hat{C}_{\text{pooled}} > \bar{C}_{\text{true}}\]
Rindorf and Lewy (2004) demonstrated analytically and via bootstrap simulations on individual cod stomachs that:

Total Consumption Overestimation: Because individual fish stomachs are highly skewed (many empty or near-empty stomachs, and a few stomachs with recently ingested large fish), applying \(\bar{S}_{\text{tot}}^{0.5}\) to pooled haul averages overestimates total food consumption by \(25\%\) to \(>100\%\)!
Prey-Composition Bias Toward Large-Meal Piscivory: When a predator occasionally eats a large fish prey item \(A\) (high \(S_{\text{tot}, k}\), so \(S_{\text{tot}, k}^{\alpha - 1} = S_{\text{tot}, k}^{-0.5}\) is small) and frequently eats small benthic invertebrate meals \(B\) (low \(S_{\text{tot}, k}\), so \(S_{\text{tot}, k}^{-0.5}\) is large), the naive pooled formula \(\hat{C}_{\text{pooled}, i} \propto \bar{S}_i \bar{S}_{\text{tot}}^{-0.5}\) applies the same average total stomach weight \(\bar{S}_{\text{tot}}^{-0.5}\) to both prey types. This overestimates the diet share of large fish prey and underestimates the diet share of small invertebrate prey (Rindorf and Lewy 2004, 2491–94)!



5.3.2 Second-Order Taylor Bias Correction (Rindorf & Lewy 2004)
When individual stomachs cannot be analyzed separately, Rindorf and Lewy (2004, Eqs. 11–14) derived a second-order Taylor series correction for total consumption among non-empty stomachs (where \(p_+\) is the proportion of non-empty stomachs in the sample and \(\text{CV}_+\) is the coefficient of variation of stomach content weight among feeding fish):
\[\bar{C}_{\text{corrected}} \approx D \, \rho \, p_{+}^{1 - \alpha} \, \bar{S}_{\text{tot}}^{\alpha} \left[ 1 + \frac{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}{2} \text{CV}_{+}^2 \right]\]
For \(\alpha = 0.5\), \(\frac{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}{2} = -\frac{1}{8} = -0.125\), reducing the pooling bias by more than an order of magnitude when \(p_+\) (fraction of non-empty stomachs) is recorded.

section: 5.4 Prey Condition, Differential Digestion, and Dietary Metrics (Hyslop 1980; Buckland et al. 2017)
text:
5.4 Prey Condition, Differential Digestion, and Dietary Metrics (Hyslop 1980; Buckland et al. 2017)
In empirical stomach content analysis, prey are quantified using one or more of four standard metrics (Hyslop 1980; Buckland et al. 2017, Table 1):

Gravimetric (\(\%W\)): Wet or dry mass of prey category \(i\) as a percentage of total stomach content mass.
Volumetric (\(\%V\)): Displaced volume, grid area, or visual points of prey \(i\) as a percentage of total volume.
Numerical (\(\%N\)): Count of prey individuals of category \(i\) as a percentage of total counted prey items.
Frequency of Occurrence (\(\%F_i\)): Percentage of sampled non-empty stomachs in which prey category \(i\) is present (binary presence/absence per stomach).


5.4.1 Biases Revealed by Prey Condition Grading (Buckland et al. 2017)
By grading stomach contents across 7 digestion states (from State 1 = intact freshly ingested prey to State 6 = isolated hard parts/otoliths/chaetae and State 7 = unidentifiable organic mush and mucus; Buckland et al. (2017, Table A1)), Buckland et al. demonstrated that:

Unidentifiable Matter & Mucus Adhesion: Unidentifiable organic tissue and stomach mucus were present in \(33\text{--}77\%\) of stomachs and physically adhered to small prey in \(>61\%\) of stomachs, making direct separation for \(\%W\) and \(\%V\) imprecise.
Differential Retention of Hard Parts: Soft-bodied prey (polychaetes, small teleost larvae, nematodes) digest rapidly into unidentifiable mush, whereas crustacean carapaces, bivalve shells, and large teleost otoliths persist in stomachs for days. Raw \(\%W\) of partially digested remains can either severely underestimate teleost importance (if only a tiny otolith remains) or overestimate shelled prey (if indigestible shells are weighed).
Prey Weight Reconstruction vs. Digested Stomach Weight:

For size-preference estimation (e.g., fitting the mizer or SMS predation kernel \(\phi(w_{\text{pred}} / w_{\text{prey}})\)), one requires the fresh ingested body weight \(w_{\text{prey}}\) of the prey at the moment of capture, which must be reconstructed from intact prey lengths or otolith/carapace allometric regressions (\(w_{\text{prey}} = a L_{\text{otolith}}^b\)).
Conversely, for evacuation-rate calculation (SMS / FishStomachs), one requires the actual digested wet mass \(S_i\) currently in the stomach to plug into \(\rho_i S_i S_{\text{tot}}^{\alpha - 1}\)! Recording both digested mass \(S_i\) and reconstructed ingested size/mass \(w_{\text{prey}}\) (as in the ICES and DAPSTOM databases) is therefore essential.

Robustness of Hierarchical \(\%F\): When comparing across studies with variable digestion states, %F (reported in a nested taxonomic hierarchy from Class \(\to\) Order \(\to\) Family \(\to\) Genus \(\to\) Species; Buckland et al. (2017, Table B1)) is invariant to mucus/evaporation weight distortion and partial fragmentation.

section: 5.5 Stomach Content Databases and Spatiotemporal Raising Pipelines (Jacobsen et al. 2023)
text:
5.5 Stomach Content Databases and Spatiotemporal Raising Pipelines (Jacobsen et al. 2023)

5.5.1 Major Open-Access Stomach Content Databases
Two primary databases underpin North Atlantic and European multispecies stock assessments (ICES 2010; Jacobsen et al. 2023), complemented by global predator–prey body-size compilations (Barnes et al. 2008, 2010):

ICES Stomach Content Database (stomachdata.ices.dk; ICES (2010)): Contains \(>800,000\) prey records from the North Sea (1981 & 1991 “Years of the Stomach” plus IBTS collections), Baltic Sea (cod and flounder stomachs 1963–2021+), and Barents/Celtic Seas. Organized into four normalized relational tables linked by tblUploadID / tblHaulID / tblPredatorID (Jacobsen et al. 2023, 13–17):

File_Information (FI): Upload metadata, country, institute, evacuation parameters.
Haul_Information (HH): ICES survey, gear, ship, haul duration, latitude/longitude, ICES statistical rectangle, bottom depth, bottom temperature \(T\), year, month, time of day.
Predator_Information (PI): Predator species (AphiaID), predator length class \(L\), individual or pooled sample flag, number of feeding stomachs \(n_+\), number of regurgitated stomachs \(n_{\text{reg}}\), number of empty stomachs \(n_0\), mean predator weight.
Prey_Information (PP): Prey species (AphiaID), digestion stage, prey length class \(l\), prey count \(N_{\text{prey}}\), total observed wet weight \(S_i\) in stomach, and gravimetric method.

CEFAS DAPSTOM Database (Pinnegar 2015; Jacobsen et al. 2023, 10–12; Morgan 2022): Contains \(>225,000\) stomach records from 1836 to 2016 across Northwest European shelf seas, providing individual predator-prey length and mass ratios (PPMR) across a 180-year historical baseline.




5.5.2 Design-Based Stratified Raising (FishStomachs R Package)
Because research vessels sample a fixed number of stomachs per length class per haul (e.g., at most 5 cod per 5-cm length bin per haul) rather than sampling proportionally to true predator density in the sea, simple arithmetic averages across all sampled stomachs are spatially biased toward areas with low predator density.
The ICES standard raising pipeline—implemented in Morten Vinther’s FishStomachs R package (Jacobsen et al. 2023, 34–38)—raises individual/haul stomach observations to the population level in three hierarchical steps:

Step 1 (Regurgitation Correction & Evacuation Conversion at Haul Level \(h\)): Within each haul \(h\) and predator length class \(L\), regurgitated stomachs (\(n_{\text{reg}, h, L}\)) are assumed to have had the same mean diet as feeding stomachs (\(n_{+, h, L}\)), so observed weights are scaled by \(\frac{n_{+,h,L} + n_{\text{reg},h,L}}{n_{+,h,L} \left(n_{+,h,L} + n_{\text{reg},h,L} + n_{0,h,L}\right)}\) and converted from stomach mass \(S_{i,h,L}\) to evacuated ration rate \(R_{i,h,L}\) using the Andersen and Beyer (2005) cylinder equation and Rindorf and Lewy (2004) pooling bias correction.
Step 2 (Haul-to-Rectangle Raising via √Stomachs or CPUE): Within each ICES statistical rectangle \(r\), haul rations \(R_{i,h,L}\) are weighted by \(\sqrt{n_{\text{stom}, h, L}}\) (or haul predator CPUE) to obtain the rectangle mean ration \(R_{i,r,L} = \frac{\sum_{h \in r} w_{h,L} R_{i,h,L}}{\sum_{h \in r} w_{h,L}}\).
Step 3 (Rectangle-to-Stock Raising via Predator Survey Abundance \(I_{r,L}\)): Across all rectangles \(r \in \mathcal{R}\) in the stock assessment area, rectangle rations are weighted by the survey abundance index \(I_{r,L}\) of predators of length \(L\) in rectangle \(r\): \[\bar{R}_{\text{pop}, i, L} = \frac{\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} I_{r, L} \, R_{i, r, L}}{\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} I_{r, L}}, \qquad \hat{W}_{\text{pop}, i, L} = \frac{\bar{R}_{\text{pop}, i, L}}{\sum_{k} \bar{R}_{\text{pop}, k, L}}\]




5.5.3 Model-Based Spatiotemporal Standardization (sdmTMB)
When stomach sampling is patchy in space and time (missing ICES rectangles in certain quarters/years), design-based raising suffers from missing-stratum bias. Jacobsen et al. (2023, 26–33) developed a model-based spatiotemporal standardization workflow using sdmTMB (Anderson et al. 2022):

Define the Feeding Ratio (FR) of prey \(i\) in individual predator \(k\) of length \(L_k\) at spatial coordinates \(\mathbf{s}_k\) and year-quarter \(t\) as: \[\text{FR}_{i,k} = \frac{S_{i,k}}{W_{\text{pred}, k}}\]
Fit a spatial/spatiotemporal Generalized Linear Mixed Model (GLMM) with a Tweedie distribution (power variance \(V(\mu) = \phi \mu^p\) with \(1 < p < 2\), which naturally models continuous positive ratios with a point mass at exact zero \(\text{FR}_{i,k} = 0\)!) and log link: \[\mathbb{E}[\text{FR}_{i,k}] = \mu_{i,k}, \qquad \ln \mu_{i,k} = \mathbf{X}_k \boldsymbol{\beta} + s(L_k) + \omega_i(\mathbf{s}_k) + \epsilon_i(\mathbf{s}_k, t)\] where \(s(L_k)\) is a smooth spline of predator length, \(\omega_i(\mathbf{s}) \sim \text{MVN}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\omega)\) is a time-invariant spatial Gaussian Markov Random Field (GMRF) approximated via SPDE on a finite-element mesh, and \(\epsilon_i(\mathbf{s}, t)\) is a spatiotemporal random field.
Predict \(\hat{\mu}_{i}(\mathbf{s}_g, L, t)\) across a fine spatial prediction grid \(g \in \mathcal{G}\), weight by spatially predicted predator density \(\hat{D}_{\text{pred}}(\mathbf{s}_g, L, t)\) (also estimated via sdmTMB on trawl survey catches), and normalize across prey types \(i\) to obtain spatially unbiased population diet proportions and their standard errors!

title: 5  Stomach Content Data, Gastric Evacuation Physics, and Diet Likelihood Formulations
section: 5.6 Statistical Observation Models and Likelihoods for Stomach Content Data
text:
5.6 Statistical Observation Models and Likelihoods for Stomach Content Data
Once population-level diet proportions \(\mathbf{W}_{U} = (W_{1,U}, \dots, W_{K,U})^\top\) (satisfying \(\sum_{k=1}^K W_{k,U} = 1\)) or individual predator-prey mass ratios (PPMR) are prepared for predator stratum \(U = (A, L, y, q)\), how should they enter the stock assessment objective function?

5.6.1 Summary Comparison of Compositional Diet Likelihoods











Likelihood Distribution
Data Support
Log-Likelihood \(\ln L(\mathbf{W}_U \mid \hat{\mathbf{p}}_U, \theta)\)
Variance Structure \(\text{Var}(W_k)\)
Handling of Zeros (\(W_k = 0\))
Used In




1. Multinomial
Proportions \(\mathbf{W}_U \in [0,1]^K\) scaled by sample size \(N_U\)
\(N_U \sum_{k=1}^K W_{k,U} \ln \hat{p}_{k,U} + \text{const}\)
\(\frac{\hat{p}_k(1-\hat{p}_k)}{N_U}\) (Fixed by \(N_U\); no free dispersion parameter)
Natural: \(W_{k,U} = 0\) simply contributes \(0 \cdot \ln \hat{p}_{k,U} = 0\)!
MSCAA, CEATTLE, Gadget, SMS (Option A)


2. Dirichlet
Strictly positive simplex \(W_{k,U} \in (0, 1)\), \(\sum_k W_{k,U} = 1\)
\(\ln\Gamma(v_U) - \sum_{k=1}^K \ln\Gamma(v_U \hat{p}_{k,U}) + \sum_{k=1}^K (v_U \hat{p}_{k,U} - 1)\ln W_{k,U}\)
\(\frac{\hat{p}_k(1-\hat{p}_k)}{v_U + 1}\) (Estimable precision \(v_U = N_U/\theta - 1\))
Undefined at \(W_k = 0\) (\(\ln 0 = -\infty\)); requires pooling zero bins or tail compression
SMS (Default), EcoState, MSCAA


3. Dirichlet-Multinomial (DM)
Count vector \(N_U \mathbf{W}_U\) with overdispersion \(\beta = \theta N_U\)
\(\ln\Gamma(N_U+1) + \ln\Gamma(\beta) - \ln\Gamma(N_U+\beta) + \sum_{k=1}^K \left[\ln\frac{\Gamma(N_U W_k + \beta \hat{p}_k)}{\Gamma(N_U W_k + 1)\Gamma(\beta \hat{p}_k)}\right]\)
\(\frac{\hat{p}_k(1-\hat{p}_k)}{N_U} \left(\frac{N_U + \beta}{1 + \beta}\right)\) (Linear or saturating parameterization; Thorson et al. (2017))
Natural: Exact handling of \(W_{k,U} = 0\) AND estimable overdispersion \(\theta\)!
SS3, LIME, WHAM, modern Rceattle


4. Additive Logistic-Normal (Aitchison)
Log-ratios \(y_k = \ln(W_k / W_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}\)
\(-\frac{1}{2}\ln|2\pi\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_U| - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{y}_U - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_U)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_U^{-1} (\mathbf{y}_U - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_U) - \sum_{k=1}^K \ln W_{k,U}\)
Arbitrary \((K-1)\times(K-1)\) covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_U\) (allows positive/negative correlations!)
Requires zero replacement or censored Tobit normal integration
SAM (compositions), gadget3 (mvlogistic)





5.6.2 Mathematical Derivation of the Compound Dirichlet-Multinomial Likelihood (Thorson et al. 2017)
Because compositional observations in both age/length sampling and stomach content analysis exhibit strong overdispersion relative to a pure multinomial draw of nominal sample size \(n\), Thorson et al. (2017) derived a model-based compound Dirichlet-Multinomial (DM) likelihood that estimates effective sample size \(n_{\text{eff}}\) simultaneously with all stock assessment parameters.

Hierarchical Compound Integral Formulation: Let \(\mathbf{p} = (p_1, \dots, p_A)\) denote the assessment model’s expected proportion vector across \(A\) categories (\(\sum_{a=1}^A p_a = 1\)), and suppose that due to process error (unmodeled spatial/temporal variation in cohort availability or predator foraging) or clustered sampling (schooling of fish within trawl hauls), the true local proportion vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_A)\) encountered during sampling is drawn from a Dirichlet distribution with expectation \(\mathbf{p}\) and concentration sum \(\beta = \sum_{a=1}^A \beta p_a > 0\), followed by a multinomial sample of size \(n\) yielding observed proportions \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}} = (\tilde{\pi}_1, \dots, \tilde{\pi}_A)\) (Thorson et al. 2017, Eqs. 2–5, p. 86):
\[\Pr(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}} \mid \mathbf{p}, n, \beta) = \int \text{Multinomial}(n\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}, n) \, \text{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol{\mu} \mid \beta \mathbf{p}) \, d\boldsymbol{\mu}\]
Evaluating this Dirichlet integral analytically yields the closed-form Dirichlet-Multinomial log-likelihood:
\[\ln f_{\text{DM}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}} \mid \mathbf{p}, n, \beta) = \ln\Gamma(n + 1) - \sum_{a=1}^{A} \ln\Gamma(n\tilde{\pi}_a + 1) + \ln\Gamma(\beta) - \ln\Gamma(n + \beta) + \sum_{a=1}^{A} \Big[\ln\Gamma(n\tilde{\pi}_a + \beta p_a) - \ln\Gamma(\beta p_a)\Big]\]
Notice that when \(\tilde{\pi}_a = 0\), the term inside the final sum is \(\ln\Gamma(\beta p_a) - \ln\Gamma(\beta p_a) = 0\), so exact observed zeros require no ad hoc constant addition or bin pooling!
Two Parameterizations of Effective Sample Size (\(n_{\text{eff}}\)): The marginal variance of an observed proportion \(\tilde{\pi}_a\) under the DM distribution is \(\text{Var}(\tilde{\pi}_a) = \frac{p_a(1 - p_a)}{n}\left(\frac{n + \beta}{1 + \beta}\right)\). Equating this to the equivalent multinomial variance \(\frac{p_a(1 - p_a)}{n_{\text{eff}}}\) yields \(n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{n + n\beta}{n + \beta}\). Thorson et al. (2017, Eqs. 9–12, p. 86) introduced two distinct parameterizations of how \(n_{\text{eff}}\) scales with input sample size \(n_y\) across years:

Parameterization #1 (Linear Scaling, \(\beta_y = \theta n_y\), Default): \[n_{\text{eff}, y} = \frac{1 + \theta n_y}{1 + \theta} = \frac{1}{1 + \theta} + n_y \left(\frac{\theta}{1 + \theta}\right)\] As \(\theta \to \infty\), \(n_{\text{eff}, y} \to n_y\) (recovering the unweighted multinomial); for small \(\theta\) and large \(n_y\), \(\frac{\theta}{1 + \theta} \in (0, 1)\) acts directly as a multiplicative data-weighting factor \(\lambda\) (analogous to McAllister–Ianelli or Francis TA1.8 reweighting), suitable when overdispersion arises from clustered/schooling sampling.
Parameterization #2 (Saturating Scaling, \(\beta_y = \beta\) constant): \[n_{\text{eff}, y} = \frac{n_y + n_y \beta}{n_y + \beta} \xrightarrow{n_y \gg \beta} 1 + \beta\] Here \(n_{\text{eff}, y}\) increases linearly with \(n_y\) at small sample sizes (\(n_y \ll \beta\)) but asymptotes at an upper ceiling \(1 + \beta\) as \(n_y \to \infty\), which is theoretically exact when overdispersion arises from process error / model misspecification in selectivity or availability (because measuring infinitely many fish in year \(y\) cannot reduce year-specific process error \(\text{Var}(\mu_a) = \frac{p_a(1-p_a)}{1+\beta}\)!).



[!TIP] Choosing Between Dirichlet, Dirichlet-Multinomial, and Logistic-Normal for Multispecies Assessments: While the Dirichlet distribution (used in SMS and EcoState) works well for aggregated species-level diet shares where all modeled prey are present (\(W_{k,U} > 0\)), when diet data are disaggregated simultaneously by prey species AND prey size bins (as required for Gadget or dynamic mizer), many \((i, l)\) prey bins have observed \(W_{k,U} = 0\). In that regime, the Dirichlet-Multinomial (Thorson et al. 2017) is strictly superior to the plain Dirichlet because \(W_{k,U} = 0\) is in the natural support of the distribution while still estimating \(\theta_{\text{stom}}\) via maximum likelihood. Note, however, that both Dirichlet and DM imply strictly negative correlations \(\text{Corr}(\tilde{\pi}_a, \tilde{\pi}_{a'}) < 0\) between bins; if positive correlations between adjacent length bins are strong, the Logistic-Normal or Tweedie spatial GLMM (sdmTMB) should be used.

section: 5.7 Fitting Exponential Family & Gamma Distributions to Predator–Prey Mass Ratios (Morgan 2022)
text:
5.7 Fitting Exponential Family & Gamma Distributions to Predator–Prey Mass Ratios (Morgan 2022)
For continuous size-spectrum models like mizer, stomach content data provide a second, uniquely powerful source of information beyond species diet shares: the empirical distribution of individual Predator–Prey Mass Ratios (PPMR), \(\text{PPMR} = w_{\text{pred}} / w_{\text{prey}}\).
In his University of York dissertation analyzing \(>300,000\) stomach records from the combined CEFAS DAPSTOM and ICES databases, Owain Morgan (Morgan 2022) derived an elegant analytical link between realized stomach log-PPMR distributions and the intrinsic mizer feeding kernel \(\varphi_{w'}(w)\) using the multiplicative closure properties of the exponential family.

5.7.1 Linking Realized Diet Size Distribution to the Feeding Kernel via the Sheldon Spectrum
Let \(w'\) denote the body mass of the predator and \(w\) denote the body mass of an individual prey item in its stomach, so the logarithmic predator-prey mass ratio is: \[x = \ln\!\left(\frac{w'}{w}\right) \iff w = w' e^{-x}\]
In mizer, the realized number density \(I_{w'}(w)\) of prey of weight \(w\) consumed by a predator of weight \(w'\) is proportional to the product of the predator’s intrinsic feeding preference kernel \(\varphi_{w'}(w) = \phi(w'/w) = \phi(e^x)\) and the ambient prey abundance spectrum \(N(w)\) in the sea (Morgan 2022, Eq. 1):
\[I_{w'}(w) \propto \varphi_{w'}(w) \, N(w)\]
By the Sheldon spectrum power law (Morgan 2022, Eq. 2), background marine abundance density scales as \(N(w) = n_0 w^{-\lambda}\) (with \(\lambda \approx 2\) for number density per unit weight, or \(w N(w) \propto w^{1-\lambda} = w^{-1}\) per logarithmic weight bin \(dx = -dw/w\)). Substituting \(w = w' e^{-x}\) into \(N(w)\) gives:
\[N(w' e^{-x}) = n_0 (w')^{-\lambda} \exp(\lambda x)\]
Therefore, in terms of the log-PPMR variable \(x = \ln(w'/w)\), the realized stomach log-PPMR probability density \(f_{\text{real}}(x)\) and the intrinsic feeding preference kernel \(\phi(x)\) are related by an exponential tilt factor \(e^{\tilde{\lambda} x}\) (where \(\tilde{\lambda} = \lambda - 1 \approx 1\) for number counts in log-bins, or \(\tilde{\lambda} = \lambda - 2 \approx 0\) for biomass shares in log-bins):
\[f_{\text{real}}(x) \propto \phi(x) \, \exp(\tilde{\lambda} x) \iff \phi(x) \propto f_{\text{real}}(x) \, \exp(-\tilde{\lambda} x)\]


5.7.2 Exact Multiplicative Closure of Exponential Family & Gamma Distributions (Morgan 2022, Section 4.6)
Morgan (2022, 7–9) showed that if the realized log-PPMR \(X = \ln(w'/w) > 0\) follows any distribution in the natural Exponential Family with sufficient statistic vector \(T(x)\) containing \(x\): \[f_{\text{real}}(x \mid \boldsymbol{\eta}) = h(x) \exp\!\left(\boldsymbol{\eta}^\top T(x) - A(\boldsymbol{\eta})\right)\] then multiplying by the Sheldon abundance correction \(\exp(-\tilde{\lambda} x)\) simply shifts the canonical parameter corresponding to \(x\) by \(-\tilde{\lambda}\), keeping the intrinsic feeding kernel \(\phi(x)\) within the exact same parametric distribution family!
Specifically:

Normal Distribution on \(x = \ln(w'/w)\) (Lognormal on \(w'/w\), as in standard mizer): If \(f_{\text{real}}(x) = \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_{\text{real}}, \sigma^2)\), then multiplying by \(e^{-\tilde{\lambda} x}\) yields another Normal distribution with the same variance \(\sigma^2\) and a shifted mean: \[\phi(x) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(x \;\middle|\; \mu_{\text{pref}} = \mu_{\text{real}} - \tilde{\lambda} \sigma^2,\; \sigma^2\right)\]
Gamma Distribution on \(x = \ln(w'/w)\) (Morgan 2022, Eqs. 19–24): Because empirical log-PPMR distributions in DAPSTOM and ICES stomachs are positively supported (\(x = \ln(w'/w) > 0\), since predators rarely eat prey heavier than themselves) and right-skewed (sharp gape-limitation cutoff at small \(x \approx 2\text{--}3\), long tail toward small benthic/planktonic prey at large \(x \approx 10\text{--}15\)), Morgan (2022) fitted a Gamma distribution to \(x = \ln(w'/w)\): \[f^{\Gamma}_{\alpha, \beta}(x) = \frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\beta x}, \qquad x > 0\] When multiplied by \(e^{-\tilde{\lambda} x}\), the Gamma density satisfies the exact algebraic identity (Morgan 2022, Eq. 24): \[e^{-\tilde{\lambda} x} f^{\Gamma}_{\alpha, \beta}(x) = \left(\frac{\beta}{\beta + \tilde{\lambda}}\right)^\alpha f^{\Gamma}_{\alpha,\; \beta + \tilde{\lambda}}(x)\] Thus, if the observed log-PPMR in stomachs is \(\text{Gamma}(\hat{\alpha}, \hat{\beta})\) (with empirical estimates across North Sea cod, haddock, whiting, plaice, and sole clustering around \(\hat{\alpha} \approx 6.8\text{--}12.3\), \(\hat{\beta} \approx 1.15\text{--}1.85\); Morgan (2022, Table 1)), the underlying mizer feeding kernel is analytically a \(\text{Gamma}(\hat{\alpha},\; \hat{\beta} + \tilde{\lambda})\) distribution on \(\ln(w'/w)\)!

section: 6.2 Data Weighting and Likelihood Conflict in Integrated & Multispecies Assessments (Francis 2011; Maunder & Punt 2013; Thorson et al. 2017)
text:
6.2 Data Weighting and Likelihood Conflict in Integrated & Multispecies Assessments (Francis 2011; Maunder & Punt 2013; Thorson et al. 2017)
When fitting an integrated single-species or multispecies model simultaneously to abundance indices (\(I_{f,y}\)), catch biomass (\(Y_{f,y}\)), length/age compositions (\(\mathbf{P}_{f,y}\)), and stomach content compositions (\(\mathbf{W}_{A,L,y,q}\)), the most critical statistical hazard is likelihood conflict and compositional domination (Francis 2011; Maunder and Punt 2013; Thorson et al. 2017).

6.2.1 Why Unadjusted Composition Likelihoods Destroy Abundance Fits (“Francis Principle 1”)
Suppose a survey measures \(10,000\) fish lengths across \(50\) length bins each year, while also providing \(1\) annual biomass index point \(I_y\) per year. If the nominal number of fish measured (\(N_y = 10,000\)) is plugged into a Multinomial likelihood \(\sum_y N_y \sum_l P_{l,y} \ln \hat{P}_{l,y}\), the composition likelihood will have \(1000\times\) larger gradient and curvature than the lognormal survey index likelihood \(\frac{1}{2\sigma_I^2}(\ln I_y - \ln \hat{I}_y)^2\). Because fish school by size and because any process model has slight misspecifications in selectivity or growth, positive correlations among bins within a year mean the true effective sample size \(N_{\text{eff}, y}\) is typically \(20\text{--}200\) (closer to the number of trawl hauls, not the number of individual fish!). If \(N_y\) is not downweighted, the optimizer will distort recruitment \(R_y\), fishing mortality \(F_y\), and biomass trends \(\hat{B}_y\) just to chase noise in the length compositions, violating Francis’s First Principle (Francis 2011, 1125): > “Do not let other data stop the model from fitting abundance data well.”


6.2.2 Three Standard Data-Weighting Algorithms for Compositional Data
Let \(O_{l,y}\) and \(E_{l,y}\) denote the observed and model-expected proportions in length (or age) bin \(l \in \{1, \dots, n_L\}\) with midpoint \(x_l\) in year \(y \in \{1, \dots, n_Y\}\), with initial nominal sample size \(N_{y}\).

McAllister & Ianelli (1997) Harmonic Mean Weighting: Estimates the effective sample size \(\hat{N}_{y} = \frac{\sum_{l} E_{l,y}(1 - E_{l,y})}{\sum_{l} (O_{l,y} - E_{l,y})^2}\) for each year and sets the dataset multiplier \(w_{\text{MI}}\) using the harmonic mean across years (used in MSCAA (Curti et al. 2013) and Rceattle (Adams et al. 2022); see McAllister and Ianelli (1997)).

Critique (Francis 2011, 1128–31): Assumes residuals across bins \(l\) within the same year \(y\) are uncorrelated. When residuals are positively correlated across adjacent length bins (the norm when growth or selectivity varies), McAllister–Ianelli dramatically overweights the composition data!

Francis (2011) Method TA1.8 (Mean-Length / Mean-Age Residual Variance): Collapses each year’s length composition into its observed mean length \(\bar{O}_y = \sum_l x_l O_{l,y}\) and expected mean length \(\bar{E}_y = \sum_l x_l E_{l,y}\), with multinomial within-year variance \(v_y = \sum_l x_l^2 E_{l,y} - \bar{E}_y^2\). Because collapsing to the annual mean \(\bar{O}_y\) absorbs all within-year inter-bin correlations, the standardized mean-length residuals \(\frac{\bar{O}_y - \bar{E}_y}{\sqrt{v_y / (w N_y)}}\) must have unit variance, yielding the Francis TA1.8 weight multiplier (Francis 2011, Appendix A, Table A1):
\[w_{\text{Francis}} = \left[ \text{Var}_{y}\!\left( \frac{\bar{O}_y - \bar{E}_y}{\sqrt{v_y / N_y}} \right) \right]^{-1}\]
Self-Weighting Likelihoods (Dirichlet-Multinomial / Logistic-Normal / SMS Dirichlet): Rather than outer fixed-point reweighting loops (Francis TA1.8 or Gadget two-stage reweighting), modern TMB and SS3 models (SMS, EcoState, LIME (Rudd and Thorson 2018), SS3 (Thorson et al. 2017)) use a Dirichlet or Dirichlet-Multinomial likelihood with an estimable dispersion parameter \(\theta\), where effective sample size is either linear in \(N_y\): \[N_{\text{eff}, y} = \frac{1 + \theta N_y}{1 + \theta}\] or saturating at \(1 + \beta\): \[N_{\text{eff}, y} = \frac{N_y + N_y \beta}{N_y + \beta}\] In a 4,500-replicate simulation study and Pacific hake application, Thorson et al. (2017) proved that simultaneous DM estimation eliminates the severe bias of unweighted multinomial likelihoods, matches the accuracy and precision of iterative McAllister–Ianelli tuning for \(M\), \(\ln R_0\), and spawning output, and propagates data-weighting uncertainty directly into the joint Hessian and MCMC posterior!

6.3 Parameter Estimation and Uncertainty Quantification Engines

6.3.1 Frequentist / Empirical Bayes State-Space Estimation in TMB (Kristensen et al. 2016)
Modern statistical stock assessment models (SAM (Nielsen and Berg 2014), smsR, Rceattle, gadget3, EcoState (Thorson et al. 2024)) are built on Template Model Builder (TMB) (Kristensen et al. 2016) or its pure-R interface RTMB.
Let \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^p\) denote the vector of fixed effects (life-history scaling parameters, selectivities, catchabilities, suitability parameters \(\beta_i, \sigma_i\), and variance parameters \(\sigma_{\text{proc}}, \sigma_{\text{obs}}\)) and let \(\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) denote the vector of latent random effects (process errors) (e.g., annual recruitment deviations \(\epsilon_{R,i,y}\), time-varying fishing mortality random walks \(\ln F_{f,y}\), or biomass process errors \(\epsilon_{B,i,y}\)). Given joint negative log-likelihood \(f(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{u}) = -\ln p(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})\), TMB approximates the marginal likelihood \(L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \int \exp(-f(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{u})) \, d\mathbf{u}\) via the Laplace Approximation (Kristensen et al. 2016, Eq. 2):
\[-\ln L^{*}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = f\!\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \hat{\mathbf{u}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right) + \frac{1}{2} \ln \det \mathbf{H}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) - \frac{m}{2} \ln(2\pi)\]
where:

\(\hat{\mathbf{u}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u}} f(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{u})\) is the inner-loop empirical Bayes mode of the random effects, and
\(\mathbf{H}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \left.\frac{\partial^2 f(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{u})}{\partial \mathbf{u} \partial \mathbf{u}^\top}\right|_{\mathbf{u} = \hat{\mathbf{u}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\) is the sparse \(m \times m\) Hessian matrix of the random effects, factored via sparse Cholesky decomposition (CHOLMOD).

Using up to third-order automatic differentiation (CppAD), TMB computes the exact gradient \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} (-\ln L^{*}(\boldsymbol{\theta}))\) of the Laplace-approximated marginal likelihood in \(O(1)\) reverse-mode sweeps, allowing nlminb or optim to estimate hundreds of fixed effects and thousands of random effects in seconds to minutes, followed by joint precision matrix inversion (sdreport) for derived quantities (\(\text{SSB}_{i,y}, M2_{i,a,y}, F_{\text{MSY}, i}\)).



6.3.2 Bayesian, Evolutionary, and Ensemble Approaches (Zhang et al. 2015, 2016; Spence et al. 2016, 2018, 2021)
When models are implemented as black-box simulation packages without automatic differentiation (or when likelihood surfaces are rugged and multimodal), researchers have developed four complementary calibration and uncertainty frameworks for mizer and LeMaRns:

Two-Step Genetic Algorithm + Parallel Tempering MCMC (Zhang et al. 2015, 2016): In calibrating a multispecies mizer model to data-poor and data-rich ecosystems (Zhang et al. 2015, 2016), Zhang et al. found that standard gradient descent or single-chain Metropolis–Hastings gets trapped in local modes where one or more species go extinct during spin-up. They introduced a two-stage global optimizer:

Stage 1: A parallel Real-Coded Genetic Algorithm (GA) searches the high-dimensional parameter space \((\ln R_{\max, i}, \kappa, q_{f,i}, F_i)\) using a survival penalty for extinct species to locate the global basin of attraction.
Stage 2: Parallel Tempering MCMC (running multiple interacting Markov chains at temperatures \(T_1 = 1 < T_2 < \dots < T_M\)) samples the posterior distribution across multimodal ridges.

History Matching + Sequential Monte Carlo (Spence et al. 2016, 2021): To calibrate mizer (Spence et al. 2016) and LeMaRns (Spence, Thorpe, et al. 2021) to North Sea time series while explicitly accounting for structural model discrepancy \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_{\text{disc}}\) (the difference between the true ocean and the best possible parameterization of the model), Spence et al. combined:

History Matching: Defines an implausibility measure \(I_k(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) for summary statistic \(k\): \[I_k(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{\left|y^{\text{obs}}_k - \mathbb{E}[f_k(\boldsymbol{\theta})]\right|}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(y^{\text{obs}}_k) + \text{Var}(f_k(\boldsymbol{\theta})) + \text{Var}(\eta_{\text{disc}, k})}}\] and rules out any parameter vector \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) where \(\max_k I_k(\boldsymbol{\theta}) > 3\) (by Pukelsheim’s \(3\sigma\) rule), rapidly shrinking the feasible space before running full time-series likelihood evaluations.
Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC): Propagates a particle cloud \(\left\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(p)}\right\}_{p=1}^P\) through sequential annealing or time-series filtering steps using Normalizing Flows / Metropolis-Hastings rejuvenation moves.

Bayesian Multi-Model Ensembles (Spence et al. 2018): Instead of selecting a single “winner” model via AIC, Spence et al. (2018) constructed a hierarchical Bayesian ensemble linking five distinct multispecies simulators (EcoPath with Ecosim, LeMans, mizer, SMS, and single-species assessments) as biased noisy realizations around a latent true ecosystem trajectory \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_t\), decomposing structural discrepancy into shared vs. simulator-specific discrepancy processes.

6.4 Architectural Blueprint for Next-Generation Statistical Dynamic Stock Assessment in mizer
In their 10-year review of mizer, Pennino et al. (2025, Section “Challenges and Future Directions”, p. 9) identify the central barrier preventing mizer from being used as a routine tactical stock assessment tool: > “First, there is a lack of a standardized optimization routine for parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification… Second, mizer models are typically calibrated to a time-averaged steady state rather than fitted dynamically to time series of catches, survey indices, and size compositions.”
Drawing together the mathematical lessons from SMS (Chapter 2), Gadget/gadget3, MULTIFAN-CL/SS3, and Punt et al. (2016) (Chapter 3), EcoState (Chapter 4), and stomach content likelihoods (Chapter 5), we can synthesize a concrete, five-pillar architectural roadmap for transforming mizer into a differentiable, state-space statistical multispecies stock assessment model (mizer-TMB / mizer-RTMB).

6.4.1 Pillar 1: Resolving Cohort Dispersion via Jump-Growth Diffusion (Datta, Delius & Law 2010)
When mizer is projected dynamically with interannual recruitment fluctuations \(R_{\text{dd}, i}(t) \exp(\epsilon_{R,i,y})\), a strong year class enters at \(w_0\) and propagates across the weight grid.

Problem: Under the standard first-order upwind scheme, cohort width is governed by numerical grid viscosity \(D_{\text{num}} \approx \frac{1}{2} g_i \Delta w\), which fails to match the true biological variance of size-at-age in survey length-frequency distributions.
Solution: Replace the first-order upwind step with the semi-implicit Crank–Nicolson / Chang–Cooper finite-volume discretization of the Jump-Growth Fokker–Planck PDE (Datta et al. 2010, Eq. 7):
\[\frac{\partial N_i}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (g_i N_i)}{\partial w} - \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^2 \left(\psi_{\text{disp}, i} \, d_i(w,t) \, N_i\right)}{\partial w^2} = -\mu_i(w,t) N_i\]
where \(d_i(w,t)\) is the mechanistic second moment of prey mass intake, optionally scaled by a species-specific dispersion multiplier \(\psi_{\text{disp}, i} \ge 1\) (analogous to Gadget’s Beta-Binomial dispersion parameter \(\beta_s\) in g3a_grow_impl_bbinom; Lentz and Elvarsson (2024)) to account for genetic growth variation and patchy foraging.
Computational Cost: Discretizing the second derivative \(\partial_w^2 (d_i N_i)\) changes the implicit linear system per species per time step from lower-bidiagonal to tridiagonal, which is still solved in exact \(O(n_w)\) operations via the Thomas algorithm (solve_tridiag) and is \(100\%\) differentiable in TMB / RTMB!




6.4.2 Pillar 2: Two-Stage Initialization (Differentiable Steady-State Spin-Up + Dynamic Projection)
In single-species assessments (SS3, SAM), the initial age vector \(N_{i,a,t_0}\) at the start of the historical time series \(t_0\) is initialized at a fished equilibrium \(N_{\text{eq}}(F_{\text{init}, i})\) plus initial deviations. For dynamic mizer:

Differentiable Steady-State Initialization at \(t = t_0\): Given trial parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) and baseline initial fishing effort \(E_{f, t_0}\), compute the steady-state spectra \(N_{i,0}(w)\) via a fixed number (\(k = 15\text{--}25\)) of damped fixed-point iterations of the analytical steady-state envelope \(N_i(w) = N_i(w_0)\frac{g_i(w_0)}{g_i(w)}\exp\!\left(-\int_{w_0}^w \frac{\mu_i(w')}{g_i(w')} dw'\right)\) (with matching resource \(N_{R,0}(w)\)). Because a fixed number of unrolled iterations uses only elementary vector operations, TMB / RTMB differentiates smoothly through the steady-state initialization!
Dynamic Time-Stepping (\(t \in [t_0, T]\)): Step forward in quarterly or monthly increments \(\Delta t\) (e.g., \(\Delta t = 0.1\) or \(0.25\text{ yr}\)) driven by time-varying fishing mortality \(F_{f,i}(w, t)\), temperature anomalies \(T(t)\) (scaling metabolic rates \(k_{s,i}\), intake \(h_i\), and search rates \(\gamma_i\) via Arrhenius activation \(e^{-E_a / k_B T}\)), and state-space recruitment deviations \(\epsilon_{R,i,y}\).




6.4.3 Pillar 3: State-Space Process Random Effects (\(\mathbf{u}\))
Following SAM (Nielsen and Berg 2014) and EcoState (Thorson et al. 2024), introduce three compact sets of latent Gaussian random effects integrated out by TMB’s Laplace approximation:

Annual Recruitment Deviations: \[R_i(t) = R_{\text{dd}, i}(t) \exp\!\left(\epsilon_{R, i, y(t)} - \frac{1}{2}\sigma_{R, i}^2\right), \qquad \epsilon_{R, i, y} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \sigma_{R, i}^2\right)\]
Resource Spectrum Productivity / Carrying Capacity Anomalies (capturing bottom-up climate/plankton regimes): \[\kappa_R(w, t) = \kappa_0 \exp\!\left(\epsilon_{\kappa, y(t)}\right) w^{-\lambda}, \qquad \epsilon_{\kappa, y} \sim \text{AR1}\!\left(\rho_\kappa, \sigma_\kappa^2\right)\]
Random-Walk Fishing Effort / Mortality (when commercial effort is noisy or unrecorded): \[\ln E_{f, y+1} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\ln E_{f, y},\; \sigma_{E, f}^2\right)\]




6.4.4 Pillar 4: Observation Operators and Joint Statistical Likelihood Function
To avoid the parameter confounding identified by Punt et al. (2016), dynamic mizer should be fitted simultaneously to four orthogonal empirical data streams:

Survey Biomass / Abundance Indices (\(I_{f,i,y}\), Lognormal Likelihood): Given survey selectivity \(S^{\text{surv}}_{f,i}(w)\) and catchability \(Q^{\text{surv}}_{f,i}\): \[\hat{I}_{f,i,y} = Q^{\text{surv}}_{f,i} \int_{w_0}^{w_{\max,i}} S^{\text{surv}}_{f,i}(w) \, w \, N_i(w, t_y) \, dw, \qquad \ln I^{\text{obs}}_{f,i,y} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\ln \hat{I}_{f,i,y},\; \sigma^2_{I,f,i,y}\right)\]
Commercial Fishery Yields (\(Y_{f,i,y}\), Lognormal Likelihood): \[\hat{Y}_{f,i,y} = \int_{y}^{y+1} dt \int_{w_0}^{w_{\max,i}} F_{f,i}(w, t) \, w \, N_i(w, t) \, dw, \qquad \ln Y^{\text{obs}}_{f,i,y} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\ln \hat{Y}_{f,i,y},\; \sigma^2_{Y,f,i}\right)\]
Survey & Commercial Length-Frequency Compositions (\(\mathbf{P}^{\text{obs}}_{f,i,y}\), Dirichlet-Multinomial or Fournier Robustified Normal Likelihood): For observed length bin \(l\) with boundaries \([L_l, L_{l+1})\) corresponding to body weights \([w_{i,l}, w_{i,l+1}) = [a_i L_l^{b_i}, a_i L_{l+1}^{b_i})\), the expected catch number in bin \(l\) is: \[\hat{C}_{f,i,l,y} = \int_{w_{i,l}}^{w_{i,l+1}} S_{f,i}(w) \, N_i(w, t_y) \, dw, \qquad \hat{p}_{f,i,l,y} = \frac{\hat{C}_{f,i,l,y}}{\sum_{m} \hat{C}_{f,i,m,y}}\] Evaluated via the self-weighting Dirichlet-Multinomial likelihood (Thorson et al. 2017) with haul sample size \(N_{\text{haul}, f, y}\) and estimated overdispersion \(\theta_{\text{comp}, f, i}\) (or Fournier’s robustified normal likelihood from MULTIFAN-CL (Fournier et al. 1998) to prevent tail outliers from distorting growth parameters).
Stomach Content Diet Shares & Log-PPMR Distributions (Dirichlet-Multinomial + Gamma Likelihood): For predator \((i, w')\) in year-quarter \(t\), the model-predicted mass share of prey species \(j\) in prey weight bin \([w_{p,m}, w_{p,m+1})\) in the diet is: \[\hat{W}_{i,w', j, m, t} = \frac{\gamma_i(w') \, \theta_{ij} \int_{w_{p,m}}^{w_{p,m+1}} \phi_i(w' / w_p) \, N_j(w_p, t) \, w_p \, dw_p}{E_i(w', t)}\]

Taxonomic Diet Shares: Fit evacuated, CPUE-weighted (or sdmTMB-standardized; Jacobsen et al. (2023)) stomach weight proportions against \(\hat{W}_{i,w',j,m,t}\) using the SMS Dirichlet (Lewy and Vinther 2004) or Dirichlet-Multinomial (Thorson et al. 2017) likelihood, which directly identifies the interaction matrix \(\theta_{ij}\)!
Predator–Prey Size Kernel Parameters (\(\beta_i, \sigma_i\) or Gamma \(\alpha_i, \beta_i\)): Fit the observed log-PPMR distribution \(x = \ln(w'/w_p)\) using the Exponential Family / Gamma likelihood of Morgan (2022).





6.4.5 Pillar 5: Stabilizing Dynamic Multi-Decadal Fits via Prey Refuges & Overconsumption Caps
A major lesson from Gadget (Lentz and Elvarsson 2024), MSCAA (Curti et al. 2013), and Ecosim/EcoState (Walters et al. 1997; Thorson et al. 2024) is that during gradient optimization over a 40-year time series, trial parameter values can easily trigger runaway trophic cascades unless two stabilizing mechanisms are included:

Holling Type III Exponent or Foraging Arena Vulnerability: Replacing linear encounter \(\theta_{ij} N_j(w_p)\) with a weakly sigmoid Type III encounter \(\theta_{ij} N_j(w_p)^{1 + \zeta}\) (\(\zeta \approx 0.1\text{--}0.3\)) or a Foraging Arena predator-interference denominator \(\frac{\theta_{ij} v_{ij}}{2 v_{ij} + \gamma_i N_i}\) provides a low-density prey refuge and prevents unrealistic species extinctions during parameter search.
Smooth Differentiable Overconsumption Cap (dif_pmin): Borrowing gadget3’s smooth logistic minimum cap on total mortality per time step ensures that \(N_i(w, t)\) remains strictly positive and gradients \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}\) remain finite across the entire parameter space.
